lessons.g: You can write a line of Python that puts text on the console.
lessons.s: A Python program is a list of instructions. The machine reads them and does them. Nothing more mystical than that. The instruction that makes a program say something is `print`. You write the word, then parentheses, and inside the parentheses you put what you want sent out: The quotes matter.

lessons.t: The console reads top to bottom
lessons.g: You can predict the order in which a program prints, and use that order to see how far it got.
lessons.s: Instructions run in the order you wrote them: first line, then the next, then the next. There is no cleverness hiding in there. Each `print` ends its own line, so three prints give you three lines in the console, in the same order as the code. That makes the console a **transcript**, not a screen.

lessons.g: You can print text and a number side by side without stitching them together by hand.
lessons.s: `print` accepts more than one value. Separate them with commas and they all go out on the same line: Python puts **one space between each value** and one line break at the end. You do not add those yourself, and if you do you get two spaces.

lessons.g: You can leave a note in the code and switch a line off without deleting it.
lessons.s: A `#` tells Python to ignore the rest of that line. The line still sits in the file, it just never runs. That is a **comment**. It has two uses, and they are different jobs. The first is a note for whoever reads the code next, which is usually you in three months.

lessons.g: You can read a Python error, find the line it points at, and fix it.
lessons.s: When Python cannot do what a line says, it stops and prints a **traceback**. It looks alarming and it is not. It is the machine telling you where it got stuck and why: Read it from the **bottom up**. The last line is the one that matters: an error type, then a detail.

lessons.g: Store a value under a name and read it back later.
lessons.s: A **variable** is a name attached to a value. You write the name, then `=`, then the value: `channel = "Cobly"`. From that line on, wherever you write `channel`, Python hands you the value back. The `=` is not the equals of mathematics. It does not claim that two things are the same.

lessons.g: Build one piece of text out of several.
lessons.s: A **string** is text. You mark it with quotes, single or double, and you close it with the same one you opened: `"Pluma"` and `'Pluma'` are the same value. The quotes are not part of the value. They are how you tell Python where the text starts and ends.

lessons.g: Do arithmetic with variables and know which type comes out.
lessons.s: Numbers are written without quotes. `12` is an **int**, a whole number. `7.5` is a **float**, a number with a decimal point. `"12"` is neither, it is a string that happens to look like a number. The usual operators work between numbers: `+`, `-`, `*` for multiplication and `/` for division.

lessons.g: Write one sentence that carries the contents of several variables.
lessons.s: An **f-string** is a string with an `f` in front of the opening quote. Inside it, anything you put between `{` and `}` is not text: Python evaluates it and drops the result in. That prints `scanning Cobly`. Without the `f`, the braces stay as braces and you get `scanning {channel}` printed literally.

lessons.g: Change what a name points at, and know what happened to the old value.
lessons.s: A name holds one value at a time. Assigning to a name that already exists does not create a second one, it repoints the same name and the previous value is gone. After those two lines there is one name and one value. Nothing remembers the `4`.

lessons.t: Asking Python what a value is
lessons.g: Find out the type of any value instead of guessing it.
lessons.s: Every value has a type, and the type decides what the value can do. `+` between two ints adds them. `+` between two strings glues them. Same operator, different behaviour, chosen entirely by the types involved. `type(x)` answers the question.

lessons.g: Convert a string into a number so you can do arithmetic with it.
lessons.s: `int("142")` gives the number `142`. `str(142)` gives the text `"142"`. `float("7.5")` gives the decimal `7.5`. Each one **returns a new value** and leaves the original untouched, so the result is worth nothing unless you assign it to a name or use it immediately.

lessons.g: Take a value from outside the program while it is running.
lessons.s: `input()` stops the program, waits until a line is typed and Enter is pressed, and returns that line. It is the first thing you have written whose result is not decided by your own code. What comes back is **always a string**. If the person types `8`, you get `"8"`, not `8`.

lessons.g: Choose names that make the next reader understand the code without running it.
lessons.s: `x = 8` is legal and tells you nothing. Six weeks later you will not know whether 8 is videos, minutes, retries or a day of the month, and you will have to reconstruct it from the lines around it. A good name says what the value **is**, and its unit when it has one. `videos_per_day` beats `videos` beats `v`.

lessons.g: You can store a yes/no fact in a variable and check that its type is bool.
lessons.s: `True` and `False` are values, exactly like `7` or `"draft"`. You can put them in a variable, print them and pass them around. The capital letter is not optional: `true` is not a Python value, and writing it gets you `NameError: name 'true' is not defined`. They have a type of their own.

lessons.g: You can turn two numbers into a True or False answer with a comparison operator.
lessons.s: You rarely type `True` by hand. You produce it by comparing two things. Python has six comparison operators and every one of them hands back a bool: - `==` equal to - `!=` not equal to - `<` less than - `>` greater than - `<=` less than or equal - `>=` greater than or equal The one that bites everybody is `==`.

lessons.t: Running code only when it matters
lessons.g: You can make a block of code run only when a condition is True.
lessons.s: `if` takes a condition and a block. If the condition is `True`, the block runs. If it is `False`, the block is skipped entirely, and the program carries on with the next line at the outer level. The shape is fixed: Two details are not decoration. The **colon** ends the condition line.

lessons.g: You can give an if a second block that runs when the condition is False.
lessons.s: `else` attaches to an `if` and holds the code for the other case. Exactly one of the two blocks runs, never both, never neither. There is no condition after `else`, only a colon, because its condition is already decided: whatever the `if` was not.

lessons.g: You can chain several conditions so the first true one wins.
lessons.s: `elif` is short for *else if*. It goes between the `if` and the `else`, and you can have as many as you need. Python checks the conditions from top to bottom, runs the block of the **first** one that is `True`, and then jumps past the whole chain without looking at the rest.

lessons.g: You can join two conditions with and or or, and flip one with not.
lessons.s: Three words build every compound condition you will ever write. - `a and b` is `True` only when **both** are true. - `a or b` is `True` when **at least one** is true. It is not the exclusive or of everyday speech: if both are true, the answer is still `True`. - `not a` flips the value. `not True` is `False`.

lessons.g: You can put an if inside another if, and you know why you should not go deep.
lessons.s: A block can contain anything, including another `if`. Each level indents four more spaces, and the inner condition is only ever asked when the outer one was true. That is legal and sometimes right. What is not right is a pyramid.

lessons.g: You can test a value directly, knowing which values Python already treats as false.
lessons.s: `if` does not require a bool. It accepts any value and decides whether that value is **truthy** or **falsy**. The falsy ones are few and worth memorising: `False`, `0`, `0.0`, the empty string `""`, and `None`. Everything else is truthy, including the string `"0"`, which is one character long and therefore not empty.

lessons.g: You can rewrite a nested pile of checks as a flat chain that rejects the bad cases first.
lessons.s: A **guard clause** is a check that handles the bad case immediately and gets it out of the way, so the code below it can assume that case is gone. Instead of wrapping the good path in condition after condition, you list the reasons to stop, one per branch, and leave the good path alone at the bottom.

lessons.t: The loop that runs while something is true
lessons.g: Repeat a block of code as long as a condition holds, and move the value that ends it.
lessons.s: Everything you have written so far runs once, top to bottom. Real work is not like that: a render is checked again and again until it is done, an upload is retried until it goes through. That is a **loop**. `while` is the plainest one.

lessons.t: Counting turns with for and range
lessons.g: Repeat a block a known number of times and use the turn number inside it.
lessons.s: `while` is for when you do not know how many turns you need. When you do know, `for` says it in one line. `range(4)` produces the numbers 0, 1, 2, 3. Four numbers, starting at zero, stopping **before** the number you gave it.

lessons.t: A range that starts and steps where you want
lessons.g: Control the first number, the last number and the size of the jump in a range.
lessons.s: `range` takes up to three numbers. `range(stop)` counts from 0. `range(start, stop)` counts from `start`. `range(start, stop, step)` counts from `start` in jumps of `step`. In every one of those, `stop` is the number the range never reaches.

lessons.t: An accumulator that grows every turn
lessons.g: Add up values across the turns of a loop using a variable created before it.
lessons.s: A loop that only prints is worth little. Most loops are there to build up a result: a total, a count, a longest title. The variable that holds that result while the loop runs is called an **accumulator**.

lessons.g: Grow, shrink or scale a variable with the short form of assignment instead of repeating its name.
lessons.s: In the last mission you wrote `total = total + day * 100`. Read that line again: the name appears twice, once on the right to be read and once on the left to be written. Python has a shorter way to write exactly that, with no second meaning: `total += day * 100`. `x += 5` **is** `x = x + 5`. `x -= 5` is `x = x - 5`.

lessons.g: Walk a string one character at a time and count only the characters that pass a test.
lessons.s: A `for` loop does not need `range`. Give it a string and it walks it one character at a time: `for letter in title:` runs once per character, with `letter` holding a one-character string each turn. A **counter** is an accumulator that only moves when a condition is true.

lessons.t: Leaving a loop the moment you have the answer
lessons.g: Stop a loop early with break instead of running turns you no longer need.
lessons.s: `break` ends the loop immediately. The rest of the current turn is skipped, the remaining turns never happen, and the program continues after the loop. You use it when the loop is a search. Once the thing is found there is nothing left to look for, and every extra turn costs time or quota.

lessons.t: Skipping one turn without stopping the loop
lessons.g: Use continue to abandon the current turn and go straight to the next one.
lessons.s: `continue` is the other half of `break`. It abandons the rest of the current turn and jumps back to the top of the loop for the next one. The loop keeps running. This is how you handle the bad entry in a batch.

lessons.g: Nest one loop in another and know how many turns the pair really runs.
lessons.s: The block inside a loop is ordinary code, so it can hold another loop. When it does, the inner loop runs **completely** on every single turn of the outer one. Two accounts with three images each is not five turns, it is six: two turns of the outer loop, three turns of the inner loop inside each.

lessons.g: Recognise an accidental infinite loop and cap a loop whose end you do not control.
lessons.s: The editor stops your program after 8 seconds and tells you a never-ending loop is the usual cause. It is right almost every time.

lessons.g: You can hold a whole set of values under a single name and ask how many there are.
lessons.s: So far every name held exactly one value. Real work never looks like that. You do not have one channel, one file or one pending render, you have a set of them, and the set changes size.

lessons.g: You can pull a single item out of a list by its position, counting from either end.
lessons.s: A list is ordered, so every item has a fixed position, and you get one item by writing that position in square brackets after the name. Positions start at **zero**. In a list of four items the valid positions are 0, 1, 2 and 3. `titles[0]` is the first, `titles[1]` the second.

lessons.t: Taking a piece of a list
lessons.g: You can cut a range of items out of a list and get a new, smaller list back.
lessons.s: One position gives you one item. Two positions separated by a colon give you a **slice**, which is a new list containing a range of items: The first number is where the slice starts, the second is where it stops, and the stop is **not included**. `queue[1:3]` gives you positions 1 and 2, two items.

lessons.g: You can add and delete items in a list that already exists, without rebuilding it.
lessons.s: A list is not frozen once you write it. It changes in place, and the name keeps pointing at the same list while the contents move under it. Three methods do almost all of that work: - `pending.append("publish")` puts one item at the end.

lessons.g: You can run the same code once per item in a list without touching positions at all.
lessons.s: In chapter 3 you drove a `for` loop with `range`, which handed you numbers. A `for` loop can walk a list directly and hand you the **items**: On each turn, `duration` is one item. No positions, no `len`, nothing to get wrong at the ends.

lessons.t: Sorting by something other than the value
lessons.g: You can sort a list by any property of its items, not just by the items themselves.
lessons.s: `sorted(titles)` gives you a **new** list in order, alphabetical for strings and numeric for numbers. The list you passed in is untouched. If you want the list itself reordered, `titles.sort()` does it in place and returns nothing. Alphabetical is rarely the order you want.

lessons.g: You can store a record whose parts are reached by name instead of by position.
lessons.s: A list answers "how many" and "which one". It is a bad answer to "what is the view count of this video", because you would have to remember that views live at position 1. A **dictionary** stores values under names.

lessons.t: Reading a key that may not be there
lessons.g: You can read a field that might be missing and get a value you choose instead of a crash.
lessons.s: The last mission ended on `KeyError`. That is the right answer when a missing key means the data is broken. It is the wrong answer when the key is simply optional: a channel registered this morning has no views yet, and a record exported months ago may not carry every field the newest ones do.

lessons.g: You can loop over a dictionary and get its keys, its values, or both at once.
lessons.s: A dictionary is a collection too, so you can walk it, but there are three things you might want on each turn and three methods that give them: - `report.keys()` hands you the names. - `report.values()` hands you the values. - `report.items()` hands you both, as a pair.

lessons.g: You can read a table of records, one dictionary per row, and total a field across all of them.
lessons.s: This is the shape almost all real data arrives in: a **list of dictionaries**. One list, one dictionary per record, every dictionary carrying the same keys. Nothing here is new. `len(videos)` is how many records. A `for` loop hands you one dictionary per turn, and inside the loop you read its fields by key.

lessons.g: You can rank a list of records by one of their fields and report the winner.
lessons.s: You have a list of dictionaries and you want them in order by views. `sorted(videos)` will not do it: Python has no idea which field decides. Sorting records directly needs a key function, and functions are the next chapter.

lessons.t: Giving a block of code a name
lessons.g: You can define a function with `def` and call it as many times as you need.
lessons.s: A **function** is a block of code with a name. You write the block once with `def`, and from then on you run it by writing its name followed by `()`. The shape never changes: - `def`, then the name, then `()` and a colon - the body, indented under it Defining a function does not run it.

lessons.g: You can pass values into a function so the same code works on different data.
lessons.s: A function with a fixed value inside it is worth almost nothing. `report()` below always says the same thing about the same channel. Written that way you would need one function per channel. Put a name between the parentheses of the `def` line and the function stops being about one channel: `name` is a **parameter**.

lessons.g: You can tell a function that prints from one that hands a value back, and you can use the value.
lessons.s: `print` writes text on the screen. That is all it does. A function whose body only prints gives nothing back to the caller, and in Python nothing has a name: `None`. Store the result of such a call and you store `None`. `return` is a different animal. It ends the function and hands a value back to whoever called it.

lessons.t: Names created inside a function stay inside
lessons.g: You know why assigning inside a function leaves the outer variable alone, and how to make the value cross.
lessons.s: Every call gets its own private set of names. The parameters, and any variable you assign in the body, live there and vanish when the function returns. That private area is the function's **local scope**. The starting code proves it. There is a `total` outside and a `total` inside.

lessons.g: You can give a parameter a default value so the caller is allowed to leave it out.
lessons.s: Write `=` and a value in the `def` line and the parameter becomes optional: Now `clip_title("...")` runs with `limit` at 30, and `clip_title("...", 20)` overrides it. Python only reaches for the default when the caller did not supply that argument. Parameters with defaults must come after the ones without.

lessons.g: You can spot the empty-list default that keeps its contents between calls, and write the version that does not.
lessons.s: A default value is evaluated **once**, when Python reads the `def` line, not again on every call. For a number or a string that makes no difference, because neither can be modified.

lessons.g: You can return several values at once and unpack them into separate names.
lessons.s: A function is not limited to one answer. Put commas in the `return` and Python packs the values together and hands back the pack: On the calling side you take it apart with commas on the left of the `=`: That is **unpacking**. The count has to match: two values returned, two names on the left.

lessons.t: A function that changes your data, and one that does not
lessons.g: You can tell whether a function edits the data you handed it, and write one that leaves it intact.
lessons.s: A function has a **side effect** when it changes something outside itself: it prints, it edits a list it was given, it touches a variable the rest of the program depends on. A function without side effects only looks at its arguments and returns a value. Call it a hundred times and nothing else in the program moves.

lessons.g: You can write the sentence that explains a function in the place where Python stores it.
lessons.s: If the first thing in a function body is a string, Python keeps it as the function's **docstring** and stores it in `__doc__`. It is not a comment. A comment above the `def` is invisible to the running program, while a docstring can be read back, printed, and shown by the editor when you type the function's name.

lessons.t: Handing a function to another function
lessons.g: You can sort records by any field by writing the key function yourself, and read the same thing written as a lambda.
lessons.s: Chapter 4 left this unfinished. You could sort titles by length with `key=len`, but you could not sort a list of dictionaries by views: `sorted` needed something that turns a record into a number, and you had no way to write one. You have `def` now, so you do. `key` takes a function.

lessons.t: Functions built out of your other functions
lessons.g: You can assemble one function from the ones you already wrote, and read the result like a sentence.
lessons.s: A function can call another function. That is how a program stops being one long block and becomes a set of parts: each one does a single job, and a function above them puts the jobs in order. You already have `watch_ratio`, which turns a video into a number. Add `verdict`, which turns a number into a decision.

lessons.g: You can clean text that came from outside your program without destroying the original.
lessons.s: A string has methods and you call them with a dot. `strip()` removes whitespace from both ends. `lower()` returns the same text in lowercase. `replace(old, new)` swaps every occurrence of one piece of text for another. None of them change the string you called them on.

lessons.g: You can cut a string on a separator and pull the filename and the extension out of a path.
lessons.s: `split(separator)` cuts a string wherever the separator appears and returns the pieces as a **list**. `"a/b/c".split("/")` gives `['a', 'b', 'c']`. The separator itself is thrown away, and the result is a list like any other, so `pieces[-1]` is the last piece and `len(pieces)` counts them.

lessons.g: You can build a path with the / operator and read its name, stem, suffix and parent without cutting text.
lessons.s: A path is text, and treating it as text is how you end up with `output//final.mp4`, or with no separator at all. The standard library has a real type for it. `from pathlib import Path`, then `Path("output/pluma-waves")`, and you have a path object instead of a string. The join operator is `/`.

lessons.g: You can turn a list of strings into one line, with the separator you choose.
lessons.s: `join` is `split` run in reverse. You call it on the **separator**, not on the list: `"/".join(folders)`. That reads inside out the first ten times, until you remember what it is doing, which is placing that separator between every pair of items. The separator can be anything, including nothing.

lessons.g: You can control width, alignment and decimals inside an f-string.
lessons.s: An f-string can carry a **format spec** after a colon: `f"{views:>10}"`. Everything after that colon is an instruction about how to print the value, and none of it appears in the output. Three specs cover most reports: - `<12` pads with spaces on the right until the field is 12 wide, `>10` pads on the left.

lessons.g: You can open a file for writing, write lines into it and know it closed.
lessons.s: `open(path, "w")` opens a file for writing. `"w"` **truncates**: whatever that file held is gone the instant you open it, before you write a single character. `"a"` appends to the end instead. Use `with`.

lessons.t: Read it back line by line
lessons.g: You can walk a file one line at a time and strip the newline that comes with it.
lessons.s: `open(path)` with no mode opens for reading. The file object is **iterable**: `for line in f:` hands you one line per turn and never loads the whole file into memory, which is exactly what you want the day the file is a 200 MB log. Every line still carries its `\n` at the end.

lessons.g: You can save Python data as JSON and load it back as real Python data.
lessons.s: JSON is text that looks like a Python list of dicts. It is the format your APIs, your config files and every export you touch already speak, so it is the default way to put data on disk. `json.dump(data, f)` writes a Python object into an open file. `json.load(f)` reads an open file back into a Python object.

lessons.g: You can write and read a CSV file and get a dict per row instead of counting columns.
lessons.s: A CSV is a text file with one record per line and fields separated by commas. Splitting a line on `","` works right up to the first video title that has a comma in it, and then it wrecks that row without an error. Use the `csv` module and let it deal with quoting.

lessons.t: Encoding, the day it bites you
lessons.g: You know why the same text is a different number of bytes and you always name the encoding.
lessons.s: A file does not hold text. It holds **bytes**. An encoding is the rule that turns one into the other, and UTF-8 is the one to use. `title.encode("utf-8")` gives you the `bytes` behind the text.

lessons.t: Read the traceback from the bottom
lessons.g: Find the error and the exact line that caused it in any traceback, without reading the middle.
lessons.s: When Python stops, it prints a **traceback**. It looks like a wall of text and most people read it top to bottom, which is the wrong direction. The top is the outermost call, usually something you did not write. The information you need is at the bottom. Read it bottom up.

lessons.t: Survive one bad value with try and except
lessons.g: Keep a job running when one item in the batch is unusable.
lessons.s: A batch job that dies on item three of two hundred is worse than one that skips item three and tells you. `try` / `except` is how you choose which one you get. Python runs the body of `try`. If nothing goes wrong, the `except` block never happens.

lessons.t: The five errors you will meet most
lessons.g: Name the error from the symptom before reading a single line of the code that raised it.
lessons.s: Almost everything that breaks in day to day Python is one of five errors. Learning their names is not trivia: the name alone tells you which kind of mistake you made, before you open the file. - **NameError**: you used a name that does not exist. Usually a typo, or a variable defined in another branch that never ran.

lessons.t: Catch the error you expected, not every error
lessons.g: Write handlers that separate two known failures instead of hiding all of them behind one message.
lessons.s: `except Exception:` catches everything. That sounds safe and it is the most expensive habit in this chapter. It swallows the typo you made ten minutes ago along with the bad data you were expecting, and turns both into the same useless line: something went wrong. A `try` can have several `except` blocks.

lessons.g: Make the close happen on the run that dies, not only on the run that works.
lessons.s: A `try` has a block most people never write. `except` runs when something broke. **`finally` runs either way**, whether the body finished, raised, or returned in the middle. Without it, the close sits on the line after the loop, and a raise inside the loop jumps straight over it.

lessons.t: Raise your own error instead of returning a lie
lessons.g: Make a function refuse impossible input rather than hand back a number that means nothing.
lessons.s: A function that gets input it cannot work with has two options. It can return something harmless looking, like 0, or it can stop. Returning 0 is how a wrong number travels: it goes into a total, into a report, into a decision, and the day you notice it you have no idea where it came from.

lessons.t: Assert the thing your code depends on
lessons.g: State an assumption in code so it fails at the cause instead of three functions later.
lessons.s: `assert` is a sentence about what must be true at that point in your own code: If the condition is true, nothing happens. If it is false, Python raises `AssertionError` with that message, right there.

lessons.t: Debug with prints when nothing crashes
lessons.g: Find which item of a batch corrupts a total, using one print inside the loop.
lessons.s: The hard bugs do not raise anything. The program finishes, prints a number, and the number is wrong. There is no traceback to read because nothing broke: your code did exactly what you wrote. The cheapest tool is a print inside the loop that shows **the name of the item and the running value** after each step.

lessons.t: Shrink the bug to three lines
lessons.g: Reproduce a failure outside the program that produced it.
lessons.s: A job over four hundred rows dies. You do not debug four hundred rows. You find the one value that breaks, and you rebuild the failure in three lines that stand alone: the value, the expression the traceback pointed at, and a print. That is a **minimal reproducible case**, and it changes the problem completely.

lessons.g: Decide what a function does with the four inputs that break every function on real data.
lessons.s: Code written against the data you have in front of you works until the day it meets one of four inputs, and it always meets all four: - **empty**: a list with no rows, a file with no lines, a string with nothing in it. - **zero**: a divisor of 0, a channel with 0 videos, a total of 0.

lessons.t: Code you did not have to write
lessons.g: You can pull a module out of the standard library and call what is inside it.
lessons.s: Python arrives with around two hundred modules already installed. Not packages you download, not something to configure: they ship with the language and they are there the moment Python starts. The word that reaches for one is `import`. `import statistics` loads the module and gives you a name to reach through.

lessons.t: Taking one tool off the shelf
lessons.g: You can import a single name out of a module instead of the whole module.
lessons.s: `import statistics` puts the whole box on your desk. `from statistics import mean` takes one tool out of the box and puts it on the bench: after that line you call `mean(numbers)` with no dot in front. Use the second form when you call the same function all over the file and its name is unmistakable on its own.

lessons.g: You know which standard library module to reach for before you start writing one yourself.
lessons.s: Most of the code a beginner writes by hand already exists, tested, in the standard library. The skill is not memorising it. The skill is recognising the shape of your problem and knowing which name to look up.

lessons.g: You can move functions into a separate file and import them back.
lessons.s: There is nothing special about the modules that ship with Python. Any file ending in `.py` is a module, and its name is the filename without the extension.

lessons.t: The line that separates running from importing
lessons.g: You can write a module that stays silent when imported and still runs on its own.
lessons.s: Every module has a variable called `__name__` that Python fills in for you. When you run a file directly, its `__name__` is the string `"__main__"`. When the same file is imported by another program, its `__name__` is the module name, `"daily_report"`. That single difference is what `if __name__ == "__main__":` uses.

lessons.g: You can lift the magic numbers out of a program into named constants at the top.
lessons.s: A number sitting in the middle of an expression tells the reader nothing. `videos * 0.42` is arithmetic; `videos * COST_PER_VIDEO` is a sentence. The `0.42` is called a magic number, and it is magic in the bad sense: it works and nobody knows why. The fix is a constant.

lessons.t: Three copies is a function waiting to happen
lessons.g: You can collapse repeated lines into one function without changing what the program prints.
lessons.s: Refactoring means changing the shape of a program without changing what it does. It is not the same as fixing or improving: the output before and the output after are identical, line for line. That is the whole safety net. Run it, keep the output, refactor, run it again, compare.

lessons.t: Code that hides what it does
lessons.g: You can rename someone else's variables until the program explains itself, without breaking it.
lessons.s: Sooner or later you open a file you did not write, or one you wrote eight months ago, which is the same thing. It runs. It is correct. And it is unreadable, because every name in it is a single letter. The method is mechanical and it works every time.

lessons.g: You can tell a comment that pays for itself from one that is only noise.
lessons.s: A comment that says what the line below it says is worse than no comment. It doubles the reading, and the day somebody changes the code without changing the comment, it starts lying. `# subtract used from the cap` above `left = DAILY_IMAGE_CAP - used` is not documentation. It is a duplicate that will rot.

lessons.g: Write the channel records to a JSON file and read them back into the program.
lessons.s: Every tool you have ever run starts the same way: data arrives on disk, the program picks it up. The final project is one program that grows across seven missions, and this is its first job. It writes `channels.json`, then it reads that same file back and prints what came out.

lessons.g: Turn one channel record into a video count, a total view count and an average, using a single function.
lessons.s: A subscriber count tells you almost nothing. What you actually rank a channel by is what its videos do. Each record carries a `videos` list, and every video in it carries a `views` number, so the numbers you want are already in the file. They just have to be computed. One function, one channel, three numbers out.

lessons.g: Add up subscribers, watch hours, videos and views across every channel and print one summary line.
lessons.s: Per channel numbers answer "which one". Fleet numbers answer "how am I doing". Both belong in the report and neither replaces the other, so the tool grows a second function instead of changing the first one. `fleet_totals(channels)` is an accumulator loop over the whole list.

lessons.g: Rank the fleet by average views per video and name the top and bottom channel.
lessons.s: The report knows the numbers, but you still have to read four lines and compare them yourself. That is work the tool should be doing. Two more lines, one naming the channel that earns the most views per video and one naming the channel that earns the least. `max` and `min` do not only take numbers.

lessons.t: The Channel With Nothing In It
lessons.g: Keep the report standing when a record is missing the fields the report reads.
lessons.s: You registered a channel today. It has a name, zero subscribers, no watch hours and no videos, and the export writes it out exactly like that: `{"name": "Detras del Enigma", "subscribers": 0}`. Feed that record to the tool as it stands and `channel["videos"]` raises `KeyError`.

lessons.g: Load the data behind a guard that survives a corrupt file and a file that is not there.
lessons.s: The record with missing keys was still valid JSON. The next two failures are not. An export that dies halfway leaves a file full of truncated garbage, and a path you typed wrong leaves no file at all. Both currently take the tool down before it prints a single line.

lessons.g: Collect the report into lines, write it to a file, and put the whole tool behind one entry point.
lessons.s: Everything works and nothing is a tool yet. The report only exists while the program is running, and the program is a pile of top level statements that fire the moment anything imports it. Two changes fix both, and neither one invents a new idea. First, `build_report(channels)` stops printing and starts returning.

lessons.g: Print text from a Python program and read the console as a robot's voice.
lessons.s: A robot that cannot talk is a robot you cannot debug. On a Raspberry Pi 4 driving a differential base, the very first thing the software does at boot is print a line saying who it is and that it is alive. That line is your only proof the program reached the start. `print()` writes text to standard output.

lessons.g: Store values in variables and reuse them instead of repeating literals.
lessons.s: A **variable** is a name attached to a value. You write `wheel_radius = 0.033` and from then on the name `wheel_radius` means 0.033 metres, the radius of the yellow wheels that come with a TT gearmotor. Why bother? Because a robot has one truth per quantity.

lessons.g: Use int and float arithmetic to compute a physical quantity from robot dimensions.
lessons.s: Python has two number types you will use constantly. An **int** is a whole number, like the 20 encoder ticks per revolution of a quadrature encoder. A **float** has a decimal point, like 0.033 metres of wheel radius. Divide two ints with `/` and you get a float back, always.

lessons.t: The Shape of a Status Line
lessons.g: Build formatted telemetry strings with f-strings and rounding.
lessons.s: Raw floats are unreadable. `0.20734493999999998` is not a status line, it is noise. An **f-string** lets you drop values inside text: put an `f` before the quotes and wrap any expression in curly braces. You can also say how it should look. `{volts:.2f}` prints the float with exactly two decimals.

lessons.t: True, False and the Bumper Switch
lessons.g: Produce boolean values with comparison operators and read them as robot conditions.
lessons.s: A bumper switch has exactly two states, pressed or not pressed. Python calls those `True` and `False`, the **bool** type. Capital letters, no quotes: `True` is a value, `"True"` is a piece of text and they are not the same thing. You rarely type `True` by hand.

lessons.t: The Line You Do Not Cross
lessons.g: Guard an action with a single if statement and correct indentation.
lessons.s: An `if` runs a block of code only when a condition is `True`. The condition goes after the keyword, the line ends with a colon, and the body is **indented four spaces**. In Python indentation is not decoration, it is the syntax. A line that is not indented is not inside the `if`.

lessons.g: Choose between two actions with if and else.
lessons.s: `else` covers everything the `if` did not. It has no condition of its own, just a colon and an indented block. Exactly one of the two branches runs, never both, never neither. In a robot this maps onto the most common decision there is: drive or stop.

lessons.g: Split a continuous sensor reading into ordered bands with elif.
lessons.s: Real robots do not have two speeds, they have a ramp. Far away, drive at cruise. Getting closer, slow down. Too close, stop. That is three cases and `elif` is how you write them. Python checks the conditions **in order** and stops at the first one that is `True`. That means order is part of the logic.

lessons.g: Combine conditions with and, or and not.
lessons.s: One sensor is never enough. A small rover carries two lever microswitches on the front bumper, left and right, and the decision depends on both. `and` is `True` only when both sides are `True`. `or` is `True` when at least one is. `not` flips a bool.

lessons.g: Nest conditions so a decision only happens once its precondition holds.
lessons.s: Some decisions only make sense after another one passed. There is no point choosing a driving speed if the battery is already below cutoff: the answer is stop, whatever the ultrasonic says. You express that by putting an `if` inside another `if`. The inner block is indented eight spaces, two levels.

lessons.g: Replace nesting with guard clauses that handle the bad case first.
lessons.s: A **guard clause** deals with the impossible case immediately and gets out of the way, leaving the rest of the code flat and readable. In a function you would `return`, and you will do exactly that in chapter three. Here you do the same with a status variable and a chain of `elif` bands.

lessons.g: Range check a value with a chained comparison and clamp it.
lessons.s: An MG996R servo accepts angles from 0 to 180 degrees. Command 200 and you push it against its mechanical stop, it stalls, it draws two amps and it cooks. Every command that leaves your code must be inside the envelope of the hardware that receives it.

lessons.g: Write a conditional expression to pick a value inline.
lessons.s: Sometimes a four line `if` and `else` exists only to give a variable one of two values. Python has a shorter form for exactly that case, the **conditional expression**: It reads value, condition, other value.

lessons.g: Repeat a block a fixed number of times with a while loop and a counter.
lessons.s: A `while` loop repeats its body as long as a condition stays `True`. Three parts have to be there or the loop misbehaves: initialise the counter before the loop, test it in the condition, and change it inside the body. Forget the third and the condition never becomes `False`, which is an infinite loop.

lessons.g: Iterate over a numeric sequence with for and range.
lessons.s: When you know how many times you want to repeat, `for` with `range()` says it in one line and cannot forget the increment. `for angle in range(0, 181, 10):` walks 0, 10, 20 and so on up to 180. `range(stop)` starts at 0. `range(start, stop)` starts where you say. `range(start, stop, step)` adds the step.

lessons.g: Walk a range backwards with a negative step.
lessons.s: A pan servo that only sweeps one way has to snap back to zero, which shakes the whole chassis and ruins the next reading. Real sweeps go out and come back, and the return leg is a `range` with a negative step. `range(180, -1, -15)` starts at 180, decreases by 15 and stops before -1, so it ends exactly at 0.

lessons.g: Accumulate a running total inside a loop and divide to get a mean.
lessons.s: An **accumulator** is a variable declared before the loop and added to inside it. Total starts at zero, each pass adds a reading, after the loop you divide by the count and you have the mean. This is the cheapest filter in robotics and it buys a lot.

lessons.g: Leave a loop early with break when the answer is already known.
lessons.s: `break` ends the loop immediately. The rest of the body is skipped and execution continues after the loop. A scanning robot does not need to finish its sweep once it has found what it was looking for.

lessons.g: Skip one pass of a loop with continue to filter invalid readings.
lessons.s: `continue` jumps straight to the next pass. Everything below it in the body is skipped, but the loop keeps going. This is how you drop garbage sensor data. An HC-SR04 returns 0 when the echo never came back, and anything above `MAX_CM`, its four metre ceiling, is beyond its usable range.

lessons.g: Nest one loop inside another to cover a two axis scan.
lessons.s: A pan and tilt head has two servos, so covering the field means two loops, one inside the other. The outer loop moves the slow axis, tilt, and the inner loop sweeps the fast one, pan. For every single tilt position, the whole pan sweep runs.

lessons.g: Structure a control loop as while True with explicit exit conditions.
lessons.s: Robot software is one big loop: read sensors, decide, write actuators, repeat, forever. You write that as `while True:` and it is the correct shape, not a beginner shortcut. Every ROS node, every Arduino sketch, every flight controller is this loop.

lessons.g: Track a running minimum through a loop to find the nearest obstacle.
lessons.s: Finding the smallest value in a stream is a loop pattern worth knowing cold. Keep two variables outside the loop: the best value so far and where it happened. On each pass, if the current reading beats the best, replace both. Initialise the best to something that any real reading beats.

lessons.t: Sealing a Behaviour in a Box
lessons.g: Define a function with def and call it by name.
lessons.s: A **function** is a block of code with a name. You write it once with `def`, and from then on you run it by writing its name followed by parentheses. Defining it does nothing on its own, the body only runs when you call it. The first reason to make one is not reuse, it is naming.

lessons.g: Pass arguments into a function through parameters.
lessons.s: A function that always does the same thing is a paragraph with a title. A function that takes **parameters** is a tool. The names in the `def` line are the parameters, the values you pass at the call are the arguments, and inside the body the parameters behave like ordinary variables.

lessons.g: Return a value from a function and use it in an expression.
lessons.s: `return` sends a value back to whoever called the function and ends the function immediately. Without a `return`, a function hands back `None`, which is Python's way of saying nothing. A function that prints instead of returning is a dead end: you cannot use its result in another calculation.

lessons.g: Give parameters default values so common calls stay short.
lessons.s: A parameter with a default becomes optional: `def drive(speed, ramp=0.2):` can be called as `drive(0.4)` or as `drive(0.4, ramp=0.05)`. Defaults are written in the `def` line and they must come after all the parameters that have none. Defaults encode the sane configuration of your robot.

lessons.g: Return several values at once as a tuple and unpack them at the call site.
lessons.s: `return x, y` hands back a **tuple**, an immutable little package of values. At the call site you unpack it with `x, y = odometry_step(...)` and the two names land in one line. Robotics is full of naturally paired values. A pose is x, y and heading. A differential drive command is left and right wheel speed.

lessons.g: Understand local scope and why shared mutable state hurts robot code.
lessons.s: A name created inside a function is **local**: it exists only while the function runs and it is invisible outside. Assigning to it does not touch a variable of the same name at module level, it creates a separate one.

lessons.g: Document a function with a docstring and type hints.
lessons.s: A **docstring** is a string on the first line of the function body, written with triple quotes. Tools read it, editors show it on hover, and `help(fn)` prints it. **Type hints** annotate what goes in and what comes out: `def clamp(value: float, low: float, high: float) -> float:`. Neither is enforced at runtime.

lessons.g: Compose small functions into one behaviour function.
lessons.s: The way real robot software is built: several tiny functions that each do one honest thing, and one function on top that calls them in order. The top one reads like a description of the behaviour and contains almost no arithmetic.

lessons.g: Use keyword arguments so a call site says what each value means.
lessons.s: `set_pid(0.8, 0.02, 0.1, 255, 0.05)` is a line nobody can review. `set_pid(kp=0.8, ki=0.02, kd=0.1, limit=255, dt=0.05)` is the same call and it needs no comment. That is a **keyword argument**: you name the parameter at the call site.

lessons.g: Create a list and read its elements by index.
lessons.s: A **list** holds several values in order, written between square brackets and separated by commas. An RPLIDAR A1 hands your program hundreds of ranges per revolution and a list is the natural container for them. You read an element with `ranges[0]`, and the first index is **zero**.

lessons.g: Take a sub list with slicing to isolate a sector of a scan.
lessons.s: A **slice** copies a range of elements: `ranges[2:5]` gives elements 2, 3 and 4. The start is included, the stop is not, exactly like `range()`. Leave a side blank and it means all the way to that end: `ranges[:4]` is the first four, `ranges[-3:]` is the last three. This is how you cut a scan into sectors.

lessons.g: Grow and shrink a list with append and pop to keep a fixed window.
lessons.s: Lists are **mutable**: you can change them after creation. `buffer.append(value)` adds one at the end, `buffer.pop(0)` removes and returns the first, `buffer.pop()` removes the last. A fixed length rolling buffer is the workhorse of sensor code.

lessons.g: Iterate a list with for and get the index too using enumerate.
lessons.s: `for r in scan:` walks the values and is the clearest way to read a list. But a lidar sample means nothing without its bearing, and the bearing comes from the index. `enumerate(scan)` hands you both at once: `for i, r in enumerate(scan):` gives the index in `i` and the value in `r`.

lessons.t: Reducing a Scan to a Number
lessons.g: Summarise a list with len, sum, min and max.
lessons.s: Four builtins collapse a whole list into one value: `len` counts, `sum` adds, `min` finds the smallest, `max` the largest. Together they replace the accumulator loops you wrote in chapter two, and they are implemented in C so they are far faster on a Raspberry Pi.

lessons.g: Sort a list and pick the middle value to reject spikes.
lessons.s: `sorted(values)` returns a new sorted list, `values.sort()` sorts in place and returns `None`. Prefer `sorted` unless you have a reason, for the same reason you prefer returning over mutating. Sorting buys you the **median**, the middle value of the sorted list.

lessons.t: Building a List in One Line
lessons.g: Transform and filter a list with a comprehension.
lessons.s: A **list comprehension** builds a new list from an old one: `[r / 100.0 for r in scan]` converts every centimetre reading to metres. Add a condition and it filters too: `[r for r in scan if r > 0]` drops the invalid zeros.

lessons.g: Represent an occupancy grid as a list of lists and index it by row and column.
lessons.s: A map is a two dimensional array, and in plain Python that is a list whose elements are lists. `grid[row][col]` reads one cell: the first index picks the row, the second picks the column inside it. Build it with a comprehension: `[[0 for _ in range(cols)] for _ in range(rows)]` creates independent rows.

lessons.g: Use tuples for fixed records and pair sequences with zip.
lessons.s: A **tuple** is written with commas, usually inside parentheses, and it cannot be changed after creation. `(1.5, 0.8)` is a waypoint. That immutability is the point: a coordinate pair has exactly two fields forever, and a function that receives it cannot append a third one behind your back.

lessons.g: Create a dict and read values by key.
lessons.s: A list is indexed by position, a **dict** is indexed by name. You write it with curly braces and colons: `{"wheel_radius": 0.033, "wheelbase": 0.16}`, and you read a value with `config["wheelbase"]`. This is how every robot stores its configuration.

lessons.t: When the Key Is Not There
lessons.g: Read optional configuration safely with get and a default.
lessons.s: `config.get("ramp_s", 0.2)` returns the value if the key exists and 0.2 if it does not, without raising. That single method is the difference between a config file that must list every parameter and one where the user only writes what differs from the defaults. Decide per parameter which behaviour you want.

lessons.g: Iterate a dict with items, keys and values.
lessons.s: `for key in d:` walks the keys. `for value in d.values():` walks the values. `for key, value in d.items():` gives both, and it is the one you will use most. A six axis arm keeps its state as a dict from joint name to angle.

lessons.g: Add, update and remove keys to maintain a live robot state dict.
lessons.s: Dicts are mutable. `state["mode"] = "AUTO"` sets or replaces a key. `state.update(other)` merges another dict in, overwriting matching keys. `del state["fault"]` removes one, and `state.pop("fault", None)` removes it without raising if it was already gone.

lessons.g: Nest dicts to describe per joint configuration and read them in two steps.
lessons.s: A value in a dict can be another dict. `limits["elbow"]["max_deg"]` reads a nested structure two levels deep, and that is exactly how a real robot description looks: one entry per joint, each holding its minimum, maximum and maximum speed.

lessons.g: Build a histogram in a dict to count events over a run.
lessons.s: To count occurrences you need a dict from event to count, and one line to increment it: `counts[code] = counts.get(code, 0) + 1`. The `get` with a default of zero handles the first time you see a code, so there is no special case. This is how you turn a log into a diagnosis.

lessons.g: Use a set for uniqueness and fast membership tests.
lessons.s: A **set** holds unique values with no order: `{"BUMPER_L", "IMU_SATURATED"}`, or `set()` for an empty one. Adding a value that is already there does nothing, which is precisely what you want for the collection of faults seen during a run. Membership testing is where sets shine.

lessons.g: Parse a delimited telemetry string with strip, split and float.
lessons.s: An MPU6050 bridged through an Arduino sends lines like `IMU,0.12,-0.03,9.81\r\n`. Your program receives text and has to turn it into numbers. Three methods do the job. `.strip()` removes the whitespace and line endings at both ends, and forgetting it is why `float("9.81\r")` fails on Windows style line endings.

lessons.g: Assemble an outgoing protocol string with join and formatting.
lessons.s: Going the other way, you have numbers and you need one line of text ending in a newline. `",".join(pieces)` glues a list of **strings** with a separator, so every number has to be formatted first. Fix the number of decimals on the way out.

lessons.g: Read a text file line by line using with open.
lessons.s: `open(path)` gives you a file object, and `with open(path) as f:` closes it automatically when the block ends, even if the code inside raises. Always use the `with` form. A robot process that leaks file handles for days eventually runs out of them and dies at the worst moment.

lessons.g: Append telemetry to a log file and control flushing.
lessons.s: The mode you pass to `open` decides everything. `"w"` truncates the file to empty before writing, `"a"` appends to what is there, `"r"` is read only and is the default. Opening a mission log with `"w"` instead of `"a"` erases yesterday's evidence, and that mistake is made once per career. Writes are buffered.

lessons.g: Read and write CSV files with the csv module.
lessons.s: Splitting on commas by hand works until a field contains a comma, and then it silently corrupts your data. The `csv` module in the standard library handles quoting, escaping and line endings correctly, and it costs one import.

lessons.g: Save and load structured configuration with json.
lessons.s: JSON is the format for anything with nesting: dicts inside dicts, lists of waypoints, per joint limits. `json.dump(obj, f, indent=2)` writes it readable, `json.load(f)` reads it back into real Python objects with the right types.

lessons.g: Handle a failure with try and except instead of crashing.
lessons.s: `try:` runs code that might fail, `except:` catches the failure and lets the program continue. Without it, one malformed serial frame kills a robot that was otherwise fine. Catch **specific** exceptions. `except ValueError:` catches a failed `float()` conversion.

lessons.g: Guarantee cleanup with else and finally.
lessons.s: The full statement has four parts. `try` holds the risky code, `except` handles a failure, `else` runs only when nothing was raised, and `finally` runs **always**, on success, on failure, and even when the block returns. `finally` is where robot code stops the motors.

lessons.g: Raise an exception yourself to reject invalid input at the boundary.
lessons.s: `raise ValueError("joint angle out of envelope")` throws an exception from your own code. You do it when a caller hands you something that cannot be honoured, and continuing would mean guessing. The rule is where to validate: at the boundary, once.

lessons.g: Import from the standard library and from your own module file.
lessons.s: `import math` brings in a module and you reach into it with a dot: `math.pi`, `math.atan2(dy, dx)`. `from math import pi, atan2` pulls specific names into your file. Never use `from math import *`, it dumps dozens of names into your namespace and one of them will collide with yours. Your own files are modules too.

lessons.g: Configure the logging module with levels, a format and a file handler.
lessons.s: `print` has one volume. `logging` has five: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL. You write `log.debug(...)` freely all over the control loop and then decide at startup whether those lines appear, without touching the code.

lessons.g: Define a class with __init__ and create instances that hold their own state.
lessons.s: A **class** is a template. It says what data every robot of this kind carries. `__init__` is the method that runs when you create one, and `self` is the instance being built, so `self.x = x` stores a value on that particular robot. Until now a robot's pose lived in three loose variables.

lessons.g: Add methods that read and modify the instance state.
lessons.s: A **method** is a function defined inside the class, taking `self` first. It can read and write the instance attributes, which is what makes an object more than a bag of values. `robot.drive(0.2)` reads better than `drive(robot, 0.2)` and it keeps the motion rule next to the state it changes.

lessons.g: Keep invariants inside the object instead of trusting every caller.
lessons.s: An **invariant** is something that must always be true about the object: the speed never exceeds the maximum, the battery reading is never negative, the heading is always in the range minus pi to pi. The object is responsible for its own invariants.

lessons.g: Give a class a readable __repr__ for debugging.
lessons.s: By default printing an object gives you `<__main__.Robot object at 0x7f8b1c0d5e50>`, which tells you nothing. `__repr__` fixes that: define it to return a string and every print, every log line, every list of robots becomes readable.

lessons.t: What Every Robot of This Kind Shares
lessons.g: Distinguish class attributes from instance attributes.
lessons.s: An attribute assigned in the class body, outside any method, belongs to the **class**: every instance sees the same value. An attribute assigned on `self` inside `__init__` belongs to that **instance** alone. The geometry of a specific model is a class attribute.

lessons.g: Extend a class with inheritance and override a method.
lessons.s: A subclass gets everything from its parent and can add or replace parts: `class Tracked(Robot):`. Inside the subclass, `super().__init__(...)` runs the parent's constructor so you do not repeat its work. Use it when the relationship is genuinely **is a**. A tracked rover is a robot.

lessons.t: The Robot Is Made of Parts
lessons.g: Build a robot by composition, holding other objects as attributes.
lessons.s: **Composition** is one object holding others: the robot has a left motor, a right motor and a range sensor, each its own object with its own class. That is the relationship almost every robot part actually has, and it is a plain attribute assignment in `__init__`.

lessons.g: Expose validated state with property and a setter.
lessons.s: A `@property` turns a method into something that reads like an attribute. `robot.speed` calls the getter, and with a matching `@speed.setter`, `robot.speed = 0.3` calls the setter, which can clamp, validate or convert. This is how you keep the clean syntax and the safety at once.

lessons.t: A Fault With Its Own Name
lessons.g: Define custom exception classes and raise them from methods so a specific handler and a family handler each have something to catch.
lessons.s: A custom exception is a class that inherits from `Exception` and often has an empty body: `class JointLimitError(Exception): pass`. That is enough to make it catchable by name. Why bother when `ValueError` exists. Because a caller can then react differently to different failures.

lessons.t: The Array That Is Not a List
lessons.g: Create numpy arrays and read their shape and dtype.
lessons.s: `numpy` is the numeric core of every Python robotics stack. `np.array([0.3, 0.1, 0.0])` builds an array, which looks like a list and behaves nothing like one: it has a fixed type, a fixed shape, and it stores its numbers packed in memory instead of as separate Python objects.

lessons.t: Doing It to All of Them at Once
lessons.g: Apply vectorised arithmetic instead of looping element by element.
lessons.s: Arithmetic on numpy arrays is elementwise and needs no loop. `scan_m = scan_mm / 1000.0` converts an entire lidar scan in one line. `p + v * dt` integrates a whole position vector at once.

lessons.g: Compute norms, unit vectors and the angle between two vectors with the dot product.
lessons.s: `np.linalg.norm(v)` is the length of a vector. For a position that is the distance from the origin, for a velocity it is the speed. Dividing a vector by its norm gives a **unit vector**, same direction, length one, which is how directions are expressed everywhere in robotics.

lessons.g: Build 2D arrays, multiply them with the matrix product, and separate it from the elementwise product.
lessons.s: A two dimensional array is a matrix: `np.array([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0]])` has shape `(2, 2)`. Index it as `M[row, col]`, take a whole row with `M[0]` and a whole column with `M[:, 0]`. The operator that matters is `@`, the matrix product.

lessons.g: Build a 2D rotation matrix and rotate a point about the origin.
lessons.s: The 2D rotation matrix is `[[cos t, -sin t], [sin t, cos t]]`, and `R @ p` rotates the point `p` counter clockwise by `t` radians about the origin. That single matrix is the backbone of every mobile robot transform you will write. Radians, always.

lessons.t: Rotation and Offset in One Object
lessons.g: Assemble a 3 by 3 homogeneous transform and chain two frames.
lessons.s: A sensor is rotated **and** offset from the robot body, and doing those as two separate steps in the wrong order is the classic transform bug.

lessons.g: Open a serial port with pyserial and read lines with a timeout.
lessons.s: A microcontroller talks to your Pi over a serial port: `/dev/ttyUSB0` or `/dev/ttyACM0` on Linux, `COM3` on Windows. `pyserial` opens it with `serial.Serial(port, baudrate, timeout=0.1)` and the three arguments all matter. The **baudrate** must match the firmware exactly.

lessons.g: Parse serial frames defensively with a checksum and a rejection counter.
lessons.s: Serial data arrives corrupted more often than beginners expect. A motor driver switching two amps next to an unshielded cable flips bits, a reset mid frame truncates a line, and the first bytes after opening a port are usually half a frame from before you connected.

lessons.g: Run a fixed rate control loop with time.monotonic and measure its jitter.
lessons.s: A control loop has a period. 50 Hz means one cycle every 20 milliseconds, and the controller you tune assumes that number is true. Sleeping a fixed 20 ms is wrong, because your own work took time that the sleep does not account for, and the loop drifts slower than intended.

lessons.t: Integrating With the Clock You Have
lessons.g: Use the measured dt to integrate motion so the estimate survives a late cycle.
lessons.s: Every integrator in a robot multiplies by `dt`: position from velocity, heading from yaw rate, the integral term of a PID. The question is which `dt` you use, the one you wanted or the one you got.

lessons.g: Build the World and Robot classes that the whole simulator will hang from.
lessons.s: The project is a two dimensional simulator of a differential drive rover: a world with walls and circular obstacles, a robot with a pose, a virtual range finder, two behaviours and a run log. Everything you have learned so far appears in it, which is the point. Start with the data.

lessons.g: Integrate the differential drive kinematics with a measured dt and reject collisions.
lessons.s: The rover is commanded with a forward velocity `v` and a yaw rate `omega`, and the pose integrates as `theta += omega * dt`, `x += v * cos(theta) * dt`, `y += v * sin(theta) * dt`. That is the unicycle model and it is what a differential drive base reduces to. Clamp the command before you integrate, not after.

lessons.g: Implement a virtual range finder by ray marching against the world.
lessons.s: The robot needs to sense. A real HC-SR04 or a lidar beam returns the distance to the first thing along a ray, and the cheapest honest way to simulate that is **ray marching**: step along the ray in small increments and return the distance at the first occupied point. The step size is the trade you are making.

lessons.g: Write a reactive avoidance behaviour that turns toward the freest side.
lessons.s: A reactive behaviour maps the current scan straight to a command with no memory. It is the simplest thing that works and it is what runs underneath every fancier planner as the last line of defence. The rule has three bands you already know.

lessons.g: Follow a path with a proportional heading controller and a wrapped angle error.
lessons.s: Avoidance keeps the robot alive, it does not take it anywhere. The goal seeking behaviour computes the bearing to the current waypoint with `atan2(dy, dx)`, subtracts the current heading, and turns proportionally to that error: `omega = KP * error`. Wrap the error into the range minus pi to pi before you use it.

lessons.g: Log the run to CSV and to a level based log file so a failure can be explained afterwards.
lessons.s: A simulator whose only output is a number at the end cannot be debugged. Every run writes two files: a CSV with one row per cycle for analysis, and a log with one line per event for reading.

lessons.g: Assemble world, robot, sensor, behaviours, logging and an ASCII render into one runnable mission.
lessons.s: Final assembly. The pieces are written and tested, and this lesson wires them into a `Simulator` class with one `run()` method: build the world, place the robot, load the path, then loop until the path is done, the collision budget is spent or the cycle cap is reached.

lessons.g: Write an open loop command and state why it cannot correct itself.
lessons.s: An **open loop** controller sends a command and never checks what happened. You tell a Pololu 25D gearmotor driver to run at 60 percent duty and you hope the wheel turns at the speed you wanted. Nothing in the code ever asks the wheel. This works while the world stays exactly as it was when you calibrated.

lessons.g: Read a measurement into the loop and compare it against the command.
lessons.s: A loop becomes **closed** the moment a sensor value enters the decision. On a wheel that sensor is usually a quadrature encoder on the motor shaft, a 12 count per revolution disc behind a 34:1 gearbox. On an oven it is a thermocouple. On a balancing robot it is an MPU-6050. The measurement is never the truth.

lessons.t: The Distance Between Want and Have
lessons.g: Compute the error signal and keep its sign meaningful.
lessons.s: The **error** is `e = setpoint - measurement`. That order is not arbitrary. Written this way a positive error means you are below target and need to push harder, which matches the intuition of every actuator command you will ever write. If you flip it to `measurement - setpoint` the whole controller inverts.

lessons.g: Choose a sign convention for the actuator and detect an inverted loop.
lessons.s: A loop with the wrong sign does not misbehave slightly. It runs away. Positive error asks for more push, the push moves the plant further from the target, the error grows, and the command saturates in under a second. The sign depends on wiring, not on theory.

lessons.g: Build the read, compute, write, wait skeleton every controller in this course uses.
lessons.s: Every controller in a real robot is the same four steps repeated forever: **read** the sensor, **compute** the command, **write** it to the actuator, **wait** until the next tick. On a Raspberry Pi 4 running a Python loop, that tick is typically 5 to 20 ms. The wait is not politeness.

lessons.g: Implement proportional control and see the command shrink as the error shrinks.
lessons.s: **Proportional control** is one line: `u = Kp * e`. The further you are from the target, the harder you push. As you arrive, the push fades to nothing. That fade is the whole point. A bang bang controller pushes at full power until it crosses the target and then slams the other way.

lessons.g: Compare rise time across several values of Kp on the same plant.
lessons.s: Raising `Kp` makes the loop react harder to the same error, so the response gets faster. On a 25D gearmotor you hear it: a soft gain makes the wheel creep up to speed, a stiff gain snaps it there. There is no free speed.

lessons.t: The Gap That Will Not Close
lessons.g: Explain and measure the steady state error left by a pure P controller.
lessons.s: Run a P loop long enough and it stops moving while still short of the target. This leftover is **steady state error**, and it is not a bug. The logic is airtight: the motor needs some duty to hold 100 rpm against friction. That duty can only come from `Kp * e`.

lessons.g: Show that a plant with delay swings harder as Kp rises, right up to the gain where it stops settling.
lessons.s: The first order plant you have been using never truly oscillates, no matter how high `Kp` goes. Real hardware does, because real hardware has **delay**. A command written to a motor driver does not reach the shaft instantly, and an encoder reading arrives from a period you already left.

lessons.g: Measure how a P loop responds to a sudden load disturbance.
lessons.s: A disturbance is anything that moves the plant without going through your command: a robot rolling onto carpet, a gripper picking up a 500 g payload, a fan blowing across a heated block. A P loop rejects disturbances the same way it tracks setpoints.

lessons.g: Add a feedforward bias to a P loop and cut the steady state error without extra gain.
lessons.s: If the droop comes from the duty the motor needs at the operating point, you can just hand it that duty. `u = u0 + Kp * e`, where `u0` is a constant chosen for the expected load.

lessons.g: Estimate the time constant of a plant from its own step response.
lessons.s: A first order plant answers a step command with an exponential rise. After one **time constant** it has covered 63.2 percent of the distance, after three it is within 5 percent, after five it is done for any practical purpose.

lessons.t: Reading the Shape of an Answer
lessons.g: Compute overshoot, rise time and settling time from a response trace.
lessons.s: Three numbers describe a step response well enough to argue about it. **Overshoot** is how far past the setpoint the peak went, as a percentage. **Rise time** is how long it took to first reach the setpoint. **Settling time** is when it stopped leaving a 2 percent band around the setpoint.

lessons.g: Wrap proportional control in a reusable class with a reset method.
lessons.s: From here on the controller carries state, so it stops being a function and becomes an object. A class gives you three things a function cannot: gains that live with the instance, memory between calls, and a `reset` you can call when the robot is disabled. That `reset` matters more than it looks.

lessons.g: Accumulate the error over time and understand what the sum represents.
lessons.s: The **integral term** adds up every error the loop has ever seen, multiplied by the time it lasted: `I = I + e * dt`. It is a running memory of how long you have been wrong and by how much. Why that helps is the key insight. Proportional control cannot produce output at zero error.

lessons.t: Ki and the Meaning of Time
lessons.g: Apply the integral gain and reason about its units.
lessons.s: The integral contribution to the command is `Ki * I`. Because `I` carries a factor of seconds, `Ki` has units of command per error per second. A `Ki` of 0.01 on a duty and rpm system means a constant error of 1 rpm adds 0.01 duty every second. That framing tells you how to pick a first value.

lessons.g: Prove that a PI loop drives the steady state error to zero.
lessons.s: Give the loop an integral term and the droop disappears. Not shrinks: disappears. As long as any error remains, the accumulator keeps growing, the command keeps rising, and the only place the system can rest is exactly at the setpoint.

lessons.g: Show that too much Ki produces a slow, growing oscillation.
lessons.s: The integral is a lagging term. It reacts to the past, so its correction always arrives late. Push `Ki` too high and the accumulator overshoots the amount of command actually needed, the plant sails past the setpoint, and the accumulator has to unwind before the loop can come back.

lessons.t: The Accumulator That Would Not Stop
lessons.g: Reproduce integral windup by driving the loop against a saturated actuator.
lessons.s: Ask a motor for 400 rpm when it can only do 180. The error never closes, so the accumulator grows every single sample, forever. The command is already at 1.0 duty and the extra accumulation does nothing except pile up. Then you lower the setpoint to something reachable.

lessons.g: Detect windup at runtime by comparing the requested command with the delivered one.
lessons.s: You cannot fix windup you cannot see. The detector is simple: keep both the raw command and the clamped command, and flag the sample whenever they differ. That flag is worth logging on real hardware, and the number it produces is meant to land between the extremes.

lessons.g: Bound the integral so it cannot grow past what the actuator can use.
lessons.s: The crudest working fix is an **integral clamp**. Decide the maximum contribution the integral is allowed to make, usually the full actuator range, and limit the accumulator to that. The clamp is expressed in accumulator units, so it is `limit / Ki`.

lessons.g: Handle setpoint changes and controller re-enable without a jump in the command.
lessons.s: Two moments break naive PID code. The first is a large setpoint step, where the accumulated history belongs to a target that no longer exists. The second is switching from manual to automatic, where the integral is stale or zero and the command jumps.

lessons.g: Assemble a PI class with output limits, integral clamp and reset.
lessons.s: Everything from this chapter belongs in one class: gains, accumulator, output limits, a clamp sized from those limits, and a reset that preloads. This is the controller that runs most of the world.

lessons.g: Compute the derivative of the error from consecutive samples.
lessons.s: The **derivative term** looks at how fast the error is changing: `D = (e - e_prev) / dt`. It is the only part of a PID that knows about the future, and it knows it the cheap way, by assuming the current trend continues.

lessons.g: Use Kd to cut the overshoot of a PI loop on a delayed plant.
lessons.s: A PI loop on a plant with delay overshoots because both of its terms react to error that already exists. The derivative reacts to error that is about to stop existing, so it pulls the command down while the plant is still approaching.

lessons.g: Show that the derivative term multiplies sensor noise by 1 over dt.
lessons.s: An encoder gives you counts, and a count either arrived or it did not. At a 5 ms loop that quantisation looks like noise of a few rpm bouncing around the true value. The proportional term sees a few rpm. The derivative sees a few rpm divided by 0.005, which is hundreds.

lessons.g: Apply a first order low pass filter to the derivative and pick its cutoff.
lessons.s: Nobody ships a raw derivative. The standard fix is a first order low pass on the D term: `d_filtered = d_filtered + alpha * (d_raw - d_filtered)`, where `alpha = dt / (tau_f + dt)`. Choosing `tau_f` is a trade. Too small and the noise survives.

lessons.g: Take the derivative of the measurement instead of the error and kill the derivative kick.
lessons.s: When you change the setpoint by 50 rpm in one sample, the error jumps 50 in one sample, and the raw derivative reports 2500 rpm per second of change that the plant never experienced. `Kd` multiplies that spike and the motor gets a violent kick.

lessons.g: Assemble the full PID sum with derivative on measurement and a filter.
lessons.s: The full parallel form is `u = Kp*e + Ki*integral(e) + Kd*d`, where `d` is the filtered derivative of the measurement, negated. Three terms answering three questions: where am I now, where have I been, where am I heading.

lessons.g: Apply setpoint weighting on the proportional term to soften step responses.
lessons.s: Derivative on measurement removed the D kick, but the P term still jumps on a setpoint step. Setpoint weighting softens it: use `Kp * (b * setpoint - measured)` with `b` between 0 and 1. With `b = 1` you have classic PID.

lessons.t: Reading a Response Without a Plot
lessons.g: Classify a response as sluggish, good or ringing from its numbers alone.
lessons.s: On a robot you often have a serial log and no plotting tool. Three numbers still tell you what to change: overshoot, number of oscillations before settling, and steady state error. High overshoot with several swings means too much `Kp` or too little `Kd`. A slow crawl to target with no overshoot means too little `Kp`.

lessons.g: Deliver a production shaped PID class with filter, weighting, limits and reset.
lessons.s: This class is the tool for the rest of the course. It holds gains, a derivative filter time, a setpoint weight, output limits and an integral it can clamp. It takes `dt` per call. It has a `reset` that preloads. Write it once, well, and stop rewriting PID in every project.

lessons.g: Follow a manual tuning procedure that converges instead of wandering.
lessons.s: Manual tuning works when you change one thing at a time and in the right order. Set `Ki` and `Kd` to zero. Raise `Kp` until the response is fast and slightly oscillatory, then back off by about a third. Add `Ki` until the offset closes in an acceptable time, no faster.

lessons.g: Measure the ultimate gain and the ultimate period of a plant.
lessons.s: Ziegler-Nichols starts by pushing the loop to the point of sustained oscillation with proportional control only. The gain that produces a steady, non growing swing is the **ultimate gain** `Ku`. The time between two peaks of that swing is the **ultimate period** `Tu`. On hardware this is a real risk.

lessons.g: Apply the Ziegler-Nichols closed loop rules to turn Ku and Tu into gains.
lessons.s: With `Ku` and `Tu` in hand the classic table gives you gains directly. For a PID: `Kp = 0.6*Ku`, `Ti = 0.5*Tu`, `Td = 0.125*Tu`, which converts to `Ki = Kp/Ti` and `Kd = Kp*Td`. For PI: `Kp = 0.45*Ku`, `Ti = Tu/1.2`. The result is aggressive.

lessons.g: Extract dead time and time constant from an open loop step and tune from them.
lessons.s: The open loop Ziegler-Nichols method never destabilises the machine. You step the command, log the response, and read two numbers off the curve: the **dead time** `L` before anything moves, and the **time constant** `T` of the rise.

lessons.g: Use the no overshoot and low overshoot variants when 25 percent is unacceptable.
lessons.s: Quarter amplitude decay is a choice, not a law. Pessen and others published variants of the same table that trade speed for calm. The **some overshoot** rule uses `Kp = 0.33*Ku`, `Ti = 0.5*Tu`, `Td = 0.33*Tu`. The **no overshoot** rule uses `Kp = 0.2*Ku`, `Ti = 0.5*Tu`, `Td = 0.33*Tu`.

lessons.t: Two Ways to Write the Same Controller
lessons.g: Convert between parallel gains and standard form times without changing behaviour.
lessons.s: Parallel form uses `Kp`, `Ki`, `Kd`. Standard form uses `Kp`, `Ti`, `Td`, with `Ki = Kp/Ti` and `Kd = Kp*Td`.
