lessons.g: Produce a clean part mask by calibrating the color gate from a sample instead of guessing.
lessons.s: The color gate for the cell should be measured, not typed. Point the camera at one part, take a small central patch, convert to HSV, and read the median hue and saturation.

lessons.g: Turn each part contour into a grasp position in millimetres and a wrist angle in degrees.
lessons.s: A grasp is a position and an angle. The position is the contour centroid from moments, pushed through the workspace homography with `cv2.perspectiveTransform` so it lands in table millimetres instead of pixels.

lessons.g: Keep identity across frames by pairing tracked boxes with new detections and predicting with a Kalman filter.
lessons.s: Detections have no memory. Frame to frame, part number two might become part number one simply because the contour list came back in a different order, and an arm following that will change target mid reach. Identity comes from association.

lessons.g: Decide when a neural network earns its place in a robot pipeline, and run one through cv2.dnn when it does.
lessons.s: The honest rule is about **variability**, not about accuracy. Classical vision wins when you control the scene: fixed camera, known lighting, parts of known colors and shapes on a known plane. It runs in milliseconds, it needs no dataset, its failures are explainable, and it never invents a class.

lessons.g: Assemble the full vision loop with explicit states, health checks and a safe output when perception fails.
lessons.s: The last piece is the state machine around the pipeline, and it is what separates a demo from something that runs a night shift. The node has four states. **CALIBRATING** while it looks for the four workspace markers. **RUNNING** while the homography is valid and detections are flowing.

lessons.g: Build a 2D occupancy grid in pure Python and read the value of any cell.
lessons.s: A planner never sees the world. It sees a **grid**: a rectangular array of cells where each cell holds one number saying whether the robot can be there. On a TurtleBot 4 the RPLIDAR A1 sweeps the room at 10 Hz and the mapping node turns those returns into cells of 5 cm on a side.

lessons.g: Convert a metric pose in meters into grid indices using resolution and map origin.
lessons.s: The robot lives in meters, the grid lives in cells, and something has to translate. Three numbers do it: the **resolution** in meters per cell, and the **origin**, the world coordinate of the lower left corner of cell (0, 0). A standard map from a ROS mapping node ships exactly these three values in its metadata.

lessons.g: Guard every cell access with a bounds test and a single free space predicate.
lessons.s: A grid has edges and a robot near them will ask about cells that do not exist. In Python that is worse than a crash: `grid[y][-1]` quietly returns the last column.

lessons.g: Generate the free neighbors of a cell under 4 connectivity and 8 connectivity.
lessons.s: A search moves from a cell to its neighbors, so the neighbor function decides the shape of every path you will ever produce. Two choices dominate. **4 connectivity** allows north, south, east and west. **8 connectivity** adds the four diagonals.

lessons.g: Render a grid, a robot pose and a goal as ASCII so you can debug a planner by eye.
lessons.s: You will spend more time looking at maps than writing planners, and you cannot look at a list of lists. Before writing a single line of search code, build a renderer. One character per cell: `.` for free, `#` for occupied, `R` for the robot, `G` for the goal, `o` for a path cell. The catch is the vertical axis.

lessons.g: Represent map knowledge as an occupancy probability per cell instead of a binary flag.
lessons.s: A binary map lies. The RPLIDAR A1 on a TurtleBot has a range accuracy of about 2 cm and it will happily return a spurious hit off a glass door, a chair leg seen edge on, or dust. If one bad beam is enough to permanently stamp `1` into a cell, your map fills with ghost obstacles within a minute of driving.

lessons.g: Convert occupancy probability to log odds so that sensor updates become additions.
lessons.s: Updating a probability with Bayes rule means multiplying and normalizing, once per cell, per beam, per scan. A 360 point scan at 10 Hz touching 200 cells per beam is 720000 updates a second. Multiplications of small floats also drift toward zero and lose precision. The standard fix is **log odds**.

lessons.g: Apply the inverse sensor model, adding a fixed hit or miss increment in log odds.
lessons.s: The **inverse sensor model** answers one question: given that a beam reported an obstacle at 2.3 meters, what does that say about each cell the beam crossed? For a lidar the answer is blunt and it works. Every cell the beam passed through is evidence of free space, a **miss**.

lessons.g: List every grid cell a straight beam crosses using integer Bresenham stepping.
lessons.s: To apply the inverse sensor model you first need the cells the beam touched. Stepping along the ray in small floating point increments and rounding works until it does not: too large a step skips cells and punches holes through walls, too small a step burns time and visits the same cell repeatedly.

lessons.g: Integrate a single lidar return into the log odds map from a known robot pose.
lessons.s: Now the pieces join. A lidar return arrives as a pair: an angle in the sensor frame and a range in meters. The robot pose is `(x, y, theta)` in the world.

lessons.g: Integrate a full lidar scan by iterating beams with the correct angle increment.
lessons.s: A scan message is an array of ranges plus three numbers: `angle_min`, `angle_increment` and the range limits. Beam `i` sits at `angle_min + i * angle_increment`. The RPLIDAR A1 gives roughly 360 beams per revolution, so the increment is about one degree in radians. Two filters belong in this loop and nowhere else.

lessons.g: Clamp log odds to a fixed band so the map stays correctable when the world changes.
lessons.s: Leave the updates unclamped and drive down a corridor for two minutes. A wall cell hit six hundred times reaches a log odds of 500, which is a probability of one to within machine precision. Then somebody opens a door.

lessons.g: Threshold a log odds map into the trinary map the planner consumes.
lessons.s: The planner does not want probabilities, it wants a decision per cell. Converting the log odds map into a **trinary map** with values `0` free, `-1` unknown and `100` occupied is the interface between mapping and planning, and it is where you set your appetite for risk.

lessons.g: Find frontier cells, the free cells adjacent to unknown space, for autonomous exploration.
lessons.s: A robot that maps a building on its own needs somewhere to go, and the answer is a **frontier**: a free cell that touches at least one unknown cell. Every frontier is a place where driving forward will produce new information.

lessons.t: Shrinking the Robot to a Point
lessons.g: Explain configuration space and convert a footprint radius into an inflation radius in cells.
lessons.s: Everything so far pretended the robot is a point. It is not. A TurtleBot 4 is a disc about 34 cm across, so its center cannot come closer than 17 cm to any wall. Checking the whole footprint against the map at every one of the two hundred thousand cells a search expands is far too slow.

lessons.g: Dilate a binary obstacle map by a radius in cells to build the C space map.
lessons.s: The direct dilation is honest and easy to get right: for every occupied cell, mark every cell within the radius as occupied in a **new** grid. The word "new" is the whole lesson.

lessons.t: How Far to the Nearest Wall
lessons.g: Compute a distance transform giving each free cell its distance to the closest obstacle.
lessons.s: Inflation throws information away. It tells you a cell is within 4 cells of a wall but not whether it is at 1 cell or at 3.9. A **distance transform** keeps that number for every cell, and once you have it, inflation at any radius is a single comparison and the cost function of the next lesson is free.

lessons.g: Turn the distance field into a continuous cost that decays away from obstacles.
lessons.s: A binary C space map gives the planner only two answers, and it will therefore route the robot along a path that shaves the inflation boundary by one cell, because that path is a few centimeters shorter and nothing in the map says it is worse.

lessons.g: Classify a cost value into the lethal, inscribed, circumscribed and free bands.
lessons.s: Production costmaps use one byte per cell and reserve specific values, and knowing the convention saves you from reinventing it badly.

lessons.g: Combine a static map layer and a live obstacle layer into one costmap by taking the maximum.
lessons.s: A real costmap is not one grid, it is a stack. The **static layer** holds the map built by SLAM or loaded from disk: walls, pillars, the shape of the building. The **obstacle layer** holds what the sensors see right now: a person, a pallet, an open door that used to be closed.

lessons.t: When the Robot Is Not a Circle
lessons.g: Test a polygon footprint against the costmap at a given position and orientation, outline and interior.
lessons.s: A rectangular robot in a corridor it barely fits through can only pass if it is aligned with the corridor. No inflation radius can express that, because inflation has no notion of heading. For those robots the planner has to check the actual footprint.

lessons.g: Estimate the size of a 3D configuration space in x, y and theta and explain why grids stop scaling.
lessons.s: Once orientation matters, the configuration space is not two dimensional any more. A pose is `(x, y, theta)` and the C space is a stack of 2D grids, one per orientation bin. With a 400 by 400 map and 72 orientation bins at 5 degrees each, that is 11.5 million states.

lessons.t: Proving the C Space Is Right
lessons.g: Verify that a point path on the inflated map corresponds to a collision free footprint path.
lessons.s: Inflation is a claim, and claims get tested. The claim is that a path of single cells through the inflated map never puts the real robot in contact with the real map. Write the checker once and run it against every planner you build for the rest of the course.

lessons.t: The Map Was a Graph All Along
lessons.g: Express a grid as an explicit graph of nodes and weighted edges and know when not to.
lessons.s: Every search algorithm in this chapter is written for graphs, not grids. A grid is just a graph with a very regular structure: each free cell is a node, each legal move is an edge, and the edge weight is the move cost.

lessons.g: Implement breadth first search with a deque and a visited set to reach a goal cell.
lessons.s: **Breadth first search** expands the frontier in rings. Start with the start cell in a FIFO queue, pop the oldest, push its unvisited neighbors, repeat. Because every cell is discovered by the shortest number of steps from the start, BFS returns a path with the minimum number of moves.

lessons.g: Reconstruct the path from the parent dictionary and return it start to goal.
lessons.s: A search does not produce a path, it produces a tree of parent pointers. Extracting the path is a walk from the goal back to the start, following parents until you hit the start whose parent is `None`, then reversing. Two guards belong in this function.

lessons.g: Implement depth first search and demonstrate why its paths are unusable on a robot.
lessons.s: Swap the queue for a stack and breadth first becomes **depth first**. One line of difference, completely different behavior: DFS charges down one branch until it dead ends, then backtracks.

lessons.t: Not Every Step Costs the Same
lessons.g: Define an edge cost that combines geometric length with the costmap value of the target cell.
lessons.s: BFS counts moves. The floor does not. A diagonal move is 1.414 times longer than a straight one, a cell near a wall is more dangerous than one in the open, and a cell on carpet may be slower than one on tile. All of that lives in one function: the **edge cost**.

lessons.g: Implement Dijkstra with a binary heap, expanding the lowest cost node first.
lessons.s: Once edges have different weights, expanding in the order cells were discovered is wrong. **Dijkstra** expands in order of cost from the start, and that requires a priority queue.

lessons.g: Run Dijkstra to exhaustion to build a cost to go field over the whole map.
lessons.s: Drop the early exit and Dijkstra stops being a path finder and becomes a field builder. Seed it at the **goal** instead of the start, keep calling `heapq.heappop` until the heap empties, and every cell now holds the exact cost of reaching the goal from there. That field is worth more than a path.

lessons.g: Instrument a planner to report expansions, heap peak and elapsed time.
lessons.s: You cannot tune a planner you do not measure. Three numbers tell you almost everything: **expansions**, the count of nodes actually popped and processed, **peak heap size**, the memory pressure, and **wall time**. Log them on every plan, in production, forever.

lessons.g: Run a bidirectional search from start and goal and stop when the frontiers touch.
lessons.s: A search from the start expands a disc of radius d. A search from the goal does the same. If the distance between them is D, the one way search expands an area proportional to D squared, while two searches meeting in the middle expand two discs of radius D over two, which is half the area.

lessons.g: Define g, h and f and state the admissibility condition a heuristic must satisfy.
lessons.s: Dijkstra expands in every direction equally because it has no idea where the goal is. Give it a hint and it stops wasting effort. Three quantities: - `g(n)`: the cost actually paid to reach n from the start. Known exactly. - `h(n)`: an **estimate** of the remaining cost from n to the goal. A guess.

lessons.g: Implement the Manhattan heuristic and know the connectivity it is admissible for.
lessons.s: On a 4 connected grid the robot can only move along axes, so the true minimum number of moves between two cells with no obstacles is `abs(dx) + abs(dy)`. That is the **Manhattan distance** and on a 4 connected grid it is not just admissible, it is exact in open space, which makes it the best possible heuristic there.

lessons.t: The Straight Line Nobody Can Walk
lessons.g: Implement the Euclidean heuristic and explain why it is safe but weak on a grid.
lessons.s: The **Euclidean** heuristic is the straight line distance, `sqrt(dx squared + dy squared)`. No path on any grid can be shorter than the straight line, so it is admissible under every connectivity you will ever use.

lessons.g: Implement the octile heuristic, the exact free space cost on an 8 connected grid.
lessons.s: On an 8 connected grid with straight cost 1 and diagonal cost 1.414, the cheapest obstacle free route between two cells is: take diagonals for as long as both axes still need progress, then go straight for the remainder.

lessons.g: Implement A star with an open heap, a closed set and a pluggable heuristic.
lessons.s: A star is Dijkstra with `f` as the priority. The structure is identical: an open heap, a `g` dictionary, a parent dictionary, and a closed set of nodes already finalized. The only new line is that `heapq.heappush` receives `(g + h(node), node)` instead of `(g, node)`. The closed set earns its keep here.

lessons.g: Show experimentally that an inadmissible heuristic returns a suboptimal path.
lessons.s: Theory says an overestimating heuristic breaks optimality. Watching it happen is what makes you careful. Take the same map you planned on in the previous lesson, plan with octile, then plan again with octile multiplied by three, and compare the two path costs and the two expansion counts.

lessons.g: Use weighted A star with a known bound so the suboptimality is a decision, not an accident.
lessons.s: The previous lesson framed an inflated heuristic as a bug. It is also a tool, provided you know the price. **Weighted A star** uses `f = g + w * h` with `w` above 1, and it comes with a guarantee: the path it returns costs at most `w` times the optimal.

lessons.g: Add a deterministic tie breaker to the open list to cut expansions on open maps.
lessons.s: On an open map, huge numbers of cells share the same `f` value, because many routes of equal length reach the same place. A star then expands all of them in whatever order the heap happens to produce, which is a wide fan of wasted work, and the path it returns often looks like a staircase because it kept switching ...

lessons.g: Benchmark Dijkstra, A star and weighted A star on one map and read the table.
lessons.s: Numbers settle arguments. Run all three planners on the same map, from the same start to the same goal, and print a table of path cost, expansions and milliseconds.

lessons.t: The World Refuses to Hold Still
lessons.g: Measure the cost of replanning from scratch every cycle and state when it stops being viable.
lessons.s: The map the robot planned on was true for about one second. A door closed, a pallet moved, a person walked into the corridor. The simple response is to run A star again every time the costmap changes, and for a small map that is entirely correct and entirely fine. It stops being fine when the numbers grow.

lessons.g: Search from goal to start so that a moving robot does not invalidate the tree.
lessons.s: The first structural idea behind D star Lite is to search **backwards**, from the goal to the start. It sounds like a detail and it is the whole thing. Search forwards from the start and the tree is rooted at the robot. The robot moves one cell, the root changes, and the entire tree is meaningless.

lessons.g: Maintain g and rhs per cell and detect local inconsistency between them.
lessons.s: D star Lite stores two values per cell. `g(s)` is the cost to go currently believed and possibly stale. `rhs(s)` is the one step lookahead: the best value you get by looking at the successors right now, `rhs(s) = min over s' of ( cost(s, s') + g(s') )` with `rhs(goal)` pinned at 0.

lessons.g: Compute the two element D star Lite priority key and order the queue with it.
lessons.s: The queue in D star Lite is ordered by a pair, not a single number. For a cell s, - `k1 = min(g, rhs) + h(start, s) + km` - `k2 = min(g, rhs)` and keys compare lexicographically: `k1` first, `k2` only to break ties.

lessons.g: Implement UpdateVertex, recomputing rhs and requeueing a cell only when it is inconsistent.
lessons.s: `UpdateVertex(s)` is the workhorse and it is short. Recompute `rhs(s)` unless s is the goal. Remove any existing queue entry for s. If `g(s)` differs from `rhs(s)`, insert s with a fresh key. That is all. The removal step is where implementations diverge.

lessons.g: Implement ComputeShortestPath, popping inconsistent cells until the start is settled.
lessons.s: `ComputeShortestPath` runs until two conditions both hold: the smallest key in the queue is not smaller than the start's own key, and the start is locally consistent. Then the values along the route from the start are correct and the robot can drive.

lessons.g: Apply an edge cost change from a new sensor reading and repair only the affected region.
lessons.s: A new scan arrives and some cells changed cost. For each changed cell, update the map, then call `UpdateVertex` on that cell and on its predecessors, then run `ComputeShortestPath` again.

lessons.t: The Robot Moved, the Keys Did Not
lessons.g: Maintain the km key modifier so old queue keys stay comparable after the robot moves.
lessons.s: Every key contains `h(start, s)`, and the start is the robot, which moves. When the robot advances one meter, every key already sitting in the queue was computed against the old position and is now wrong. Recomputing all of them each cycle would undo the entire point of the algorithm. The fix is elegant.

lessons.g: Decide between incremental repair and a full replan from the change size and map size.
lessons.s: D star Lite is not automatically the right answer. It wins when the map is large, the changes are small and local, and the goal is fixed. It loses in three cases worth naming. If the **goal changes**, the entire tree is rooted at the wrong place and there is nothing to repair. Rebuild.

lessons.g: Explain why sampling replaces enumeration above three dimensions and what it gives up.
lessons.s: Chapter two ended with the number that kills grid search: a 6 degree of freedom arm discretized into 100 bins per joint has 10 to the 12 states. You cannot allocate it, let alone search it. And yet a robot arm plans a motion in 50 ms every day. The trick is to stop describing the free space and start **sampling** it.

lessons.g: Write a point collision check against a costmap that respects the inflation radius.
lessons.s: A sampling planner calls the collision checker far more than anything else, typically 90 percent of its runtime. Everything else you optimize is noise next to this function. For a planar robot on a costmap, the check is what chapter two prepared: convert the continuous point to a cell and look up the cost.

lessons.g: Implement steering, extending from a node toward a sample by at most one step length.
lessons.s: A sample is a direction, not a destination. If you connected the tree directly to every sample, the tree would make huge jumps across the space and every edge would need a long expensive collision check, most of which fail.

lessons.g: Check a straight segment for collisions by sampling it at a resolution below one cell.
lessons.s: Both endpoints of an edge can be free while the segment passes straight through a pillar. Checking only endpoints is the second classic mistake of sampling planners, right after forgetting the bounds check. The pragmatic method is discrete sampling along the segment.

lessons.g: Implement the RRT main loop: sample, find the nearest node, steer, check and attach.
lessons.s: RRT is five steps in a loop. Sample a random configuration. Find the **nearest** node already in the tree. Steer from it toward the sample by one step. If the resulting segment is collision free, add the new point as a node with that nearest node as its parent. Repeat.

lessons.g: Add goal biasing and a goal region test so the tree terminates instead of wandering.
lessons.s: Plain RRT explores beautifully and arrives at the goal by accident. Two additions turn it into a planner. **Goal biasing**: with probability around 5 to 10 percent, use the goal itself as the sample instead of a random one. The tree then grows toward the goal whenever it can while still exploring the rest of the time.

lessons.g: Implement the RRT star parent selection, attaching a new node to the cheapest reachable neighbor.
lessons.s: RRT returns a valid path and there is no reason to believe it is a good one. It attaches every new node to the **nearest** existing node, which is fast and arbitrary. RRT star fixes it with two changes, and this lesson is the first. Keep a `cost` per node, the total path length from the root.

lessons.g: Implement RRT star rewiring so existing nodes adopt the new node when it lowers their cost.
lessons.s: The second half of RRT star looks the other way. Having attached the new node, check every neighbor within the radius and ask: would routing that neighbor through the new node give it a lower cost? If yes and the segment is free, change its parent. This is what makes RRT star asymptotically optimal.

lessons.g: Compute the RRT star connection radius that shrinks with node count, and sample an informed ellipse.
lessons.s: The radius in RRT star is not a constant. Optimality requires it to shrink as the tree grows, following `r(n) = min(gamma * (log(n) / n) ** (1 / d), step)` where `n` is the node count and `d` the dimension.

lessons.g: Quantify the defects of a raw grid path: staircases, redundant waypoints and sharp turns.
lessons.s: The path A star returns is optimal on the grid and wrong for the vehicle. It has three specific defects and you should be able to measure each one. **Staircases.** On an 8 connected grid every heading is a multiple of 45 degrees, so a route at 20 degrees becomes a sawtooth.

lessons.t: If You Can See It, Go Straight There
lessons.g: Shortcut a path by removing waypoints whenever a direct segment is collision free.
lessons.s: The cheapest and most effective smoother is **line of sight shortcutting**. Start at waypoint 0, then look as far ahead as possible: find the furthest waypoint j such that the straight segment from i to j is collision free, keep j, and continue from there. A staircase path across an open room collapses to two points.

lessons.g: Smooth a path with gradient descent balancing fidelity to the original against curvature.
lessons.s: Shortcutting removes waypoints. **Gradient descent smoothing** moves them. Each interior point is pushed by two competing terms: - a data term pulling it back toward its original position, weighted `alpha` - a smoothing term pulling it toward the average of its two neighbors, weighted `beta` Iterate until the total ...

lessons.g: Compute path curvature and check it against the vehicle minimum turning radius.
lessons.s: A differential drive can turn in place, so any path is geometrically drivable, just slowly and with a jerk at every corner. An Ackermann vehicle cannot.

lessons.g: Resample a path at uniform spacing so the controller gets evenly distributed waypoints.
lessons.s: After shortcutting, a path has two waypoints twelve meters apart. After a grid search it has waypoints every five centimeters. Neither is what a controller wants. Pure pursuit needs to find a lookahead point on the path, and searching a path with wildly uneven spacing is both slower and less accurate.

lessons.g: Build an attractive potential field and derive the force vector toward the goal.
lessons.s: Potential fields are a completely different way to think about navigation. Instead of searching for a route, define a scalar field over the space and let the robot roll downhill. The goal is a valley and every obstacle is a hill.

lessons.g: Build a repulsive potential with a finite influence radius and sum the obstacle forces.
lessons.s: Each obstacle produces a repulsive force that is strong up close and exactly zero beyond an influence radius `rho_0`, typically one to two meters.

lessons.t: The Valley That Is Not the Goal
lessons.g: Follow the total gradient and reproduce a local minimum where the robot stalls short of the goal.
lessons.s: Sum the attractive and repulsive forces, step in that direction, repeat. On an open map the robot glides to the goal and the method looks wonderful.

lessons.g: Detect a stall in a potential field and apply an escape strategy, then state the honest verdict.
lessons.s: You can patch local minima and you cannot cure them. Three patches are worth knowing. **Random walk.** Detect the stall, apply random displacements for a second or two, resume. Cheap, sometimes works, and gives no guarantee: a deep well swallows the random walk too.

lessons.g: Compute the dynamic window of reachable velocities from current speed and acceleration limits.
lessons.s: A global path says where to go. The local planner decides what to send the motors, and it works in **velocity space** rather than position space. For a differential drive the command is a pair `(v, w)`: linear and angular velocity. Not every pair is available. Three constraints intersect.

lessons.g: Forward simulate a differential drive trajectory for a constant velocity pair.
lessons.s: To judge a velocity pair you have to see where it leads. Forward simulate the unicycle model for a horizon of one to three seconds in small steps: - `theta += w * dt` - `x += v * cos(theta) * dt` - `y += v * sin(theta) * dt` With constant `v` and `w` the exact trajectory is a circular arc of radius `v / w`, and a ...

lessons.g: Score a candidate trajectory by heading alignment, obstacle clearance and forward speed.
lessons.s: Every candidate arc gets one number, a weighted sum of three normalized terms. **Heading**: how well the trajectory endpoint points at the goal or the next path point. Usually `1 - abs(angle_error) / pi` so that 1 is perfect.

lessons.g: Implement the full dynamic window approach loop selecting the best velocity command.
lessons.s: Now the loop. Compute the dynamic window. Sample it on a grid, typically 10 by 20 pairs, which is 200 candidates. Simulate each, compute its clearance, score it, keep the best. Send that `(v, w)` to the motors and repeat next cycle.

lessons.g: Compute the distance from a simulated trajectory to the nearest obstacle in the local costmap.
lessons.s: The clearance term needs a real number and it must be honest. For each pose on the trajectory, look up the distance to the nearest obstacle, which is exactly the distance transform from chapter two applied to the local costmap. The clearance of the trajectory is the **minimum** over all its poses.

lessons.g: Find the pure pursuit lookahead point where the path crosses a circle around the robot.
lessons.s: Pure pursuit is the simplest path tracker that works, and it has been steering vehicles since the 1980s. Draw a circle of radius `L`, the lookahead distance, around the robot. Find where the path crosses it ahead of the robot. Drive an arc to that point. Repeat. Finding the crossing has a robust recipe.

lessons.g: Convert a lookahead point into a curvature and a differential drive velocity command.
lessons.s: Transform the lookahead point into the robot frame, giving `(x_r, y_r)` with x forward and y to the left. The unique arc from the robot through that point has curvature `kappa = 2 * y_r / L squared` That is the whole of pure pursuit. The lateral offset of the target divided by the square of the lookahead, times two.

lessons.g: Scale the lookahead distance with velocity and add the approach and arrival behavior.
lessons.s: A fixed lookahead is wrong at one of the two ends of the speed range. Short `L` at speed makes the robot oscillate, chasing a point it reaches before it can settle. Long `L` at low speed makes it cut every corner and it will not turn into a doorway at all.

lessons.g: Implement the safety and recovery layer: emergency stop, oscillation detection and recovery behaviors.
lessons.s: Under the planner and the controller sits a layer that exists to stop the robot. It is the simplest code in the stack and the only code whose absence is dangerous. **Emergency stop.** If any obstacle is inside the stopping distance for the current speed, zero the command immediately, before any planning logic runs.

lessons.g: Build a particle set and propagate it through the odometry motion model with noise.
lessons.s: Every planner so far assumed the robot knows where it is. It does not. Wheel odometry on a differential drive accumulates error at roughly one to three percent of distance travelled, so after 50 meters the estimate can be off by more than a meter, which is more than the width of a doorway.

lessons.g: Weight particles with a likelihood field measurement model built from the map.
lessons.s: The correction step asks each particle: if the robot were here, how well would the actual lidar scan match the map? Particles that explain the scan gain weight, particles that do not lose it. Ray casting the full scan per particle is the exact method and it is far too slow at 1000 particles times 360 beams.

lessons.g: Implement low variance resampling and extract the pose estimate from the weighted set.
lessons.s: After weighting, most particles have negligible weight and are wasting compute. **Resampling** draws a new set of the same size, with replacement, in proportion to the weights. The naive method draws N independent random numbers.

lessons.g: Explain the SLAM chicken and egg problem and build a pose graph with loop closure candidates.
lessons.s: Localization needs a map. Mapping needs a pose. **SLAM** solves both at once, and the reason it is hard is that the errors are coupled: a wrong pose writes a wall in the wrong place, and that wrong wall then corrupts every later pose estimate. Modern SLAM is **graph based**. Nodes are robot poses over time.

lessons.g: Assemble the global planner module: inflate the map, run A star, shortcut and resample.
lessons.s: Time to build the stack. The global layer is one function with a clear contract: given a costmap, a start pose and a goal pose in world coordinates, return a list of world waypoints that a controller can follow, or an explicit failure. The pipeline is everything from chapters two, three, four and seven in order.

lessons.g: Assemble the local controller: pure pursuit for steering, the dynamic window for feasibility and safety.
lessons.s: The local layer runs at 10 to 20 Hz and its contract is equally clear: given the current pose, the current velocity, the global path and the local costmap, return a `(v, w)` command. Order matters. First find the lookahead point on the global path, which gives the desired direction.

lessons.g: Run the full navigation stack: localize, plan, control, replan on change and terminate honestly.
lessons.s: The last piece is the loop that ties the layers together and decides when to give up. Each cycle: read odometry and the scan, run the particle filter to get the pose, update the local costmap, and check whether the global path is still valid.

lessons.g: Start a ROS 2 context from Python, create a node and log a line from it.
lessons.s: ROS 2 is not an operating system and not a library you import into one big program. It is middleware: a set of rules and libraries that let many small programs on the same robot talk to each other. Each of those programs is a **node**.

lessons.g: Keep a node alive with rclpy.spin and exit cleanly on Ctrl-C.
lessons.s: A node that reaches the end of `main` dies immediately. That is fine for a one shot script, useless for a laser driver that has to run for hours. To stay alive a node has to be handed to an **executor**, and the simplest way to do that is `rclpy.spin(node)`. Spin is a blocking loop.

lessons.g: Declare a Python node as an executable of an ament_python package in setup.py.
lessons.s: ROS 2 code does not live in loose scripts. It lives in **packages**. A Python package built with `ament_python` has a fixed shape: a `package.xml` with metadata and dependencies, a `setup.py` that installs it, a folder with the same name as the package holding the modules, and a `resource/` marker file so the package ...

lessons.g: Give a node a namespace and read back its name, namespace and fully qualified name.
lessons.s: Every node has a name and a namespace. The name identifies it in the graph, the namespace groups it with others. A node called `laser` in namespace `/front` is `/front/laser` fully qualified, and that string has to be unique on the whole network.

lessons.g: Query the ROS graph from inside a node to list the other nodes and topics that exist.
lessons.s: The **graph** is the live picture of who is running and who talks to whom. Nodes are the vertices, topics and services are the edges. You do not build the graph, DDS discovery builds it as nodes appear and vanish, and every node can read it.

lessons.g: Write a node as a subclass of rclpy.node.Node instead of a loose script.
lessons.s: The script style from chapter 0 does not scale. As soon as a node owns publishers, timers and state, you need somewhere to keep them, and that place is a class. Every real ROS 2 Python node subclasses `rclpy.node.Node` and calls `super().__init__('node_name')` in its constructor. Inside the class, `self` is the node.

lessons.g: Run work periodically inside a node with create_timer.
lessons.s: Robots run on a clock. A motor driver has to send a velocity command every 20 ms or the wheels stop, a battery monitor checks the pack once a second. In ROS 2 you never write `while True` with a `sleep` inside a node, because that blocks the executor and every other callback starves. You create a **timer**.

lessons.g: Choose log severities and throttle a message that would otherwise flood the console.
lessons.s: Logging is the only window you have into a robot that is driving away from you. ROS 2 gives five severities: debug, info, warn, error and fatal.

lessons.g: Use spin_once with a timeout to drive a node from your own loop.
lessons.s: `rclpy.spin` never returns, which is wrong for programs that have their own main loop. A test harness, a GUI or a script that has to talk to a piece of hardware in a blocking way needs to give the executor a slice of time and take control back. That is `rclpy.spin_once(node, timeout_sec=...)`.

lessons.g: Shut a node down without leaving DDS resources or a half open context behind.
lessons.s: Shutdown order matters. The node owns DDS entities: publishers, subscriptions, timers, service servers. `destroy_node()` releases them. `rclpy.shutdown()` tears down the context that those entities were created in. Call shutdown first and destroy after, and you get warnings about operating on an invalid context.

lessons.g: Run two nodes in a single process using an explicit executor.
lessons.s: `rclpy.spin(node)` is a shortcut that builds a `SingleThreadedExecutor`, adds one node and spins it. Once you want two nodes in one process, you build the executor yourself. Why would you? Because processes are expensive on an embedded board.

lessons.g: Use a MultiThreadedExecutor so a slow callback does not block the rest of the node.
lessons.s: A single threaded executor runs one callback at a time. If your image processing callback takes 300 ms, the 50 Hz safety timer that watches the bumper does not run for 300 ms. On a moving robot that is fifteen centimetres of blindness.

lessons.g: Separate callbacks with MutuallyExclusiveCallbackGroup and ReentrantCallbackGroup.
lessons.s: A **callback group** is a promise about concurrency. Every callback belongs to one, and the executor honours the group's rule. `MutuallyExclusiveCallbackGroup` means no two callbacks in that group ever run at the same time. That is the default group of a node, and it is why single threaded code is safe by accident.

lessons.g: Read time from the node clock and measure an elapsed Duration.
lessons.s: Never call `time.time()` inside a ROS 2 node. The node has its own clock, `self.get_clock()`, and it is the one that follows simulation time. When you launch with `use_sim_time` true, that clock is driven by the `/clock` topic that Gazebo publishes, so your node slows down and speeds up with the simulator.

lessons.g: Create a publisher and send a std_msgs/String message onto a topic.
lessons.s: A **topic** is a named stream of messages. Publishers write to it, subscribers read from it, and neither knows the other exists. That anonymity is the reason you can swap a real laser for a simulated one without touching the node that consumes the scan.

lessons.g: Publish at a fixed rate by driving the publisher from a timer.
lessons.s: Publishing once from the constructor is almost always a bug. At that moment no subscriber has discovered you yet, so the message goes nowhere. Sensor data, odometry and velocity commands are streams, and streams come from timers.

lessons.g: Subscribe to a topic and react to every message in a callback.
lessons.s: `self.create_subscription(msg_type, topic, callback, qos_depth)` is the mirror of a publisher. The callback receives one argument, the message, already deserialised into a Python object. It runs on the executor, so a slow callback delays everything else in its group. The type has to match.

lessons.g: Publish a geometry_msgs/Twist on cmd_vel to drive a differential base.
lessons.s: `cmd_vel` is the most standardised topic in ROS 2. Nearly every mobile base, from a TurtleBot 4 to a custom rover with RoboClaw drivers, subscribes to `geometry_msgs/Twist` on that name. If your node publishes a correct Twist, it can drive hardware it has never seen.

lessons.g: Read a sensor_msgs/LaserScan and extract the distance straight ahead.
lessons.s: A `sensor_msgs/LaserScan` is not a list of points, it is a polar sweep. The fields that matter are `angle_min`, `angle_max`, `angle_increment` and the `ranges` array. Range index `i` corresponds to angle `angle_min + i * angle_increment`, measured in the frame named in `header.frame_id`.

lessons.g: Fill a std_msgs/Header with a frame id and a timestamp from the node clock.
lessons.s: Any message that describes something physical carries a `std_msgs/Header` with two fields you must fill: `stamp` and `frame_id`. Without them the data is unusable. A distance of 1.2 m means nothing until you know it was measured at time t from the frame `laser_link`.

lessons.g: Define a custom .msg interface and declare the generator in CMakeLists.
lessons.s: When no existing message fits, you define your own. Interface definitions live in a package of their own, built with `ament_cmake` even if all your nodes are Python, because the code generator `rosidl` runs from CMake. A `.msg` file is a list of `type name` lines.

lessons.g: Inspect a live topic with the ros2 topic commands and reproduce their output from a node.
lessons.s: Before you write a subscriber, interrogate the topic. `ros2 topic list` shows what exists. `ros2 topic info /scan --verbose` shows the type and every publisher and subscriber with its QoS. `ros2 topic echo /scan` prints messages as YAML.

lessons.g: Understand topic remapping and write nodes with relative topic names so they can be moved.
lessons.s: Hardcoding `/scan` with a leading slash pins a node to one absolute name forever. Writing `scan` without the slash makes it **relative**, so it resolves under the node namespace: the same node launched in `/front` publishes `/front/scan` and in `/rear` publishes `/rear/scan`.

lessons.g: Build a colcon workspace and understand what src, build, install and log hold.
lessons.s: A **workspace** is a folder with a `src/` inside it and nothing else that you write by hand. You clone or create packages under `src`, run `colcon build` from the workspace root, and colcon creates three siblings: `build/` with intermediate artefacts, `install/` with what actually gets used, and `log/` with the record ...

lessons.g: Declare a package and its runtime dependencies in package.xml.
lessons.s: `package.xml` is the manifest every ROS 2 package must have. It gives the package a name, a version, a licence, a maintainer, and the list of packages it needs. Tools read it: `rosdep` to install system dependencies, `colcon` to order the build, the package index to find the package at runtime.

lessons.g: Expose several nodes of one package as separate ros2 run executables.
lessons.s: One package normally holds several nodes. The laser driver, the odometry publisher and the safety filter of the same robot belong together, and each one needs its own entry point. Every line in `console_scripts` is independent, so a package with three nodes has three lines pointing at three modules.

lessons.g: Resolve system and ROS dependencies of a workspace with rosdep.
lessons.s: `rosdep` reads every `package.xml` in your workspace and installs what is missing. It maps a ROS key such as `sensor_msgs` or a system key such as `python3-serial` to the actual apt package for your distribution. This is why a correct manifest matters beyond documentation: it is executable.

lessons.g: Explain overlays and sourcing order, and detect which workspace a node was loaded from.
lessons.s: Sourcing `/opt/ros/humble/setup.bash` gives you the **underlay**, the distribution. Sourcing `~/nebula_ws/install/setup.bash` afterwards adds your **overlay** on top. If a package name exists in both, the overlay wins. That is how you patch a system package without touching the system. Order is not symmetric.

lessons.g: Map each ros2 command line verb to the graph concept it inspects.
lessons.s: The `ros2` command is a family, and every branch of it has the same shape: `ros2`, the concept, then a verb. `ros2 node list` and `ros2 node info` cover nodes. `ros2 topic list` and `ros2 topic info` cover streams.

lessons.g: Detect a topic that has publishers but no subscribers by querying the graph counts.
lessons.s: `rqt_graph` draws the running system as a picture. It is the fastest way to see that two nodes you thought were connected are actually publishing to two different topic names, one with a typo. The picture comes from the same graph API you used in chapter 0. The counts are the useful part in code.

lessons.g: Record and replay topics with ros2 bag to debug a run that already happened.
lessons.s: A **bag** is a recording of messages with their timestamps. `ros2 bag record /scan /odom /cmd_vel` writes an sqlite3 file plus a metadata yaml. `ros2 bag record -a` records everything, which on a robot with cameras fills a disk in minutes, so name your topics.

lessons.g: Open a bag from Python with rosbag2_py and deserialise its messages.
lessons.s: Sometimes replaying is not enough and you want the numbers. `rosbag2_py` opens a bag directly. You build a `SequentialReader`, open it with a `StorageOptions` pointing at the folder and a `ConverterOptions`, then call `read_next()` until `has_next()` is false.

lessons.g: Serve a ROS 2 service and fill its response from the request.
lessons.s: A topic is a broadcast with no answer. A **service** is a request and one reply, addressed to a specific node. Use it for questions and for short commands: reset the odometry, read the firmware version, compute an inverse kinematics solution.

lessons.g: Call a service asynchronously and read the result from the future.
lessons.s: `self.create_client(srv_type, name)` builds the caller. Calls are asynchronous: `client.call_async(request)` returns a `Future` immediately, it does not block. The future is filled by the executor when the reply arrives, which means someone has to be spinning for it ever to complete.

lessons.t: Waiting for the Door to Open
lessons.g: Block until a service server is available before sending the first request.
lessons.s: Nodes start in an unpredictable order. A client created half a second before its server exists will send a request into nothing. Discovery is asynchronous, so the topic of failure here is timing, not correctness.

lessons.g: Define a custom .srv interface with request and response halves.
lessons.s: A `.srv` file lives in `srv/` inside an interface package and is split by a line of exactly three dashes. Everything above is the request, everything below is the response. The generator produces `Package.srv.Name.Request` and `.Response` classes plus the type support the middleware needs.

lessons.g: Call a service from inside a callback without blocking the executor.
lessons.s: Here is the trap. Your subscription callback needs an answer from a service. You call `spin_until_future_complete` inside it. The executor thread is already running your callback, so it cannot process the reply, so the future never completes and the node freezes with no error at all. There are two correct escapes.

lessons.g: Call and inspect a service from the command line without writing a client.
lessons.s: `ros2 service list` shows every service in the graph, including the six parameter services every node exposes automatically. `ros2 service type /add_two_ints` gives the type, and `ros2 interface show example_interfaces/srv/AddTwoInts` gives the fields.

lessons.g: Use std_srvs Trigger and SetBool for enable and disable commands.
lessons.s: Not every command needs a custom type. `std_srvs` ships three that cover most of a robot: `Empty` for a command with no arguments and no answer, `Trigger` for a command that answers `success` and `message`, and `SetBool` for an on or off switch that answers the same pair.

lessons.g: Decide between topic, service and action for a given robot interaction.
lessons.s: Three channels, three shapes of problem. A **topic** is for data that flows: sensor readings, velocity commands, state estimates. Many to many, no answer, drop tolerant.

lessons.g: Write an .action interface with its goal, result and feedback sections.
lessons.s: An **action** is the channel for work that takes time. It is built on top of topics and services: a goal service, a cancel service, a result service and two topics for feedback and status. You never touch those, `rclpy.action` hides them. An `.action` file has three sections separated by two lines of three dashes.

lessons.g: Create an ActionServer and finish a goal with succeed and a result.
lessons.s: `ActionServer(node, action_type, name, execute_callback)` registers the server. The execute callback receives a `ServerGoalHandle`, reads the request from `goal_handle.request`, does the work, and must end by calling exactly one of `goal_handle.succeed()`, `goal_handle.abort()` or `goal_handle.canceled()`, then ...

lessons.g: Publish feedback from an action server while the goal is running.
lessons.s: Feedback is what separates an action from a slow service. `goal_handle.publish_feedback(msg)` sends a `Type.Feedback()` to every client watching this goal. It is a normal topic underneath, so it is best effort in spirit: a client that misses one feedback message is not broken.

lessons.g: Send a goal from an ActionClient and receive its feedback.
lessons.s: `ActionClient(node, action_type, name)` builds the caller. `client.wait_for_server()` blocks until the server is discovered, same reasoning as with services. `client.send_goal_async(goal_msg, feedback_callback=...)` returns a future that resolves to a **goal handle**, not to the result.

lessons.g: Check whether a goal was accepted and then wait for its result.
lessons.s: A server is allowed to reject a goal. `goal_future.result()` gives you a goal handle with `handle.accepted` as a boolean. If it is false, there is no result coming and any code that waits for one waits forever. When accepted, ask for the result with `handle.get_result_async()`, which returns the second future.

lessons.g: Handle cancellation on the server side and stop the work cleanly.
lessons.s: Cancellation is the reason actions exist. The client calls `handle.cancel_goal_async()`, and on the server side the running goal handle reports `goal_handle.is_cancel_requested`. Your execute callback has to check that flag in its loop.

lessons.g: Reject a new goal while another is running using a goal_callback.
lessons.s: By default an `ActionServer` accepts every goal, and under a multi threaded executor two goals can run at once. For a robot with one base and one set of wheels that is nonsense: two goals fighting over `cmd_vel` produce motion neither one asked for.

lessons.g: Drive an action from the command line and read its feedback live.
lessons.s: `ros2 action list` shows the actions in the graph, `ros2 action info /drive_distance -t` shows the servers and clients with the type. `ros2 interface show nebula_interfaces/action/DriveDistance` prints the three sections.

lessons.g: Declare a parameter with a default and read its value inside the node.
lessons.s: A **parameter** is a named value owned by a node and settable from outside it. Anything a field engineer might want to change without editing code is a parameter: the maximum speed, the serial port of the laser, the frame id to publish in. ROS 2 requires you to declare parameters before use.

lessons.g: Declare parameters of several types and read them without losing the type.
lessons.s: A parameter has one of a fixed set of types: bool, integer, double, string, byte array, bool array, integer array, double array, string array. The type is fixed at declaration, inferred from the default you give. The trap is the numeric literal.

lessons.g: Attach a ParameterDescriptor with a range and a description to a parameter.
lessons.s: A bare declaration accepts any value of the right type, including a speed limit of 40 m/s on a robot that tips over at 1.2. A `ParameterDescriptor` lets you state the constraint so the middleware enforces it before your code sees the value.

lessons.g: Validate parameter changes at runtime with a set parameters callback.
lessons.s: Ranges cover numeric bounds. Everything else is your job. `self.add_on_set_parameters_callback(self.on_set)` registers a function that runs before any change is applied, receives the list of proposed `Parameter` objects, and returns a `SetParametersResult`.

lessons.g: Write a YAML parameter file with the node name and namespace structure ROS 2 expects.
lessons.s: A parameter yaml file has a shape that is easy to get wrong. The top level key is the fully qualified node name, then a literal `ros__parameters` key, then the values. The double underscore is not a typo. A node in a namespace needs its namespace in the key: `/front/laser_driver:` and not `laser_driver:`.

lessons.g: List, read, set and dump parameters of a running node from the command line.
lessons.s: Every node automatically serves six parameter services, which is why `ros2 param` works without you writing anything. `ros2 param list /pilot` shows the names, `ros2 param get /pilot max_speed` reads one, `ros2 param describe /pilot max_speed` prints the descriptor with its range.

lessons.g: Build a QoSProfile with best effort reliability for a high rate sensor stream.
lessons.s: Quality of Service is the contract between a publisher and a subscriber. The depth number you have been passing to `create_publisher` is a shortcut for a default profile. The full form is a `QoSProfile` object. `ReliabilityPolicy.RELIABLE` retransmits until the message arrives.

lessons.g: Use transient local durability so late subscribers still receive the last message.
lessons.s: `DurabilityPolicy.VOLATILE`, the default, means a subscriber that joins after a message was published never sees it. For a stream that is correct. For a map published once at startup it is a disaster: any node that starts thirty seconds later has no map and no way to ask for one.

lessons.g: Choose history and depth so a slow subscriber drops old data instead of lagging.
lessons.s: `HistoryPolicy.KEEP_LAST` with a `depth` keeps a ring buffer of that many messages. `HistoryPolicy.KEEP_ALL` keeps everything the middleware can hold, bounded by DDS resource limits rather than by you. Depth is a latency decision, not a memory decision.

lessons.g: Detect a missing publisher with a QoS deadline and its event callback.
lessons.s: A **deadline** is a promise about rate. Setting `deadline=Duration(seconds=0.2)` on a subscription says you expect a message at least every 200 ms. When one does not arrive, the middleware calls your deadline missed event handler. You did not have to write a watchdog timer, DDS did it.

lessons.g: Write a Python launch file that starts several nodes at once.
lessons.s: A robot is a dozen nodes. Starting them by hand in a dozen terminals is not a workflow, it is a memory test. A **launch file** describes the whole system and starts it with one command. ROS 2 launch files are Python.

lessons.g: Pass parameters to a node from a launch file, inline and from a yaml file.
lessons.s: The `parameters` argument of a `Node` action takes a list. Each element is either a dictionary of inline values or a path to a yaml file. They are applied in order, so a later entry overrides an earlier one, which is how you load a base configuration and then override one value for a test.

lessons.g: Declare a launch argument and use its value inside the launch description.
lessons.s: Hardcoding a value in a launch file means editing the file to change it. `DeclareLaunchArgument('max_speed', default_value='0.5')` creates a switch that the operator sets on the command line: `ros2 launch nebula_bringup base.launch.py max_speed:=0.3`. Reading it back is `LaunchConfiguration('max_speed')`.

lessons.g: Run the same node twice under different namespaces with remapped topics.
lessons.s: This is where relative topic names from chapter 2 pay off. A `Node` action takes `namespace`, and every relative name inside that node is pushed under it. The same laser driver launched with `namespace='front'` and `namespace='rear'` produces `/front/scan` and `/rear/scan` with zero code changes.

lessons.g: Include one launch file from another and pass arguments through.
lessons.s: A real robot has one launch file per subsystem and one that ties them together. `IncludeLaunchDescription` pulls in another file, so `robot.launch.py` can include `base.launch.py`, `sensors.launch.py` and `navigation.launch.py`. The include needs a source.

lessons.g: Run a process at startup and react to its exit with an event handler.
lessons.s: Not everything in a launch file is a node. `ExecuteProcess` runs any command, which is how you start `ros2 bag record` alongside a test, or call a calibration script before the drivers come up. `RegisterEventHandler` with `OnProcessExit` fires an action when a process ends.

lessons.g: Describe the managed lifecycle states and the transitions between them.
lessons.s: A plain node starts doing its job the moment its constructor runs. For a laser driver that means opening a serial port during construction, and if the port is missing the process dies before anything can react. A **lifecycle node** separates existence from activity.

lessons.g: Implement a LifecycleNode with on_configure, on_activate and on_deactivate.
lessons.s: `rclpy.lifecycle.LifecycleNode` is the base class. You override the transition callbacks, each receiving the previous state and returning `TransitionCallbackReturn.SUCCESS`, `FAILURE` or `ERROR`. Returning failure keeps the node in the old state and the supervisor learns the driver could not open its port.

lessons.g: Trigger lifecycle transitions from the command line and from a launch file.
lessons.s: A lifecycle node exposes services for its transitions. `ros2 lifecycle list /managed_laser` shows what is available from the current state, `ros2 lifecycle get /managed_laser` prints the state, and `ros2 lifecycle set /managed_laser configure` performs a transition.

lessons.g: Explain the TF2 tree and name the standard frames of a mobile robot.
lessons.s: A distance of 1.2 metres is meaningless on its own. It is 1.2 metres from the laser, which sits 18 cm above and 10 cm in front of the wheel axis, on a robot that is somewhere in a room.

lessons.g: Publish a fixed sensor offset with a StaticTransformBroadcaster.
lessons.s: A laser bolted to the chassis never moves relative to it. Publishing that transform at 50 Hz would waste bandwidth forever. `StaticTransformBroadcaster` publishes it once on `/tf_static`, a transient local topic, so every node that starts later still receives it. The message is a `geometry_msgs/TransformStamped`.

lessons.g: Broadcast a changing odom to base_link transform on every odometry update.
lessons.s: The pose of the robot changes, so its transform has to be republished continuously. `TransformBroadcaster` sends on `/tf`, and the usual rate is whatever your odometry produces, 20 to 50 Hz on a wheeled base.

lessons.g: Look up a transform between two frames with a Buffer and a TransformListener.
lessons.s: To read the tree you need two objects: a `Buffer`, which stores the last few seconds of transforms, and a `TransformListener`, which fills that buffer from `/tf` and `/tf_static`. Create both in the constructor and keep both on `self`. `buffer.lookup_transform(target_frame, source_frame, time)` answers the question.

lessons.g: Transform a stamped point into another frame and handle extrapolation errors.
lessons.s: Looking up a transform is half the job. `tf2_geometry_msgs` adds the other half: `buffer.transform(point_stamped, 'base_link')` takes a stamped message and returns it expressed in the target frame, using the stamp inside the message to pick the right moment in the tree. The import looks unused and is not.

lessons.g: Describe a robot in URDF with links, a fixed joint and a continuous joint.
lessons.s: **URDF** is the XML that describes the physical robot: which parts exist, where they sit, how they are connected. Two element types carry everything. A `<link>` is a rigid body with visual, collision and inertial blocks. A `<joint>` connects a parent link to a child link and says how they may move.

lessons.g: Factor repeated URDF into a xacro macro with parameters.
lessons.s: A four wheeled robot written in plain URDF is the same twenty lines four times, with one number different. **xacro** is the macro language that fixes that. The file becomes `robot.urdf.xacro`, declares the namespace `xmlns:xacro`, and is expanded before anything reads it.

lessons.g: Launch robot_state_publisher so the URDF becomes live TF frames.
lessons.s: `robot_state_publisher` is the node that turns a URDF into transforms. You give it the description as the `robot_description` parameter, it publishes every fixed joint on `/tf_static` and computes the moving joints from `/joint_states`.

lessons.g: Configure RViz displays and pick a fixed frame that does not jitter.
lessons.s: RViz2 draws the robot and its data in 3D. It is a viewer, not a simulator: everything it shows comes from topics and from TF2. If something is missing in RViz, it is missing in the graph. The **fixed frame** is the single most important setting. Everything is drawn relative to it.

lessons.g: Spawn the robot in Gazebo and bridge the simulated topics into ROS 2.
lessons.s: Gazebo runs the physics. It is a separate process with its own transport, and the two worlds meet through `ros_gz_bridge`. Nothing crosses that boundary unless you bridge it explicitly, which is why a freshly spawned robot appears in the simulator and publishes nothing to ROS 2.

lessons.g: Decide the node split, the topics and the channel of each interaction for a complete robot.
lessons.s: The project of this chapter is a full differential drive robot in ROS 2: a laser, wheel odometry, a safety layer, a behaviour that drives to a target, and a supervisor that brings everything up in order. Every piece is a node, and the design work is deciding where the boundaries go.

lessons.g: Write the laser driver node with parameters, sensor QoS and a stamped message.
lessons.s: The first node of the robot is the sensor driver, and it puts together most of what this course covered. It reads its port and frame from parameters, publishes with a best effort sensor profile, stamps every message with the node clock and names the frame it measured from.

lessons.g: Write the odometry node that publishes nav_msgs/Odometry and the matching TF.
lessons.s: The odometry node integrates wheel velocities into a pose and tells the rest of the system two things at once: a `nav_msgs/Odometry` message on `/odom` for anything that wants the pose with covariance, and a transform from `odom` to `base_link` handed to TF2 through `TransformBroadcaster.sendTransform()`, camelCase in ...

lessons.g: Write the safety filter that caps speed and blocks motion when an obstacle is close.
lessons.s: The safety node sits between the behaviour and the wheels. It subscribes to `cmd_vel_raw`, subscribes to `scan`, and publishes the real `cmd_vel`. Nothing else may publish `cmd_vel`, and that is enforced by the launch file through remappings rather than by convention. It does two jobs.

lessons.g: Write the behaviour action server that drives a distance with feedback and cancellation.
lessons.s: The behaviour node is the only one that decides where the robot goes. It offers the `drive_distance` action, reads `/odom` to know how far it has come, and publishes to `cmd_vel_raw` so the safety filter always gets the last word.

lessons.g: Write a supervisor node that configures and activates the managed nodes in order.
lessons.s: The supervisor is the node that decides the robot is ready. It calls the lifecycle services of the managed nodes: `configure` on all of them, wait for each to reach inactive, then `activate` in dependency order, sensors first, then estimators, then behaviour.

lessons.g: Write the bringup launch file that starts the whole robot with its wiring and its recording.
lessons.s: The last piece is the launch file that starts the robot: the description through `robot_state_publisher`, the laser driver, the odometry node, the safety filter, the behaviour, and a bag recording of the three topics that matter. One command, one system. The wiring lives here and nowhere else.

lessons.g: Compute how fast a standing humanoid falls once it tilts, and explain why two legs is an unstable problem.
lessons.s: A wheeled robot is stable by construction. Turn it off and it stays where it is. A humanoid turned off falls over. That single sentence is the whole difficulty of this course. The reason is **underactuation**. A humanoid has plenty of motors, but none of them connects to the ground.

lessons.g: Build the joint map of a humanoid and count its degrees of freedom by limb.
lessons.s: A **degree of freedom** is one independently commanded joint axis. Counting them tells you how much machine you have to control and how much of it you actually need.

lessons.g: Compute the whole body center of mass from a list of links with mass and position.
lessons.s: The **center of mass**, or CoM, is the mass weighted average of every link position. For a rigid body chain it is `sum(m_i * p_i) / sum(m_i)`. It is the single point that gravity acts on, and almost every balance law in this course is written in terms of it. Mass in a humanoid is not spread evenly.

lessons.g: Build the support polygon of a standing humanoid from the rectangles of both feet.
lessons.s: The **support polygon** is the convex hull of all contact points with the ground, projected onto the floor plane. It is the region where the robot is allowed to push. Outside of it there is nothing to push against. A flat humanoid foot is a rectangle. HRP-2 uses roughly 0.23 m by 0.13 m.

lessons.g: Decide whether a static posture is stable by testing the center of mass projection against the support polygon.
lessons.s: **Static equilibrium** has one rule: the vertical projection of the center of mass must fall strictly inside the support polygon. If it does, the robot can hold that posture forever with zero velocity. If it does not, it is already falling and no amount of joint torque will save it without moving a foot.

lessons.g: Build a homogeneous transform and compose two of them.
lessons.s: Every link of a humanoid carries its own coordinate frame. To know where the right hand is, you chain the transforms from the pelvis outward. A **homogeneous transform** packs a rotation and a translation into one 4 by 4 matrix so that chaining is a single matrix product.

lessons.g: Compute forward kinematics of a planar leg with hip, knee and ankle pitch.
lessons.s: Start in the **sagittal plane**, the side view. A leg reduced to three pitch joints, hip, knee and ankle, is enough to explain most of walking, because forward motion happens almost entirely in this plane. Forward kinematics is the easy direction: given joint angles, where is the foot.

lessons.t: Six Ways to Place a Foot
lessons.g: Extend the leg to the full 6 degree of freedom chain and compute the foot pose in three dimensions.
lessons.s: Six is not an arbitrary number. Placing a rigid body anywhere in space takes exactly 6 parameters, 3 for position and 3 for orientation. A leg with 6 joints can therefore put the foot at any reachable pose, and only one set of joint angles gets you there for a given configuration branch.

lessons.g: Clamp joint commands to their mechanical limits and keep the knee away from full extension.
lessons.s: Every joint has a hard limit, and a command that exceeds it does not produce a bigger motion, it produces a fault or a broken gearbox. The controller must clamp before the command leaves the machine, never after. The knee gets a second, softer limit.

lessons.g: Compute analytic inverse kinematics for the leg using the law of cosines on the knee.
lessons.s: Walking is planned in terms of foot poses, not joint angles, so you need the inverse: given a desired foot position, find the joints. For a 6 degree of freedom leg with a single knee this has a closed form solution, no iteration and no Jacobian. The key step is the triangle formed by hip, knee and ankle.

lessons.g: Compute arm forward kinematics and show the redundancy of the elbow swivel.
lessons.s: An arm with 7 joints is redundant: 7 commands for 6 constraints, so an infinite family of postures reaches the same hand pose. The free parameter is the **elbow swivel**, the rotation of the elbow around the line from shoulder to wrist. Your own arm does this. Hold a cup still and move your elbow up and down.

lessons.g: Compute the whole body center of mass by pushing each link mass through forward kinematics.
lessons.s: In lesson h0-3 the link positions were handed to you. On a real robot they are not. Each link has a center of mass expressed in its own frame, and you get the world position by running forward kinematics for that link and applying its local offset.

lessons.g: Express the pelvis pose in the world using the IMU orientation and the stance foot as an anchor.
lessons.s: Forward kinematics tells you where every link is relative to the pelvis. It says nothing about where the pelvis is in the world, because no joint connects the robot to the ground. That is the **floating base** problem. The standard trick is to invert the chain.

lessons.t: One Loop for the Whole Body
lessons.g: Represent the robot as a parent index tree and write a single forward kinematics pass over it.
lessons.s: Hand written chains do not scale to 30 joints and two branches. The standard representation is a **kinematic tree** stored as a flat array, where each entry holds its parent index, its joint axis and its fixed offset.

lessons.g: Compute the ground reaction force of a standing humanoid and split it between both feet.
lessons.s: Standing still, the floor pushes up with exactly the weight of the robot. For a 45 kg machine that is about 441 N, spread over two feet. Nothing else holds the robot up, so the **ground reaction force**, or GRF, is the only actuation channel that matters for balance.

lessons.g: Compute the center of pressure of one foot from four load cell readings.
lessons.s: Pressure under a foot is not a single point, it is a distribution. The **center of pressure**, or CoP, is the point where the resultant vertical force acts, the pressure weighted average of the contact area. The cheapest way to measure it is four load cells, one near each corner of the sole.

lessons.g: Compute the foot center of pressure from a six axis force torque sensor mounted above the sole.
lessons.s: Production humanoids do not use four cells, they use one **six axis force torque sensor** in the ankle. It reports three forces and three moments in its own frame, which sits a few centimeters above the sole. Getting the CoP from it requires moving the measurement down to the floor.

lessons.g: Merge the center of pressure of both feet into the global center of pressure.
lessons.s: With both feet on the ground you have two local CoPs, one per sole, and one global point that the balance controller cares about.

lessons.g: Compute the true convex hull of the contact points instead of the axis aligned box.
lessons.s: The box from chapter 0 works only when both feet point forward and sit square. The moment the robot turns a foot, steps onto a ledge or stands with one foot ahead, the real support polygon is the **convex hull** of all contact corners, and the box overestimates it badly.

lessons.g: Compute the signed distance from a point to a convex polygon and use it as the stability margin.
lessons.s: Once the support polygon is a real hull, the margin is the shortest distance from the point to any edge. For a convex polygon in counterclockwise order there is a shortcut: for each edge, the signed distance is the cross product of the edge with the vector to the point, divided by the edge length.

lessons.t: The Point That Rules Them All
lessons.g: Define the zero moment point and show it coincides with the center of pressure on flat ground.
lessons.s: The **zero moment point**, or ZMP, is the point on the ground where the horizontal components of the moment produced by inertia and gravity are zero. Miomir Vukobratovic introduced it in 1968, and it is the concept the entire first generation of walking humanoids, from Honda E series to ASIMO to HRP, was built on.

lessons.g: Model the support polygon through a step cycle and measure how much of the time the robot is on one foot.
lessons.s: Walking alternates between **double support**, both feet down, and **single support**, one foot down and one in the air. In double support the polygon is roughly 0.23 by 0.31 m. In single support it is one shoe, 0.23 by 0.13 m, an area cut by more than half, and the lateral direction loses almost everything.

lessons.g: Decide whether a reaching posture stays statically stable, and how far the robot can lean before it must step.
lessons.s: This lesson closes the static chapter with the problem that actually shows up on a real machine: the robot reaches forward for an object and quietly falls on its face. Reaching moves mass. An arm holding a 2 kg tool at 0.6 m in front of a 45 kg robot moves the whole body CoM forward by `2 * 0.6 / 47`, about 0.026 m.

lessons.g: Compute the ground reaction force required for a commanded center of mass acceleration.
lessons.s: The whole robot, all 30 joints of it, obeys one equation at the center of mass: `F_grf = m * (a_com + g)`. Nothing else. Every joint torque you will ever command is just a way of producing that force through the contacts. Read the equation both ways.

lessons.g: Derive the zero moment point from the cart table model and check that it stays inside the foot.
lessons.s: The **cart table model** is the simplest picture that gets the ZMP right. Imagine a cart of mass m sliding on a table at constant height z, with the table supported only by the small foot area. Moving the cart shifts the moment about the table edge.

lessons.g: Write the linear inverted pendulum dynamics and integrate it for one second.
lessons.s: Constrain the CoM to a horizontal plane of constant height and the inverted pendulum becomes linear: `x_ddot = (g / z) * (x - p)` where `p` is the ZMP. That is the **linear inverted pendulum model**, or LIPM, and it is the workhorse of humanoid walking.

lessons.g: Compute the analytic solution of the LIPM and compare it against the numerical integration.
lessons.s: The LIPM is linear with constant coefficients, so it has a closed form. With a fixed ZMP at `p`: - `x(t) = p + (x0 - p) * cosh(w t) + (v0 / w) * sinh(w t)` - `v(t) = w * (x0 - p) * sinh(w t) + v0 * cosh(w t)` This matters for three reasons.

lessons.g: Compute the orbital energy of the linear inverted pendulum and use it to predict whether the robot crosses over the foot.
lessons.s: The LIPM has a conserved quantity, the **orbital energy**: `E = 0.5 * v^2 - 0.5 * (g / z) * (x - p)^2` Its sign answers a question you need constantly. If `E` is negative, the CoM does not have enough speed to pass over the support point, so it slows, stops and comes back, like a normal pendulum swing.

lessons.g: Split the pendulum state into its stable and divergent components and compute the divergent component of motion.
lessons.s: The hyperbolic solution of h3-4 is a sum of two exponentials, one decaying and one growing. Change coordinates so each has its own variable and the problem becomes trivial.

lessons.g: Compute the instantaneous capture point and the foot placement that stops the robot in a single step.
lessons.s: The **capture point** is where you must place the foot to bring the robot to a complete stop in one step. Under the LIPM it is exactly the DCM: `x_cap = x + v / w`. The reason is the orbital energy of the previous lesson.

lessons.t: Checking a Trajectory Before It Runs
lessons.g: Given a center of mass trajectory, compute the required zero moment point over time and verify it stays inside the foot.
lessons.s: Planning produces a CoM trajectory. Before it goes anywhere near the machine, you check that the ZMP it implies is physically available, meaning inside the support polygon for the whole horizon. This is the cheapest safety net in the entire stack.

lessons.g: Compare the static and dynamic stability verdicts on the same motion and show where the static test is wrong.
lessons.s: Time to retire the chapter 0 rule. The static test asks whether the CoM projection is inside the polygon. The dynamic test asks whether the ZMP is. They disagree constantly, in both directions. A robot leaning far forward with the right backward acceleration is dynamically fine and statically condemned.

lessons.g: Define the phases of the gait cycle and locate any time inside the cycle.
lessons.s: A **gait cycle** is one full stride, from left heel strike to the next left heel strike. It contains two steps, one per leg. The naming trips people up constantly: a step is half a cycle, a stride is a whole one.

lessons.g: Generate a straight line footstep plan with the correct alternating lateral offset.
lessons.s: Before any trajectory exists, walking is a list of **footsteps**: where each foot lands, in what order, and when. Everything downstream reads this list. Two numbers define a straight walk.

lessons.g: Extend the footstep planner to turning, rotating each footprint and its lateral offset.
lessons.s: Turning while walking is not a different gait, it is the same footstep list with a heading that changes step by step. Each footprint carries a yaw, and the lateral offset is applied in the rotated frame, not in the world frame. The limit is the hip yaw joint and the risk of scuffing.

lessons.g: Build the gait state machine with double and single support states and explicit transitions.
lessons.s: The gait is driven by a **finite state machine** with four states: double support left to right, single support right, double support right to left, single support left. Every module in the stack asks it two questions: which foot is the support, and how far into the current phase are we.

lessons.g: Generate the horizontal swing foot trajectory with a fifth order polynomial.
lessons.s: The swing foot has to travel from the previous footprint to the next one in the single support time, and it must arrive with **zero velocity and zero acceleration**. Anything else lands as an impact, and impacts inject impulses that the balance controller has to absorb after the fact.

lessons.g: Generate the vertical swing profile with a controlled apex height and flat contact at both ends.
lessons.s: The vertical profile is not symmetric with the horizontal one. It has to rise, reach an apex around mid swing, and come back down to exactly zero. A useful shape is two quintics back to back, up to the apex and down again, or a single sine arc if you do not need to place the apex freely.

lessons.g: Compute the impact impulse of a touchdown and size the landing velocity that keeps it acceptable.
lessons.s: Touchdown is a collision. The swing leg carries momentum, and the moment the foot meets the floor that momentum has to go somewhere. The impulse is roughly `J = m_eff * v_touchdown`, where the effective mass is somewhere between the leg mass and the whole body mass depending on how stiff the leg is at that instant.

lessons.g: Generate the foot pitch profile for heel strike and toe off, and check the foot does not scuff.
