The robot drove a single lap of the Cartographer Hold, a 16 by 12 m floor with five obstacles, carrying a 240 beam lidar with 2 percent range noise and wheel encoders calibrated 1.2 percent large with a heading rate that leans.

lessons.g: Turn the log into graph nodes and odometry edges and report the quality of every match it made.
lessons.s: The front end is chapters one through three in one call: pick keyframes, match each against the last, store the answer as an edge with its quality, and chain the answers into an initial pose for each node. What it returns is a graph with no cycles, and its report has to say three things.

lessons.g: Run the whole closure pipeline on the front end output and report what each veto refused.
lessons.s: Chapter five in one call, and it is four stages that narrow in turn. The **radius**, sized from the front end drift rate, turns 780 possible pairs into a handful. The **descriptor** orders those by how alike the two scans look. The **correlative verifier** scores each survivor geometrically with no usable prior.

lessons.g: Optimize the full graph with a redescending kernel and score the trajectory before and after.
lessons.s: Chapters six and seven in one call. Build the graph from the front end edges and the accepted closures, anchor node zero, and run Gauss Newton with the Tukey kernel until the step stops moving anything. The kernel stays on even though the detector believes every closure it accepted.

lessons.g: Render the submaps at the optimized anchors and measure the map error against the trajectory error.
lessons.s: The trajectory improved. That is not the deliverable. The deliverable is a map, and the map improves only when somebody redraws it, which is exactly what chapter four built the submaps for. Nothing inside a submap changes.

lessons.g: Run every check the course promised against one pipeline run and print a verdict beside each number.
lessons.s: A SLAM system that produces a map and no verdict is a system nobody can sign off. Every chapter of this course produced a number that has to hold, and the last mission is to check all of them on one run and print the answer beside the threshold, not instead of it. Nine checks, and each one belongs to a chapter.

lessons.t: When SLAM Is the Wrong Tool
lessons.g: Localise against a surveyed map of the same floor and compare the accuracy and effort against full SLAM.
lessons.s: The last mission of the Hold is the one nobody wants to run. Everything in this course exists because the map is unknown. In a warehouse that is not true: the floor plan exists, it does not move, and somebody can survey it once. So measure the alternative honestly.

lessons.g: Compute the gravity force vector on a part and decide whether it is inside the gripper payload rating.
lessons.s: Everything in this workshop starts with a part sitting on a bench and a hand that has to pick it up. The arm already knows how to reach the pose, that was the Joint Cathedral. What nobody has told it yet is whether the part will still be in the fingers a second later. The first number is the easy one.

lessons.g: Compute the inward unit normal of a contact point on a box shaped part.
lessons.s: A contact is not a point. It is a point plus a direction, and the direction is the one thing beginners drop. The **inward normal** at a contact is the unit vector that points from the surface into the material.

lessons.g: Split a contact force into its normal component and its tangential component in the contact plane.
lessons.s: Every contact force splits into two parts that behave nothing alike. The part along the normal is the squeeze. It is bounded below by zero, because a finger cannot pull, and bounded above by what the part survives. The part in the tangent plane is friction, and it is bounded by the squeeze itself.

lessons.g: Turn a contact force into a six dimensional wrench about the object centre of mass.
lessons.s: A force applied off centre does two things at once: it pushes and it turns. Adding the turn is what promotes a force to a **wrench**, the six number object that the rest of this course speaks in. Stack the three force components first and the three moment components second.

lessons.g: Sum every contact wrench plus gravity and read the residual wrench the object is left holding.
lessons.s: A grasp holds when the contacts cancel everything the world does to the object. Sum the wrenches, subtract gravity, and whatever survives is the **residual**: the wrench that is going to accelerate the part out of the hand.

lessons.g: Decide whether a contact blocks a candidate object motion from the sign of the normal component.
lessons.s: There are two ways to hold something. **Form closure** holds it with geometry alone: the fingers are placed so that no motion of the object is possible, and you could switch the motors off.

lessons.g: Compute the velocity of a material point under a planar twist and use it to test whether a candidate twist survives every contact.
lessons.s: Objects do not only translate. A planar rigid motion is a **twist**, three numbers, two of linear velocity and one of angular velocity, and every material point of the body moves at a different speed under it.

lessons.g: Sample the twist space and give a form closure verdict, then show two four contact layouts that disagree.
lessons.s: Form closure means **no** twist survives. That is a statement about an infinite set, and the honest engineering answer is to sample it densely and see whether anything gets through. One detail decides whether the sampling means anything: units.

lessons.g: Build the contact wrench matrix, read its rank, and show that full rank does not imply form closure.
lessons.s: There is a cheap test that people reach for instead of sampling, and it is worth knowing exactly how much it buys. Each frictionless contact can only push along its normal, and that push produces one wrench on the object.

lessons.g: Compute the width of a polygonal part along a direction and find the direction where it is narrowest.
lessons.s: A jaw does not care about the bounding box of a part. It cares about the width the part shows **along the line the jaws close on**, and that number changes with every degree of rotation.

lessons.t: A Cage Is Not a Grip
lessons.g: Test whether a part can escape between two fingers by comparing the finger gap against the narrowest width of the part.
lessons.s: **Caging** is the weak cousin of form closure and it is more useful than it sounds. The object is free to move and rattle inside the fingers, but it cannot get out. A hook carrying a bucket cages it. A two finger gripper closing around a part before it touches it cages it first and grips it second.

lessons.g: Measure how far a pair of contacts is from being antipodal, in degrees.
lessons.s: A two finger grip wants its contacts **antipodal**: the segment joining them should run straight down both inward normals. When it does, the squeeze goes entirely into pressing the part and none of it into spinning the part out of the jaws.

lessons.t: Firing a Ray Across the Part
lessons.g: Find the contact on the far side of a part by casting a ray along the inward normal and keeping the nearest edge it hits.
lessons.s: You do not get contact pairs handed to you. You pick a point on the surface, fire a ray straight into the part along its inward normal, and whatever the ray leaves through is the other jaw. That is how every antipodal grasp sampler in the field generates candidates, and it is thirty lines.

lessons.t: Which Line the Jaws Should Take
lessons.g: Score every candidate contact pair on alignment and offset from the centre of mass, and pick the best one.
lessons.s: Now the two halves join. Fire rays from points along every edge, keep the pairs that come back, and you have a candidate list. Choosing among them is a ranking problem, and the ranking is where a grasp planner earns its keep. Two penalties are enough at this stage.

lessons.g: Convert a friction coefficient into a friction cone half angle and into the tangential force a squeeze buys.
lessons.s: Form closure is rare in a real cell. Almost everything a robot picks is held by friction, and friction has exactly one parameter that matters at this level: the coefficient `mu` between the pad and the part. It buys two things and it is worth seeing both.

lessons.g: Test whether a contact force lies inside its friction cone, and reject one that tries to pull.
lessons.s: A contact force is **feasible** when two things hold at once, and code that checks only the second one is the classic bug. First, the normal component has to be positive. A pad pushes; it does not pull.

lessons.g: Size the normal force two pads need to hold a hanging part, and check it against what the part survives.
lessons.s: Here is the calculation that decides whether a pick is possible at all. A part hangs between two pads. Each pad carries at most `mu` times its normal force sideways, and between them they have to carry the weight, so the smallest squeeze that works is `mass * G / (2.0 * mu)` newtons. Nobody ships that number.

lessons.g: Approximate a three dimensional friction cone with a set of edge vectors that a linear solver can use.
lessons.s: The friction cone is round, and round is inconvenient. Every practical grasp solver replaces it with a pyramid: a handful of **edge vectors**, and any nonnegative combination of them is a force the solver is allowed to use.

lessons.g: Add a torsional friction limit to a contact and show why a point fingertip cannot resist a twist at all.
lessons.s: A hard fingertip touching a flat face is a **point contact with friction**: it resists a push and a slide and nothing else. Spin the part about the contact normal and the fingertip offers no resistance, because a point has no area to generate a moment over.

lessons.t: The Line Has to Fit in Both Cones
lessons.g: Give a two finger force closure verdict by comparing the antipodal error against the friction angle.
lessons.s: For two fingers in the plane there is a force closure test you can do in your head, and it joins the two halves of this course. If the segment joining the contacts lies inside **both** friction cones, the fingers can squeeze along that line and generate any force the part needs without sliding.

lessons.t: The Matrix the Fingers Speak Through
lessons.g: Build the planar grasp matrix that maps a stack of contact forces to the wrench on the object.
lessons.s: Two fingers with a hand test is fine. Three fingers, or four, or a hand with a thumb, needs the general machinery, and the general machinery is one matrix. The **grasp matrix** `G` takes the contact forces stacked into one long vector and returns the wrench they produce on the object.

lessons.g: Decide force closure by checking that every sampled wrench direction has at least one cone edge pushing against it.
lessons.s: The general force closure question is: can the fingers produce **every** wrench, in every direction, using only forces inside their cones? There is a linear program for it and there is a sampling test, and the sampling test is the one you can write today and debug tomorrow.

lessons.g: Find the null space of the grasp matrix and show that squeezing harder changes the contact forces without changing the object wrench.
lessons.s: Two fingers pressing on opposite sides of a part with 5 N each, and the same two fingers pressing with 50 N each, apply exactly the same wrench to the object: none. That difference lives in the **null space** of the grasp matrix, and it has a name, the **internal force**, or in shop language the squeeze.

lessons.t: A Number Instead of an Opinion
lessons.g: Score a grasp with the smallest singular value of its grasp matrix and compare three finger layouts.
lessons.s: A planner produces hundreds of candidate grasps and has to sort them. Sorting needs a number, and the cheapest honest number comes straight out of the grasp matrix. The singular values of `G` say how much object wrench you get per unit of finger force, direction by direction.

lessons.t: The Direction It Is Weakest In
lessons.g: Read the left singular vector of the smallest singular value and name the wrench direction the grasp resists worst.
lessons.s: A score tells you that a grasp is weak. The singular vector tells you **what** it is weak against, and that is the part you can act on. The full decomposition returns three things, `u, s, _ = np.linalg.svd(G)`, and the columns of `u` are directions in wrench space.

lessons.g: Compute the isotropy and the condition number of a grasp and say what each one is good for.
lessons.s: The smallest singular value is an absolute capacity, and it changes if you double every finger force. Sometimes you want the **shape** of the capacity instead of its size, and that is a ratio.

lessons.t: The Largest Push It Always Survives
lessons.g: Compute the epsilon quality of a grasp as the smallest support of its cone wrenches over all directions.
lessons.s: The metric the field actually ranks grasps on is geometric: how big a ball of wrenches, centred on the origin, fits inside everything the fingers can produce?

lessons.t: The Metric That Cannot See Friction
lessons.g: Show that two grasps with identical grasp matrices have opposite epsilon qualities, and say which metric to trust.
lessons.s: Here is a test worth running on any metric before you ship it: delete the thing the metric is supposed to measure and see whether the number moves. The grasp matrix is built from contact **positions** only. Nowhere in it does a contact normal appear.

lessons.t: How Close Each Finger Is to Sliding
lessons.g: Solve the contact forces for a task wrench, add internal force, and report the cone margin of every finger.
lessons.s: Epsilon scores the grasp against every possible wrench. Once you know the wrench the task actually needs, there is a sharper question: with the forces the hand is really applying, how much room does each finger have left? Solve the forces first.

lessons.g: Compare the moment an off centre grasp has to resist against the moment two pads can generate.
lessons.s: Grip a 60 mm bar 30 mm off its centre of mass, accelerate it, and the part tries to rotate in the jaws. Nothing about the friction coefficient stops that; what stops it is the pair of pads being far enough apart to make a couple.

lessons.g: Measure the area of the triangle three fingers make and reject a layout that has collapsed onto a line.
lessons.s: A three finger hand has a cheap sanity check that catches the worst layouts before any decomposition runs: the area of the triangle the contacts make.

lessons.t: One Score the Planner Sorts On
lessons.g: Combine epsilon, alignment error and offset into a single weighted grasp score and rank five candidates.
lessons.s: A planner cannot act on four numbers. At the end of the chapter they collapse into one, and the collapse is a design decision you should write down rather than tune until the demo works.

lessons.g: Build the pre grasp and retreat poses from a grasp pose, a standoff and a lift height.
lessons.s: A pick is never one pose. It is at least three, and skipping the other two is how a gripper knocks a part over on the way in. The **pre grasp** sits back along the approach axis by a standoff, `grasp - standoff * approach`, where `approach` is the unit vector the gripper travels along.

lessons.g: Interpolate the approach into waypoints and verify that no single step is longer than the servo can track.
lessons.s: A straight line between two poses is a plan, not a trajectory. The controller wants waypoints, and the spacing of those waypoints is a safety property: a 50 mm jump commanded to a position servo becomes a lunge, and the part is gone before the force sensor has a chance to say anything. Interpolating is one expression.

lessons.g: Check the pads against the table along the whole approach and find the first waypoint that would strike it.
lessons.s: The planner has been treating the gripper as a point, and the gripper is a pair of 16 mm rubber pads with a body behind them. The tool centre sits in the middle of the pads, so the bottom of the hand is `PAD_BELOW_TCP` below the pose you commanded, 8 mm on a 2F-85 with the standard fingers.

lessons.g: Reject a grasp whose open fingers would strike a neighbouring part before the pads reach the target.
lessons.s: In a bin the target is not alone. The jaws have to fit into the gap around it, and a grasp that is perfect in isolation is worthless if a neighbouring part sits where a finger has to go. Model it flat: each part is a disc in the horizontal plane, and each open finger is a disc of half width `JAW_HALF_WIDTH`.

lessons.t: How Far the Wrist Can Lean
lessons.g: Compute the largest approach tilt a part near a bin wall allows, and reject the grasps that exceed it.
lessons.s: A part in the middle of a bin can be approached from any angle. The same part 15 mm from the wall cannot, because the gripper body is 140 mm tall and leaning it towards the wall drives the elbow end into the steel. The geometry is a right triangle.

lessons.g: Resolve the 180 degree ambiguity of a grasp axis by choosing the wrist angle inside the joint limit and nearest the current one.
lessons.s: A parallel jaw grasp does not care which finger goes on which side, so the grasp axis gives you an angle and that angle plus 180 degrees, and both are correct grasps. The wrist cares very much, because one of them may be past a joint limit and one of them may need a 300 degree unwind.

lessons.g: Shape the approach speed so the last centimetres are travelled at creep speed with a linear ramp above it.
lessons.s: Speed on approach is a trade you make twice. Far from the part, fast is free. Near the part, fast is the difference between detecting contact at 3 N and detecting it at 40 N, because the force you measure is the speed you were carrying when you hit. The profile has three pieces and one of them is the important one.

lessons.g: Implement a guarded move that steps down until the measured force crosses a threshold, and measure the overshoot it leaves.
lessons.s: The surface is never where the model says it is. A **guarded move** solves that by not caring: command small steps towards the surface and stop when the force sensor says you have arrived. The loop is short. Step, read the force, and `if force >= FORCE_THRESHOLD:` record `contact_z = z` and break.

lessons.g: Build the traverse of a retreat from the top of the lift and check that the carried part clears the bin wall.
lessons.s: More parts are lost on the way out than on the way in. The gripper is holding something now, the something hangs below the jaws, and the bin wall is exactly at the height the operator finds convenient. The retreat is two segments and only one of them needs checking.

lessons.g: Decide whether a part fits a parallel jaw gripper once the pad thickness and the approach gap are counted.
lessons.s: A 2F-85 opens 85 mm, and the largest part it picks is nowhere near 85 mm wide. Two 6 mm pads eat 12 mm of that, and you want a couple of millimetres either side so the fingers do not scrape the part on the way in.

lessons.t: Current Is the Only Force Sensor You Have
lessons.g: Turn a gripper motor current into an estimated jaw force and mark the readings that are below the noise floor.
lessons.s: Most industrial grippers have no force sensor. What they have is a motor, and the current that motor draws is roughly proportional to the force at the jaws once the drivetrain is loaded. That is the whole force feedback path on a cell that costs a hundred thousand euros.

lessons.t: The Window Between Slipping and Cracking
lessons.g: Command a grip force inside the window between the friction minimum and the crush limit, and refuse when the window is empty.
lessons.s: Two chapters ago you computed the smallest squeeze that holds a part, and the largest squeeze the part survives. A gripper driver has to turn those two numbers into one command, or into an honest refusal. The floor is `lo = SAFETY * mass * G / (2.0 * mu)`, the friction minimum with the safety factor already applied.

lessons.t: The Cup Holds Because Air Pushes
lessons.g: Size a vacuum cup by turning its diameter and its vacuum level into a holding force.
lessons.s: A suction cup does not pull. The atmosphere pushes, and the cup simply removes some of the air on one side so the push stops being balanced. That framing makes the arithmetic obvious and stops people believing a cup can exceed one atmosphere.

lessons.g: Find the largest tilt a vacuum cup can carry a part at, given that shear is limited by friction and not by vacuum.
lessons.s: The number on a cup datasheet is a lift rating, measured straight down the cup axis. Tilt the part and the load splits, and the two halves are limited by completely different physics. The part of the weight along the cup axis is `weight * math.cos(math.radians(tilt))`, and that is what the vacuum resists directly.

lessons.g: Model the vacuum decaying through a leaking seal and compute how long the cup can still hold the part.
lessons.s: A cup on machined aluminium seals. A cup on corrugated cardboard leaks through the flutes, and on a system with a small pump the vacuum starts falling the moment the ejector cycles off.

lessons.g: Split the tendon tension of an underactuated finger between its two phalanges and detect the ratio that ejects the part.
lessons.s: An underactuated finger has two joints and one motor. A tendon runs over a pulley at each joint, and the finger closes around whatever shape it meets without any sensing. That is why fruit picking hands and prosthetic hands are built this way, and why they occasionally throw the object out of the hand.

lessons.g: Compute the contact patch a compliant pad makes on a round part and turn it into torsional grip capacity.
lessons.s: The soft finger contact of the second chapter needed a patch radius and you were handed one. It is not a constant: it grows with the squeeze, which means the twist a grip resists grows with the squeeze twice over, once through the normal force and once through the patch.

lessons.t: Choosing the Tool Before the Grasp
lessons.g: Select a gripper type from the properties of a part with an ordered rule chain, and see what reordering the rules costs.
lessons.s: Everything so far assumed a gripper was already bolted on. Choosing it is a decision that a short ordered rule chain makes better than a long argument, provided the order is written down and defended. The chain here is three tests and a default.

lessons.g: Compute the force a stiff position servo generates from a small commanded overshoot into a surface.
lessons.s: A position controller has one job and it does it without judgement: go to the commanded pose and stay there. When the commanded pose is inside a solid object, staying there means pushing as hard as the arm can push.

lessons.t: The Spring You Get to Choose
lessons.g: Pick a virtual stiffness from a force budget and a position uncertainty, then compute the force it produces.
lessons.s: The fix for the last lesson is not a better position controller. It is a controller that behaves like a **spring** instead of like a vice, so that a position error turns into a bounded force rather than an unbounded one. The spring is virtual and you choose it.

lessons.g: Add damping to a virtual spring, sweep the damping ratio, and measure the overshoot each one leaves.
lessons.s: A spring on its own oscillates forever. Add a virtual damper and the second order system you have built gets the behaviour you asked for, which is arriving once rather than seven times.

lessons.g: Run an impedance controller into a surface and show that the contact force it settles at depends on where the surface is.
lessons.s: Here is the thing about impedance control that catches people who expected a force controller. It does not control force. It controls the **relation** between position error and force, and the force you end up with depends entirely on how far past the surface you told it to go.

lessons.t: Admittance Is the Other Way Round
lessons.g: Implement an admittance update and show that the gain that behaves on foam diverges on steel.
lessons.s: Impedance reads position and writes force. **Admittance** reads force and writes position, which is what you do when the arm underneath you only accepts position commands, and that is most industrial arms.

lessons.t: Asking For a Force and Getting It
lessons.g: Close a proportional integral loop on force error with a clamped integrator and show the offset the integral removes.
lessons.s: Impedance gives you a spring and its force depends on where the surface is. Closing a loop on the force error itself fixes that, and the loop is a standard PI whose output is a **position offset** into the surface. Proportional alone cannot get there and the arithmetic says why.

lessons.g: Show a force integrator winding up while the tool is in free air and add the guard that stops the slam on re contact.
lessons.s: A force controller in free air is asking for a force nothing is providing. The error sits at the full target, the integrator accumulates every cycle of it until it hits its clamp, and the reference sinks into a surface that is not there. Then the part arrives and everything the integrator saved up is spent in one hit.

lessons.g: Split a Cartesian command with a selection matrix so one axis tracks position while another regulates force.
lessons.s: Wiping a surface, deburring an edge, seating a connector: all of them want position control along some axes and force control along others, at the same time. **Hybrid control** does that with a diagonal selection matrix and no cleverness at all.

lessons.t: The Torque the Joints Have to Make
lessons.g: Map a desired fingertip force into joint torques through the Jacobian transpose and check them against the motor ratings.
lessons.s: All of this chapter has been asking for forces at the fingertip. The motors do not make forces, they make torques, and the bridge between the two is the transpose of the Jacobian you built in the Joint Cathedral. The relation is `tau = J.T @ f`, and it is exact, not an approximation.

lessons.g: Reduce a tactile pressure array to a total normal force and a centre of pressure.
lessons.s: A tactile pad is a grid of pressure cells, sixteen of them on a modest fingertip and several hundred on a research one. Nothing downstream wants a grid. What the grasp controller wants is two numbers.

lessons.g: Detect slip from the drift of the centre of pressure across a window, and see why consecutive frames cannot do it.
lessons.s: When a part slips through the fingers, the contact patch does not stay where it was. The centre of pressure walks across the pad, and that walk is one of the earliest signals you get, well before the part is visibly moving. The obvious implementation does not work and it is worth knowing why.

lessons.g: Compute how much of the friction cone a contact is using and raise a warning before the whole contact lets go.
lessons.s: A contact does not go from stuck to sliding in one step. The edge of the patch starts sliding first while the middle is still stuck, and that state, **incipient slip**, is the last moment at which squeezing harder still fixes anything.

lessons.g: Detect slip from the high frequency energy of a tactile signal instead of from its mean level.
lessons.s: Rubber sliding on a rigid part does not slide smoothly. It sticks, releases, sticks again, hundreds of times a second, and that stick slip cycle puts a buzz into the tactile signal that a mean pressure reading averages straight out. You do not need a spectrum to find it.

lessons.t: The Slip That Measured Your Pad
lessons.g: Estimate the real friction coefficient from a recorded slip event and recompute the squeeze the part actually needs.
lessons.s: Every slip is a free measurement, and it is the only honest one you will get. At the instant the part let go, the contact was exactly on the edge of its cone, so the ratio of the two forces at that instant **is** the friction coefficient: `estimate = ft_at_slip / fn_at_slip`.

lessons.g: Build an adaptive grip controller that steps the force up on a slip event and lets it decay back down between events.
lessons.s: Holding everything at maximum force is a policy, and it is the one most cells run. It marks soft parts, wears pads, costs cycle time on release, and it is what you do when you have no slip sensing.

lessons.g: Distinguish an object translating through the fingers from one rotating between them, using two tactile pads.
lessons.s: One pad cannot tell you whether the part slid or turned. Two can, and the test is a sign. When the part slides through the jaws, both centres of pressure walk the **same** way, because both pads are being dragged over the same moving surface.

lessons.g: Estimate the mass of the held part from a wrist force reading and use it to catch a double pick.
lessons.s: The wrist force torque sensor is measuring the gripper before it measures anything else. Take the reading with an empty gripper hanging still, call it the **tare**, and everything after that is the part.

lessons.g: Classify the outcome of a close from the jaw width, the grip force and the number of live tactile cells.
lessons.s: The last thing a pick routine does is decide whether it worked, and the answer has to be more specific than yes or no, because the recovery is different for each way of failing. Three signals separate four outcomes.

lessons.t: The Pose You Think It Is
lessons.g: Compute where the pads actually land when the estimated part pose is wrong, and decide whether the grasp still lands on the part.
lessons.s: Every grasp so far assumed the part was exactly where the estimate said. It is not. A calibrated camera at 600 mm gives you a couple of millimetres on a good day, a part sitting on a chamfer adds a couple more, and nothing in the pipeline tells you which day it is. The geometry is simple and the consequence is not.

lessons.t: The Grasp That Survives Being Wrong
lessons.g: Score a grasp by the fraction of perturbed poses it still succeeds on, and rank two candidates on robustness instead of on quality.
lessons.s: The metrics of the third chapter score a grasp at the pose you gave them. Reality gives a different pose every cycle, so the number that predicts the cell is not the quality of the nominal grasp, it is the fraction of the neighbourhood that still works. That is a Monte Carlo and it is thirty lines.

lessons.g: Decide whether a closing chamfered jaw can slide a misplaced part into the centre against table friction.
lessons.s: Closing jaws are not only a clamp, they are a funnel. A chamfered or V shaped jaw face turns the closing motion into a sideways push on the part, and if that push beats the friction holding the part to the table, the part slides into the middle by itself.

lessons.g: Predict which way a pushed part rotates from the moment of the push about its centre of friction.
lessons.s: Sometimes the right move is not to grasp at all. Pushing a part across a table is how you separate it from a neighbour, bring it out from a wall, or turn it into an orientation you can pick. To do that on purpose you have to predict which way it turns.

lessons.t: Push It Off the Wall First
lessons.g: Compute how far a part flush against a bin wall has to be pushed before a jaw fits behind it, and confirm the pick becomes legal.
lessons.s: A part lying flat against the bin wall is not a hard grasp, it is an impossible one. The far jaw has to occupy space the wall is already using, and no amount of scoring finds a grasp that fits. The fix is a **pre manipulation** action: push the part away from the wall by exactly enough and then run the normal pick.

lessons.t: How Fast You Are Allowed to Move
lessons.g: Compute the largest transport acceleration a grip survives, from the squeeze and the friction coefficient.
lessons.s: A grip that holds a part standing still is not a grip that holds it through a move. During transport the part needs a force of `mass` times the vector sum of gravity and the acceleration, and the fingers have `2 * mu * fn` of friction to supply all of it.

lessons.g: Invert the transport budget to get the squeeze a planned acceleration needs, and decide which knob to turn when it does not fit.
lessons.s: The last lesson answered how fast you may move at a given squeeze. Turn it round and you get the question a cell scheduler asks, which is how hard to squeeze for the move it already wants to make.

lessons.g: Turn slip margin, pose drift and in hand rotation into one ordered recovery decision.
lessons.s: By now you can measure four things about a grip in flight: how much of the friction cone it is using, how far the contact has drifted, how far the part has turned in the jaws, and whether the mass is what it should be. A cell needs one decision out of them, and the decision has more than two values.

lessons.t: Putting It Down Without Dropping It
lessons.g: Release a part only once the surface has taken its weight, and measure what releasing too early costs.
lessons.s: A place is a pick run backwards and it has one extra failure mode that a pick does not: the moment of release. Open the jaws while the arm is still pressing and the stored energy in the arm, the pad and the part goes somewhere, and where it goes is the part. The signal is the wrist.

lessons.g: Turn a bin of part records into a manifest with the weight and the commanded squeeze each part needs.
lessons.s: The last chapter of this workshop builds one pipeline out of the nine that came before it, and it starts where every real one starts: a list of parts and their properties, arriving from a database that nobody in robotics wrote.

lessons.t: What the Gripper Can Even Reach
lessons.g: Filter the bin on stroke, payload and wall clearance, and return a specific reason for each refusal.
lessons.s: The first filter is the hardware one and it has nothing to do with grasp quality. Either the gripper physically fits around the part and can carry it, or the rest of the pipeline is wasted work.

lessons.g: Refuse the parts whose friction minimum is above their crush limit, and report the window for the ones that pass.
lessons.s: The second filter belongs to the part rather than to the gripper, and it is the one that catches the foam. The floor is the friction minimum with the safety factor, `lo = SAFETY * mass * G / (2.0 * mu)`, and the ceiling is the crush limit.

lessons.g: Rank the surviving parts on grasp alignment and centre of mass offset so the cell picks the easy ones first.
lessons.s: Three parts are left and the order they are picked in matters more than it looks. Picking the easiest first empties the bin faster, exposes the harder parts to a clearer camera view, and means a cell that stops halfway has still delivered something.

lessons.g: Execute one pick with a creeping guarded descent and classify the close from width, force and tactile cells.
lessons.s: Now one part gets picked, and the execution is the fourth and seventh chapters wired together. The descent creeps and stops on force, exactly as in the guarded move: step down, read, and `if force >= FORCE_THRESHOLD:` record the contact height and stop.

lessons.g: Cap the transport acceleration to what the grip supports and step the squeeze up when the slip monitor fires.
lessons.s: The part is in the hand and the move is the part of the cycle where it gets dropped. Two mechanisms from the last two chapters do the work, and they answer different failures. The first is planning.

lessons.g: Run the whole bin through every stage and report the parts placed, the parts refused and the reason for each refusal.
lessons.s: Everything joins here. Seven parts go in, four stages run, and what comes out is a placed count, a refusal list with a reason on every line, and the sentence a shift supervisor can act on. The structure is the one that survives contact with a real cell.

lessons.g: Count how many times a robot routine crosses from user space into the kernel and back.
lessons.s: Your robot program does not touch the hardware. It cannot. The processor runs it in **user mode**, where the memory management unit hides every peripheral register behind a page table the process does not own. A write to the GPIO data register from user mode is a segmentation fault, not a moving wheel.

lessons.g: Turn the errno of a failed system call into the repair it actually points at.
lessons.s: A system call that fails returns -1 and leaves a number in `errno`. Python turns that into an `OSError` whose `.errno` attribute carries the same number, so nothing is lost. The number is not decoration: on an embedded board it is usually the whole diagnosis. Four of them cover most of what goes wrong on a robot.

lessons.g: Tell a regular file, a directory, a pipe and a character device apart from their stat mode.
lessons.s: Linux gives you one vocabulary for very different things: you `open` them, you `read` and `write` them, you `close` them. A configuration file, a serial port, a GPIO chip and a socket all answer to the same four verbs. That is why a robot program can be written without a single hardware specific API.

lessons.t: Three Filesystems That Hold No Disk
lessons.g: Read a mount table and separate the filesystems the kernel invents from the ones stored on media.
lessons.s: Run `mount` on a board and most of what you see is not storage. The kernel exports its own state as filesystems, so you can read it with `cat` instead of with a special tool. - **procfs**, mounted on `/proc`.

lessons.g: Judge a measured latency sample against a loop budget and decide whether the work belongs on Linux at all.
lessons.s: This is the honest lesson of the bay, and it decides the shape of every robot you build on Linux. Linux is a **throughput** operating system. Its scheduler, `SCHED_OTHER`, hands out fair shares of processor over time.

lessons.g: Claim a GPIO line by writing its number, as text, into the sysfs export file.
lessons.s: `/sys/class/gpio` is the oldest way to move a pin from a shell, and it is still on every board you will meet. It works by writing text into files.

lessons.g: Set the direction of an exported line and use the atomic forms that never glitch the output.
lessons.s: Once a line is exported it has a `direction` attribute holding one of four words. - `in`, the pin reads. - `out`, the pin drives, and the level it drives is whatever was in `value` before, which is usually 0 but is not promised. - `low`, the pin becomes an output already driving 0.

lessons.t: The Value That Arrives as Text
lessons.g: Read a sysfs attribute and turn it into the type your program actually wanted.
lessons.s:
Every sysfs attribute is text with a trailing newline. Reading `value` on an input line gives you `"0
"` or `"1
"`, three bytes at most, and never an integer. This is where a whole family of quiet bugs lives. `"0
"` is a non empty string, so `if read_value(line):` is true for a pin that is low.

lessons.g: Poll a sysfs attribute through a descriptor you keep open, without reading an empty string forever.
lessons.s: Opening and closing a file for every sample costs three system calls, and in a loop that reads six lines at 200 Hz that is thirty six hundred crossings a second for nothing. The obvious fix is to open the attribute once and keep the descriptor. The obvious fix has a trap in it. A descriptor carries an offset.

lessons.t: The Pin That Lies On Purpose
lessons.g: Use active_low so a wire that is inverted in hardware stops being inverted in your code.
lessons.s: Half the buttons on a robot are wired to ground with a pull up resistor, so pressing them reads 0. Half the enable lines on motor drivers are active low, so a 0 means run.

lessons.g: Translate the pin number printed on the board into the global line number the kernel uses.
lessons.s: The number you write into `export` is not the number silkscreened on the header. Sysfs numbers lines in one global space shared by every controller on the board, and each controller gets a slice of it.

lessons.g: Convert a servo specification in hertz and milliseconds into the nanosecond attributes sysfs wants.
lessons.s: PWM has its own class, `/sys/class/pwm/pwmchipN`, and it works like GPIO: write a channel number into `export`, get a `pwm0` directory with `period`, `duty_cycle`, `polarity` and `enable` inside. Both times are in **nanoseconds**, integers, no exceptions.

lessons.g: Write the PWM attributes in the only order the kernel accepts, and reject a duty cycle that cannot fit.
lessons.s: The PWM attributes are not independent, and the driver enforces the relationship on every write. `duty_cycle` must be less than or equal to `period`. A fresh channel comes up with `period` at 0, so the very first write of a duty cycle, no matter how small, is compared against zero and rejected with `EINVAL`.

lessons.t: Leave the Bay As You Found It
lessons.g: Release an exported line even when the code between export and unexport raises.
lessons.s: An exported GPIO line outlives your process. Nothing in the kernel notices that the program that exported it is gone, so the `gpio17` directory stays, the pin keeps driving whatever it was driving, and the next run of your service gets `EBUSY` on export and dies at startup.

lessons.t: A Node Is a Pair of Numbers
lessons.g: Split a device node identifier into its major and minor numbers and say what each one selects.
lessons.s: A device node in `/dev` carries almost no information. It has a type, character or block, and it has two numbers. That is the whole interface between a file name and a driver. The **major** number selects the driver.

lessons.g: Separate the entries in /dev the kernel creates by itself from the ones that only exist because udev ran.
lessons.s: `/dev` is a `devtmpfs`, and the kernel fills the first layer of it. When a driver binds to a device it registers a character or block device and `devtmpfs` immediately creates the node, owned by root, group root, mode 0600. No user space program is involved, which is what makes a board bootable before udev exists.

lessons.t: The Handle That Belongs to You
lessons.g: Claim GPIO lines through the character device, where the claim dies with the descriptor that made it.
lessons.s: The replacement for `/sys/class/gpio` is a character device per controller, `/dev/gpiochip0`. You open it, and then you ask it for the lines you want with an ioctl, giving a consumer name. What you get back is another file descriptor that represents **your claim on those lines**.

lessons.g: Build a real ioctl request number out of its direction, group, index and payload size.
lessons.s: `ioctl` takes a file descriptor, a request number and a pointer. The request number looks like a magic constant and it is not: it is four fields packed into 32 bits, and the kernel checks them.

lessons.g: Lay out the bytes an ioctl expects, and let the format string tell you the size instead of counting.
lessons.s: The pointer you hand to `ioctl` points at a C structure the kernel will read or fill in. Python has no C structures, so you build the bytes yourself with the `struct` module, and the format string is the contract.

lessons.t: The Port With a Name That Sticks
lessons.g: Resolve a stable by-id path to whatever ttyUSB number the adapter got on this boot.
lessons.s: `/dev/ttyUSB0` is not the name of your lidar. It is the name of whichever USB serial adapter was enumerated first, and enumeration order depends on which port the kernel scanned first, how fast each device answered, and whether somebody plugged the hub in the other way round.

lessons.g: Read a fixed length frame from a stream that hands you whatever happens to be in the buffer.
lessons.s: `read` on a character device returns what is available, not what you asked for. A serial port at 115200 baud delivers about eleven bytes per millisecond, so a request for a 12 byte frame typically returns three or five, whatever the driver had when your call arrived. The rest is still on the wire.

lessons.t: The Descriptor That Would Not Wait
lessons.g: Read a descriptor that refuses to block, and wait on it properly instead of spinning.
lessons.s: A blocking `read` on a serial port stops your thread until a byte arrives. If nothing ever arrives, the thread is gone. That is fine in a dedicated reader thread and fatal in a control loop.

lessons.g: Split a peripheral address into the page you can map and the offset inside it.
lessons.s: `/dev/mem` is the last resort. It hands you physical memory, so with a map of the chip you can write a GPIO register from user space and toggle a pin in nanoseconds instead of microseconds. Every bare metal habit works, and none of the kernel safety does. `mmap` cannot start wherever you like.

lessons.g: Decide which peripherals the kernel can find on its own and which ones have to be written down.
lessons.s: A PC never needed a device tree. PCI and USB are **discoverable**: the bus can be asked what is on it, every device answers with a vendor and product identifier, and the kernel loads a driver for the answer. Plug in a webcam and it works because it announced itself.

lessons.t: A Node, a Property, a Cell
lessons.g: Write a device tree node for an I2C sensor with its compatible string, its address and its interrupt.
lessons.s: A device tree source file is a tree of **nodes**, and a node holds **properties**. A node is written `name@address { ... };`. The part after the at sign is not decoration, it has to agree with the first cell of the `reg` property, and `dtc` warns when it does not.

lessons.g: Match a node against the drivers a kernel has, taking the most specific compatible string that anybody claims.
lessons.s: `compatible` is a list on purpose. A node writes down every identity it can honestly claim, from the most specific to the most generic, and the kernel walks the list in that order and takes the first one a driver has registered for. That single rule is what lets one kernel serve boards it was built before.

lessons.g: Decode a reg property into addresses and sizes, using the cell counts the parent node declares.
lessons.s: `reg` is a flat list of 32 bit cells, and on its own it means nothing. What it means is decided by two properties on the **parent**: `#address-cells`, how many cells make one address, and `#size-cells`, how many make one length.

lessons.g: Use status to enable the buses this robot uses and switch off the ones it does not.
lessons.s: A chip has more blocks than any board uses. The vendor writes them all into the shared include file, and each one carries `status = "disabled";`. A node that is disabled is parsed, kept in the tree, and never bound to a driver: no `/dev` entry, no clock enabled, no pins claimed.

lessons.g: Find the pins two enabled nodes are both trying to claim before the board boots and one of them loses.
lessons.s: Every pin on the package can do several things. GPIO 14 and 15 on a Broadcom part are a UART, or an I2C bus, or plain GPIO, depending on which alternate function the pin controller selects.

lessons.t: The Overlay That Patches a Board
lessons.g: Write a device tree overlay that enables a bus and adds a sensor to it without touching the board file.
lessons.s: You do not own the board file. It ships with the operating system image, it is replaced on the next update, and your change to it disappears. An **overlay** is the supported way to add your hardware: a separate blob, loaded on top of the base tree at boot, that says which node it is patching and what to put inside it.

lessons.g: Read the tree the kernel actually booted with out of /proc/device-tree.
lessons.s: The tree in the source file is not proof of anything. The tree the kernel booted with is, and the kernel exports it at `/proc/device-tree`, which is a symlink into sysfs. The layout is the tree itself.

lessons.g: Follow a phandle from one node to the node it points at, the way the kernel does after dtc has run.
lessons.s: `&gpio` is source code, not data. When `dtc` compiles the tree it replaces every reference with a plain 32 bit number called a **phandle**, and it gives the referenced node a `phandle` property holding that same number. The blob has no labels in it at all.

lessons.g: Parse a kernel uevent into its properties and decide whether a rule should fire on it.
lessons.s: Nothing in udev is magic and nothing polls. When a driver binds or a device disappears, the kernel sends a **uevent**: a small block of `KEY=value` lines over a netlink socket. `systemd-udevd` is listening, reads the block, runs it through every rule, and applies whatever the rules assigned.

lessons.t: A Rule Is Matches and Assignments
lessons.g: Write a udev rule that recognises one specific USB serial adapter and gives it a name of its own.
lessons.s: A rule is one line, a list of comma separated pairs, and every pair is either a **match** or an **assignment**. The operator is what tells them apart, and confusing the two is the single most common mistake in this file. - `==` and `!=` are matches. The rule only continues if they hold.

lessons.t: The Attributes of the Whole Chain
lessons.g: Find the one ancestor that carries every attribute a rule matches, and see why two attributes from different parents never match together.
lessons.s: `ATTR{...}` looks at the device the event is about. `ATTRS{...}`, with the S, walks **up** the chain of parents until it finds one that has the attribute. That is why a rule about `/dev/ttyUSB0` can match on `idVendor`, which belongs to the USB device three levels above the tty. Now the part that costs an afternoon.

lessons.t: A Link That Always Points Home
lessons.g: Give two identical looking adapters two stable names, told apart by the only thing that differs.
lessons.s: Two FTDI adapters on the same robot report the same vendor and the same product. `idVendor` and `idProduct` cannot tell them apart, and neither can `KERNEL`, because the number in `ttyUSB0` is the enumeration order that this whole chapter exists to escape from.

lessons.g: Hand a device node to the group the robot runs as, instead of running the robot as root.
lessons.s: The node the kernel creates is owned by root with mode 0600, so an ordinary user gets `EACCES` on `open`. There are two ways out and only one of them is acceptable. The bad one is running your robot as root.

lessons.t: The File Name Decides the Order
lessons.g: Work out what a device ends up with after every rules file has had its turn.
lessons.s: udev reads every file in `/lib/udev/rules.d` and `/etc/udev/rules.d`, sorts them all together by **file name**, and runs them in that order against every event. The numeric prefix is the whole mechanism: `50-udev-default.rules` runs before `60-rover.rules`, which runs before `99-last-word.rules`.

lessons.g: Catch the rule that assigns where it meant to compare, before it renames every device on the board.
lessons.s: One missing equals sign turns a filter into a catch all. Write `SUBSYSTEM="tty"` instead of `SUBSYSTEM=="tty"` and the rule stops asking anything: it assigns, so it matches every event on the system, and then applies its group, its mode and its symlink to all of them.

lessons.g: Read the properties udev ended up with for a node, and pull the links and the identity out of them.
lessons.s: `udevadm info --query=property --name=/dev/ttyUSB0` prints what udev knows about a node after all the rules have run. It is the fastest answer to "did my rule work", and unlike unplugging the device it can be done over a network connection to a robot that is bolted to something.

lessons.t: The Rule Must Not Start Your Robot
lessons.g: Decide what belongs in a rule and what has to become a service the rule only asks for.
lessons.s: `RUN+="/usr/bin/something"` looks like the answer to every bring up problem, and it is a trap. The program runs **inside the udev event**, so udev is blocked while it runs, every other device event on the board is queued behind it, and udev kills anything still alive after its timeout, by default around three minutes.

lessons.t: Three Digits and Who You Are
lessons.g: Turn a numeric mode into the nine permission bits it stands for.
lessons.s: `0660` is not a number anybody picked for looks. It is three octal digits, and each digit is three bits, in the order read, write, execute. The three digits are, in order, the **owner**, the **group** and **everybody else**. So 6 is 110, read and write and no execute.

lessons.t: The Group That Opens the Port
lessons.g: Work out every group a user really belongs to, primary and supplementary together.
lessons.s: A user has one **primary** group, written in their line in `/etc/passwd`, and any number of **supplementary** groups, written as membership lists in `/etc/group`. A permission check considers all of them, so the answer to "can this user open the port" starts with building the full set.

lessons.g: Run the real permission check, where the three sets of bits are alternatives and not a total.
lessons.s: The check the kernel runs is shorter than people think, and the surprise is in its shape. If your user identifier is 0, you are root and it stops there, allowed. Otherwise: if you own the file, only the **owner** bits are considered, and the check stops.

lessons.g: Predict the mode a new file will really get, once the umask has taken its share.
lessons.s: A program asks for a mode when it creates a file, and it never gets exactly that. The **umask** of the process removes bits from the request before the file is made. It is a mask of what to take away, which is why it reads backwards from everything else. The arithmetic is `requested & ~umask`.

lessons.g: Replace root with the two or three capabilities a robot service actually uses.
lessons.s: Root is not one permission, it is about forty. Linux splits them into **capabilities**, and a process can hold exactly the ones it needs and none of the rest. A service that runs as root because of one privileged operation is carrying thirty nine it will never use, and every one of them is available to any bug in it.

lessons.g: Find the component of a path that blocks a user, which is almost never the file at the end.
lessons.s: On a directory the three bits mean something else. `r` lets you list the names inside it. `x` lets you **enter** it, which means resolving a name through it. `w` lets you create and delete entries in it, and notice that deleting a file is a write to the directory, not to the file.

lessons.t: The Service That Drops What It Does Not Need
lessons.g: Build the smallest privilege set a service can run with and still do its job.
lessons.s: Now put the last five lessons together, because this is the decision you make for every service on the robot. Start from nothing: an ordinary user, no capabilities, no write access outside its own directory. Then add, one at a time, only what the service demonstrably needs.

lessons.t: The Bit That Protects a Shared Directory
lessons.g: Use the sticky bit so two services can share a directory without deleting each other's files.
lessons.s: Two services both write into `/run/rover`. The directory has to be group writable or neither can create anything. But write on a directory means create **and delete**, so each service can remove the other's socket, and one day one of them does, during cleanup, at start up, and the other one has been dead for an hour ...

lessons.g: Sweep every node the robot will open and report the ones that are wrong in either direction.
lessons.s: Two failures live at opposite ends of the same scale and both belong in one report. A node the robot **cannot** open stops the machine at start up, loudly, and gets fixed in ten minutes. A node that is **world writable** does not stop anything.

lessons.g: Follow the handover chain from the boot ROM to init and find the first stage that can do a given job.
lessons.s: Nothing on an embedded board goes straight to Linux. Four programs run first, each one bigger and more capable than the last, and each one exists because the one before it could not do the job. - The **boot ROM** is burned into the chip and cannot be changed.

lessons.t: The Line the Kernel Was Given
lessons.g: Parse the kernel command line into its settings and its bare flags.
lessons.s: The bootloader hands the kernel one string, and `/proc/cmdline` is that string, unchanged. It is the first thing to read when a board behaves differently from the one next to it, because a surprising amount of behaviour is decided here and nowhere else. The syntax is space separated tokens of two shapes.

lessons.t: The Root That Does Not Move
lessons.g: Choose a root specification that survives somebody plugging in a second disk.
lessons.s: `root=/dev/mmcblk0p2` works until the day it does not. Add a USB stick to a board that boots from an SD card and the enumeration can shift; move the same image to a board with eMMC and `mmcblk0` is the internal storage while the card became `mmcblk1`.

lessons.g: Decide whether this board needs an initramfs, instead of shipping one because everybody does.
lessons.s: An **initramfs** is a small filesystem the bootloader loads into RAM alongside the kernel. The kernel unpacks it, runs `/init` from it, and that script does whatever is needed to reach the real root, then hands over.

lessons.g: Write the init script of an initramfs: mount the kernel filesystems, find the real root, and hand over.
lessons.s: The kernel unpacks the initramfs and runs `/init` as **process 1**. Process 1 is special: it is never allowed to exit. If it does, the kernel panics with `Attempted to kill init`, which is the message you get when your script has a typo on the last line. The script does four things, always in this order.

lessons.g: Find where the boot really went by reading the gaps between kernel messages, not the messages.
lessons.s: Every line of `dmesg` starts with the seconds since the kernel started, in brackets, with six decimals. On a board that takes eleven seconds to boot, the interesting information is not in any single line, it is in the **distance** between two of them.

lessons.t: A Budget for the First Second
lessons.g: Turn a boot into a table of stages against a budget and name the one worth attacking.
lessons.s: A robot that has to be moving five seconds after power on needs a boot budget, and a budget is a table, not a feeling. Measure each stage once, write down what it cost, and compare against what you promised. The measurements come from four places. `dmesg` gives you kernel time, the first stamp to the last.

lessons.t: The Root That Cannot Be Written
lessons.g: Make a robot survive having its power cut by deciding, per path, what may be written and where it goes.
lessons.s: A robot loses power without warning. Not gracefully, not with a shutdown: somebody hits the emergency stop, or the battery protection cuts out mid write. A read only root filesystem is what turns that from a corrupted image into an event nobody notices.

lessons.t: Two Slots and a Way Back
lessons.g: Update a robot in the field without being able to visit it when the update is bad.
lessons.s: A robot in a field, on a roof or inside a machine cannot be recovered with an SD card reader. So the update scheme has to assume the new image is broken and still leave the machine reachable. The answer is **two slots**. The storage holds two complete root filesystems, A and B.

lessons.g: Write the service unit that starts a robot driver as an unprivileged user at boot.
lessons.s: A service on a modern Linux is a text file in `/etc/systemd/system` called `something.service`, and it has three sections. `[Unit]` is about the service as a thing in the system: what it is called in the logs, and how it relates to other units.

lessons.g: Separate ordering from requirement, and see which of the four combinations is the one you meant.
lessons.s: These two are confused more than anything else in systemd, and they are completely independent. `After=` is **ordering only**. It says: if both of us are being started, do not start me until it has finished starting.

lessons.g: Turn a pile of After= lines into the start up order they add up to, and refuse a set that eats itself.
lessons.s: No unit knows the whole order. Each one names the two or three things it must follow, and systemd works the rest out. What it is doing is a **topological sort**: repeatedly start everything whose dependencies are already up, until nothing is left.

lessons.t: When It Dies, Bring It Back
lessons.g: Restart a crashed driver automatically, and stop restarting it when it is clearly never going to work.
lessons.s: A robot driver that dies at three in the morning should come back by itself. `Restart=on-failure` does that: systemd notices the process exited with a non zero status or a signal, waits `RestartSec=`, and starts it again.

lessons.t: The Rate Limit That Gives Up
lessons.g: Run the start limit yourself and see exactly which restart is the one that stops the machine trying.
lessons.s: The rule is a sliding window and nothing more. Keep the times of the recent starts, throw away everything older than `StartLimitIntervalSec`, and if what is left is more than `StartLimitBurst`, refuse.

lessons.g: Make a service report that it is ready and keep proving it, so a hung loop is noticed instead of tolerated.
lessons.s: A process that is running is not the same as a service that is working. A control loop deadlocked on a mutex is still a live process, still `active (running)` in `systemctl status`, and completely useless. `Type=simple` cannot tell the difference, because all it knows is that the process exists.

lessons.t: The Log Has Fields, Not Lines
lessons.g: Query the journal the way it is actually stored, by field, instead of grepping text.
lessons.s: `journalctl` looks like a file of lines and is not. Every entry is a set of **fields**, and the human readable line is one field among many. That is why `journalctl -u rover-lidar -p err --since "10 min ago"` is exact where a `grep` over a text log is a guess. The fields you will use: `MESSAGE` is the text.

lessons.t: The Service That Waits for the Device
lessons.g: Bind a driver to the device it drives, so it starts when the hardware appears and stops when it is unplugged.
lessons.s: This closes the race from chapter 2. Every device udev knows about is also a **device unit**: `/dev/rover/lidar` is `dev-rover-lidar.device`, with the slashes turned into dashes.

lessons.g: Generate the hardening lines for a service from what it genuinely touches.
lessons.s: systemd can take things away from a service, and each one costs a line. The four that pay for themselves on a robot: - `ProtectSystem=strict` mounts the whole filesystem read only for this service, and then `ReadWritePaths=` lists the exceptions.

lessons.t: The Machine That Builds Is Not the Machine That Runs
lessons.g: Name the kind of build you are doing from the three machines involved in it.
lessons.s: Three machines take part in a build, and they have names that are worth learning once because every toolchain error message uses them. The **build** machine is the one running the compiler. The **host** machine is the one the program you are producing will run on.

lessons.g: Read a toolchain prefix and say what machine it produces code for.
lessons.s: `aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc` is not a name somebody invented, it is four fields with dashes between them and a trailing dash before the tool. The fields are **architecture**, **vendor**, **operating system** and **ABI**.

lessons.g: Read the ELF header of a compiled file and say which machine it is really for.
lessons.s: Every executable and every shared library on Linux starts with an **ELF header**, and the first 24 bytes of it answer the question you care about after a cross build: is this actually for the board. The first four bytes are the magic, `\x7fELF`. Byte 4 is the class, 1 for 32 bit and 2 for 64 bit.

lessons.t: Hard Float Is Not a Suggestion
lessons.g: Catch an ABI mismatch between a program and a library before the linker does it with a worse message.
lessons.s: Two binaries for the same architecture can still be unable to speak to each other, because the **ABI** decides how arguments are passed and they have to agree. On 32 bit ARM the split that bites is floating point.

lessons.t: The Root That Is Not Yours
lessons.g: Point every include and library path at the sysroot, and find the flag that is still reaching into your laptop.
lessons.s: A cross compiler needs headers and libraries for the **board**, not for the machine it is running on. That collection is the **sysroot**: a directory that looks like the root filesystem of the target, with `usr/include` and `usr/lib` inside it, usually copied from the board or unpacked from the image.

lessons.g: Turn a native Makefile into one that builds for the board by changing the tools, not the rules.
lessons.s: Almost every embedded Makefile, including the kernel's own, uses one variable for this. `CROSS_COMPILE` holds the prefix, trailing dash included, and every tool is that prefix followed by its name: `$(CROSS_COMPILE)gcc`, `$(CROSS_COMPILE)ld`, `$(CROSS_COMPILE)objcopy`, `$(CROSS_COMPILE)strip`.

lessons.t: Teaching CMake Where the Robot Lives
lessons.g: Write the toolchain file that makes CMake build for the board, and stop it finding your laptop's libraries.
lessons.s: CMake does not take a `CROSS_COMPILE` variable. It takes a **toolchain file**, passed once at configure time with `cmake -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=aarch64.cmake ..`, and read before anything else so the compiler tests run against the right compiler. The first two lines say what the machine is.

lessons.t: Static Costs Space, Dynamic Costs Trust
lessons.g: Choose between linking statically and dynamically for each program on the robot, with a reason you can defend.
lessons.s: Linking statically copies the library into your binary. Linking dynamically leaves a reference that `ld.so` resolves at start up from the shared object on the board. Static is tempting on a robot.

lessons.g: Work out what a binary actually occupies on the board, which is a small fraction of the file you built.
lessons.s: A freshly built binary with debug information can be four megabytes while the code inside it is a hundred and fifty kilobytes. On a board with a small flash that difference decides whether the image fits, and it is worth being able to compute rather than guess. Sections split into three kinds.

lessons.g: Walk sysfs and produce the list of every device this board actually has.
lessons.s: The project of this chapter is a commissioning pass: a program you run once on a new board, or on every boot of a robot you care about, that answers whether the machine is what you think it is. It starts with an inventory, because every check after this one is a comparison against a list.

lessons.t: The Names the Robot Will Use
lessons.g: Run your own rules over the inventory and produce the name every device will answer to.
lessons.s: Now apply chapter 4 to the inventory. Each rule is a subsystem, a set of attributes that must all match, and the link name to give whatever matches. Running them yourself, before the board is in the robot, answers two questions that udev will not answer for you.

lessons.t: The Order It Comes Up In
lessons.g: Build the start up order for the robot and hold back the services whose hardware is not on this board.
lessons.s: Chapter 7 sorted units by their dependencies. On a real machine there is a second question that has to be asked at the same time: is the device this unit is bound to actually here. A unit with `BindsTo=` a device that does not exist will never start, and systemd is right not to start it.

lessons.g: Turn a pin configuration into the exact sequence of sysfs writes, refusing a plan that claims a line twice.
lessons.s: This is chapter 1 turned into something you can put in a file. A robot has a table of pins: which line, what it is for, whether it is an input or an output, and what the PWM channels should be set to. The bring up program reads that table and produces writes. Two things have to happen before any write.

lessons.t: The Permissions Audit Before First Power
lessons.g: Check every node the robot will open against the user it will run as, before the robot runs as that user.
lessons.s: Chapter 5 built the pieces. This is where they are run against a real list, and the value of doing it here is that every failure it finds is a failure that would otherwise happen at three in the morning with the machine on a table you cannot reach.

lessons.g: Cut a real boot log into named stages and say which stage owns the time.
lessons.s: The budget from chapter 6 was a table somebody typed. This is the same table built from the log the machine produced, which is the only version that stays true. The method is markers.

lessons.g: Put the whole chapter into one verdict, and make the fixes change it.
lessons.s: The last thing. Six checks have run, each one producing findings, and now somebody has to decide whether this machine goes into a robot. That decision needs a report with exactly three properties. It has to be **short**: one line per check, a verdict, and the count of findings.

lessons.g: Convert a load quoted in milliamps into the watts it takes off a rail.
lessons.s: Every part bolted to a robot is bought with three numbers: the **volts** its rail must supply, the **amps** it pulls from that rail, and the product of the two, the **watts** it burns. Volts alone say nothing about cost. Amps alone say nothing either. Datasheets almost never quote amps.

lessons.g: Turn watts and hours into watt hours, and watt hours back into hours.
lessons.s: A watt is a **rate**. A watt hour is an **amount**. Confusing the two is the most common mistake in a power review, and it always shows up as a runtime that is off by a factor of somebody guessed. A robot that burns `12 W` and runs for `8 h` has spent `96 Wh`.

lessons.g: Convert a cell label in milliamp hours into energy in watt hours.
lessons.s: A cell is labelled in **milliamp hours**, and that number is not energy. It is charge: how many milliamps the cell can push for one hour. To turn charge into energy you have to know the voltage it comes out at. A Samsung INR18650-35E is `3500 mAh` at `3.6 V` nominal. Divide by `1000.0` and you have `3.5 Ah`.

lessons.g: Rank two packs by energy and show why the amp hour figure cannot rank them.
lessons.s: A shop lists a `5000 mAh` pack at 12 V and a `2500 mAh` pack at 24 V. The first number is twice the second, and the two packs hold exactly the same energy: 60 watt hours each. The bigger label sold nothing but volts you were not told about.

lessons.g: Estimate runtime by dividing capacity by draw and name the three reasons it reads high.
lessons.s: Divide milliamp hours by milliamps and the milli cancels on both sides, leaving hours. A `3400 mAh` cell feeding a steady `850 mA` gives exactly 4 hours. That is the whole calculation, and it is the number every datasheet and every forum post quotes.

lessons.g: State the nominal, full and empty voltage of a cell and compute the swing between them.
lessons.s: A cell does not have a voltage. It has a **window**, and it walks across that window as it empties. Lithium ion leaves the charger at `4.2 V` and is considered flat at `3.0 V`. LiFePO4 goes from `3.65 V` down to `2.5 V`. A NiMH cell runs `1.45 V` to `1.0 V`, and one lead acid cell `2.4 V` to `1.75 V`.

lessons.g: Stack cells in series and scale the whole voltage window by the count.
lessons.s: Wire the positive of one cell to the negative of the next and the voltages add while the amp hours stay exactly where they were. Three lithium ion cells in series is a **3S** pack, and every point of the window multiplies by three: `10.8 V` nominal, `12.6 V` full, `9.0 V` empty.

lessons.g: Stack cells in parallel and scale capacity and current limit while the voltage stays put.
lessons.s: Wire all the positives together and all the negatives together and you get a **parallel group**. The voltage window does not move at all. What grows is the amp hours and the current the group can deliver without cooking.

lessons.g: Compute the voltage, capacity and energy of a pack described as SxP.
lessons.s: A pack is named by the two counts together. **3S2P** means three cells in series repeated twice in parallel: six cells, `10.8 V` nominal, `7000 mAh`, and `75.6 Wh` of energy. The arithmetic has one rule and it is easy to get backwards. The series count owns the volts. The parallel count owns the amp hours.

lessons.g: Remove a reserve fraction from a pack and compare the honest runtime with the ceiling.
lessons.s: A lithium ion pack taken down to `3.0 V` per cell on every cycle will not see many cycles. Take the same pack to `3.5 V` per cell instead and it lasts several times longer, at the cost of leaving perhaps twenty percent of the energy in the pack.

lessons.g: Convert a C rate into amps using the capacity of the pack it refers to.
lessons.s: Cells are compared with a rate that carries no amps in it at all. **1C** is whatever current empties the pack in one hour, so on a `3.4 Ah` cell 1C is `3.4 A`, and on a `100 Ah` truck battery 1C is `100 A`. The point of the notation is that it travels between sizes.

lessons.t: What the Cell Will Not Give
lessons.g: Compute a pack current limit from the per cell rating and judge a load against it.
lessons.s: Every cell has a **continuous discharge** rating, and pulling above it does not blow anything up on the spot. It heats the cell, and a hot cell ages fast. The damage is invisible until the pack that used to run four hours runs two.

lessons.g: Judge a short high current pulse against both an amp limit and a time limit.
lessons.s: A drive motor that stalls against a table leg pulls four or five times its running current until something gives. A cell datasheet answers that case with a second rating: a **pulse** or burst current, valid for a stated number of seconds. So a burst has two numbers and both of them can fail.

lessons.g: Estimate pack mass from energy and chemistry, including the overhead around the cells.
lessons.s: Energy has a mass, and on anything that moves you pay for it twice: once to carry it and once to accelerate it. The figure that matters is **energy density** in watt hours per kilogram. At cell level, lithium ion 18650 cells land near `250 Wh/kg`, LiFePO4 near `120`, NiMH near `90`, and lead acid near `35`.

lessons.g: Add a table of consumers into a single figure in watts.
lessons.s: A power budget is a table, and the discipline is that nothing on the robot is allowed to be missing from it. Every board, every motor, every sensor, every indicator LED gets a line with the rail it sits on and the current it pulls. The rails differ, so the currents cannot be added.

lessons.g: Turn on and off times into a duty cycle and an average current.
lessons.s: The headlight bar on a delivery robot pulls `1200 mA`, and it is on for two seconds out of every twenty. Budgeting it at 1200 mA sizes the pack for a robot that does not exist. The **duty cycle** is the fraction of the time a load is actually drawing.

lessons.g: Compute the peak and the average of the same budget and say which one sizes what.
lessons.s: A budget produces two totals and confusing them ruins hardware in both directions. The **average** is what the pack has to store. It is every line multiplied by its duty, and it decides how many amp hours you buy.

lessons.g: Add up a standby budget and compute how long the pack survives with the robot switched off.
lessons.s: A robot that is off is not drawing zero. The BMS is watching the cells, the microcontroller is in stop mode waiting for a button, the radio is in deep sleep, and somebody left a status LED on. Those numbers are tiny and the time is enormous, which is exactly the combination that empties packs.

lessons.g: Weight a budget by the minutes each phase lasts and find the true average watts.
lessons.s: A duty cycle per part is the small version of this idea. The large version is that a robot has **phases**, and each one has its own power and its own length.

lessons.t: From Watts to the Shopping List
lessons.g: Convert an average power and a target runtime into the amp hours a pack must hold.
lessons.s: A budget in watts does not buy anything. Cells are sold in amp hours at a voltage, so the last step of any budget is a conversion the other way. It has three parts and they go in this order. Multiply the average watts by the hours you want and you have the **energy** the mission needs.

lessons.g: Apply an unknowns margin and an ageing margin to a budget and judge two pack sizes against it.
lessons.s: The budget you just built is a best case built from datasheet numbers, and datasheet numbers are measured by people who wanted a good number. Two margins cover most of the gap.

lessons.g: Rank the consumers of a budget by average watts and report each share of the total.
lessons.s: A budget that is only a total tells you whether the design fits. A budget that is **ranked** tells you what to do about it when it does not. The rule of thumb is brutal and reliable: one or two lines are most of the sheet.

lessons.t: The Sheet That Buys the Pack
lessons.g: Assemble average, margin, mission energy and pack amp hours into one report.
lessons.s: Everything in this chapter exists to produce four numbers, and a power review is over when somebody can read them off one screen. The **average** is the honest draw of the robot as it really runs. The **design** figure is that average with the margins on it.

lessons.g: Compute the terminal voltage of a cell under load from its internal resistance.
lessons.s: A cell is not a voltage source. It is a voltage source with a resistor welded inside it, and that resistor is the reason a robot browns out the instant the motors start. The number is called **internal resistance** and it is quoted in milliohms. A healthy 18650 sits somewhere near `40 mohm` when new and warm.

lessons.g: Compute pack internal resistance from the series and parallel counts and see the sag shrink.
lessons.s: Internal resistance follows the stack exactly the way you would expect from any other resistor. Series **adds** it, parallel **divides** it, and a pack of `40 mohm` cells arranged 3S1P is a `120 mohm` pack. That is the hidden cost of a tall pack.

lessons.g: Derive internal resistance and open circuit voltage from two loaded measurements.
lessons.s: The internal resistance of the pack on your bench is not the one in the datasheet. It depends on the cells, the welds, the age and the temperature, so you measure it. Two points are enough. Read the terminal voltage at a light load and again at a heavy one.

lessons.g: Predict whether a peak current drives the pack below the brownout floor at each state of charge.
lessons.s: A robot that reboots when it accelerates is not a software problem. The peak current sagged the pack below what the converters needed, they dropped their rails, and the computer that was mid sentence stopped existing. The test is arithmetic and you can do it before you build anything.

lessons.g: Add cable and connector resistance to the pack and see what share of the sag they own.
lessons.s: The pack is not the only resistor between the cells and the motors. The wire is one, and so is every connector, every fuse holder and every switch on the way. Copper is quoted in milliohms per metre: `13.17` for 16 AWG, `8.28` for 14 AWG, `5.21` for 12 AWG.

lessons.g: Compute the internal heating loss at a current and its share of the power delivered.
