lessons.s: The volts lost to internal resistance do not disappear, they become heat inside the pack. The power spent that way is the current **squared** times the resistance, and the square is what makes it a design problem rather than a footnote.

lessons.g: Compensate a loaded voltage reading back to open circuit before judging the pack.
lessons.s: A robot reads `10.4 V` at its pack terminals while both motors pull `20 A`. If the low battery threshold is `10.6 V` the machine parks itself and reports an empty pack that is in fact two thirds full.

lessons.g: Scale internal resistance by temperature and recompute the sag at each one.
lessons.s: Internal resistance is a chemistry rate, and chemistry slows down in the cold. A lithium ion cell that measures `60 mohm` as a pack at 25 degrees measures well over twice that near twenty below.

lessons.g: Trip a low voltage cutoff only after the loaded rail stays down for several samples.
lessons.s: A pack under a heavy pulse dips below the cutoff and climbs straight back the moment the pulse ends. A controller that trips on the first sample will park a robot with a third of its energy left, every single time it accelerates near the end of a run.

lessons.t: The Linear Rail Pays Full Price
lessons.g: Show that a linear regulator draws the load current from the pack whatever the voltage drop is.
lessons.s: A linear regulator is a valve. The current that leaves it is the current that entered it, and the extra volts it did not pass on are burned. That second half is the famous one. The first half is the one that decides your runtime. A 5 V rail delivering `1 A` from an `11.1 V` pack pulls exactly `1 A` off the pack.

lessons.t: The Switching Rail Buys the Ratio
lessons.g: Compute pack current for a buck converter, where power is conserved instead of current.
lessons.s: A switching converter does not pass current through, it passes **power** through. What comes out is what went in minus a loss, so the input current is set by the voltage ratio rather than by the load current. The arithmetic is three steps. The rail power is its volts times its amps.

lessons.g: Interpolate a converter efficiency from a load table instead of using one headline figure.
lessons.s: The `94` percent on the front page of a converter datasheet is measured at one load, usually the one that flatters the part. Efficiency is a **curve**, and the ends of it are where robots live.

lessons.t: The Day the Rail Gives Up
lessons.g: Compute the minimum pack voltage a regulator needs and the share of the window it costs you.
lessons.s: Every regulator needs its output plus some headroom at the input, and below that it stops regulating. That headroom is the **dropout** voltage, and it decides when your pack is empty far more often than the cells do. An old LM7805 wants about `2.0 V` of it, so a 5 V rail needs `7.0 V` at the input.

lessons.g: Compute boost converter input current and show it rising as the pack empties.
lessons.s: A boost converter makes a rail higher than the pack. Power still crosses it, so making volts out of nothing means taking **more amps in than it gives out**. A 12 V motor rail at `3 A` is 36 watts. From a 3S pack at `12.6 V` and `0.90` efficiency the input is `3.17 A`.

lessons.g: Sum the pack current of a mixed tree of linear and switching rails.
lessons.s: A real robot has three or four rails and they are not the same kind of converter. The 12 V motor rail is a boost, the 5 V logic rail is a buck, and the quiet 3.3 V rail for the analogue sensors is a linear regulator precisely because it is quiet.

lessons.g: Cost a converter quiescent current in watt hours per week and compare two parts.
lessons.s: A converter with nothing connected to its output is still drawing. That is its **quiescent current**, and the spread between parts is enormous in a way that no other specification is. A general purpose buck like the TPS5430 sits near `15 mA` doing nothing.

lessons.g: Compare a linear and a switching rail by the runtime each one leaves on the same pack.
lessons.s: The usual way to choose between a linear regulator and a switcher is heat: work out the watts burned and decide whether you can get rid of them. On a machine that plugs into a wall that is the whole question. On a battery it is the wrong question, or at least the second one.

lessons.g: Find which converter loses regulation first and recompute the real empty voltage of the pack.
lessons.s: A pack is empty when the robot stops working, and that is almost never when the cells are flat. It is when the **first** converter on the tree runs out of input voltage.

lessons.t: The Curve That Tells the Truth
lessons.g: Map a rested cell voltage to a state of charge by interpolating an open circuit table.
lessons.s: A rested lithium ion cell has a repeatable relationship between its voltage and how full it is. That relationship is a **curve**, not a line, and it is the cheapest fuel gauge in existence. The shape matters.

lessons.g: Model voltage relaxation after a load and show the charge reading climbing to the truth.
lessons.s: The open circuit table is only valid for a cell that is **at rest**, and a cell does not rest the instant the load goes away. It climbs back over minutes as the chemistry inside settles. A reasonable model is an exponential recovery with a time constant of a couple of minutes.

lessons.g: Integrate current over time into milliamp hours spent and a remaining state of charge.
lessons.s: The other way to know how full a pack is does not look at voltage at all. It measures the current and adds it up. That is **coulomb counting**, and it is what every serious fuel gauge chip does. The arithmetic is one line and the units are the whole difficulty.

lessons.g: Show a small current sense bias growing into a large charge error over hours.
lessons.s: A coulomb counter adds up its own mistakes. If the current sense reads two percent high, then every hour it invents two percent of an hour of current, and nothing ever takes it back. Two percent sounds harmless.

lessons.g: Count coulombs while the robot works and snap the estimate to the voltage curve when it rests.
lessons.s: The two gauges have opposite faults, so the standard answer is to use both. Count coulombs continuously, because that is accurate over minutes, and **re anchor** to the open circuit curve whenever the robot has been still long enough for the reading to mean something.

lessons.t: The Pack Is Not Its Label
lessons.g: Apply cycle fade to the nameplate capacity and show the gauge error it causes.
lessons.s: A pack loses capacity as it is used. A reasonable figure for good lithium ion cells worked gently is about **three percent per hundred cycles**, and it is worse if the pack is run hot, charged to the very top, or emptied to the very bottom.

lessons.g: Turn a state of charge and a present draw into remaining hours above the reserve.
lessons.s: A percentage on a screen is not an answer. The question a robot has to answer is how many minutes of work are left, and that needs three numbers: the charge, the capacity and the current it is drawing right now. The subtlety is the **reserve**.

lessons.g: Compute the energy a return trip needs and decide whether to carry on or turn back.
lessons.s: The reserve is a blunt instrument. A robot two metres from its dock and a robot at the far end of a warehouse need very different amounts of energy held back, and a fixed twenty percent is wrong for both. The sharp version computes the **return cost** from where the robot actually is.

lessons.g: Judge a pack on its lowest cell rather than on the average and show the two disagreeing.
lessons.s: A pack voltage is a sum, and a sum hides everything. Three cells at `3.55`, `3.52` and `3.10` volts average `3.39`, which looks like a pack with charge left. The third cell is nearly flat and it is the one that will be damaged.

lessons.t: Two Phases and a Full Stop
lessons.g: Classify a charging cell into constant current, constant voltage or finished.
lessons.s: A lithium cell is charged in two phases and then left alone, and mixing them up is how packs catch fire. In **constant current** the charger pushes a fixed current and lets the cell voltage climb wherever it wants.

lessons.g: Turn a charge C rate into amps and into the hours the constant current phase lasts.
lessons.s: Charging has its own C rate and it is not the discharge one. Most lithium ion cells accept `0.5C` comfortably, many accept `1C`, and almost none should be charged faster than that without a datasheet in front of you saying so. On a `7 Ah` pack, `0.5C` is `3.5 A`.

lessons.g: Model the constant voltage taper and compute how long it runs before termination.
lessons.s: Once the cell reaches its ceiling voltage the charger stops pushing and starts holding. The current then falls away roughly **exponentially**, because what drives it is the shrinking difference between the charger and the cell.

lessons.t: Why Faster Is Not Twice as Fast
lessons.g: Add both charging phases and show that doubling the current barely shortens the total.
lessons.s: Put the two phases together and something uncomfortable appears. The constant current phase halves when you double the current, exactly as promised. The constant voltage phase gets **longer**, because it starts from a higher current and has further to fall.

lessons.g: Compute the energy drawn from the mains for one charge, including both efficiency losses.
lessons.s: The energy that leaves the wall is more than the energy that ends up in the pack, and it is lost in two places. The cells themselves are not perfectly efficient.

lessons.g: Return the charge rate a cell temperature allows, including the temperatures that allow none.
lessons.s: A lithium ion cell must not be charged below **zero degrees**. Not slowly, not gently: the lithium plates out as metal on the anode instead of intercalating, the damage is permanent, and enough of it makes an internal short. Discharging in the cold is merely inefficient.

lessons.g: Estimate calendar ageing from the charge level a pack is stored at.
lessons.s: A pack sitting in a cupboard loses capacity even though nobody used it. This is **calendar ageing**, it is separate from cycle wear, and the charge level it is stored at changes it by a factor of five.

lessons.t: Sizing the Thing on the Wall
lessons.g: Compute the supply power a charger needs at full pack voltage and pick a standard size.
lessons.s: The charger supply is sized at the **worst** moment, which is the end of the constant current phase: the current is still at its maximum and the pack voltage is nearly at its maximum too. For a 4S pack that means `16.8 V`, not the `14.4 V` nominal that a careless calculation would use.

lessons.g: Work out how many robots a shared supply can charge at once and how long a fleet rotation takes.
lessons.s: One robot is a power budget. A fleet is a **schedule**, and the constraint moves from the pack to the building. A charging room with a `600 W` supply and robots that need `67 W` each can run eight of them at once, not nine, because the remainder is not a slot.

lessons.g: Compare the sum of the cell taps against the measured pack voltage to detect a broken sense wire.
lessons.s: A battery management system exists because a pack terminal voltage tells you almost nothing. What it watches is **every cell separately**, through a set of thin sense wires called taps, plus the current through the pack and the temperature of the cells. Those taps are the most fragile thing in the whole assembly.

lessons.g: Classify one cell against its undervoltage and overvoltage limits.
lessons.s: Every cell has two hard limits and crossing either one damages it permanently. The **undervoltage** wall for lithium ion is around `2.50 V`, and a protection cutoff is normally set above it, at `3.00 V` or higher, so the pack stops with margin rather than at the edge.

lessons.g: Measure cell spread in millivolts and classify how urgent the imbalance is.
lessons.s: Cells in series start matched and slowly stop being matched. Small differences in self discharge and internal resistance accumulate, and after a few hundred cycles the pack has a leader and a straggler.

lessons.g: Compute passive balancing current and the hours it takes to remove an imbalance.
lessons.s: The common cure for imbalance is embarrassingly crude. A resistor is switched across the cell that is ahead and the excess charge is turned into heat until the others catch up. That is **passive balancing**, and almost every small BMS does it that way.

lessons.t: How Long May It Be Wrong
lessons.g: Apply an inverse time overcurrent curve so brief peaks ride through and sustained ones trip.
lessons.s: An overcurrent protection with a single threshold is useless on a robot. Motors draw several times their running current every time they start, and a BMS that trips on that never lets the machine move. The answer is a **trip curve**: the further over the limit you are, the less time you are allowed to stay there.

lessons.t: The Part That Is Meant to Die
lessons.g: Size a fuse from the derated continuous current and check a burst against its energy rating.
lessons.s: A fuse is the last protection and the only one with no software in it. Sizing it has two halves and people usually do only the first. The first half is the continuous current. A fuse does not carry its printed rating forever in a warm enclosure, so **derate** it, typically to seventy five percent.

lessons.g: Apply separate temperature limits for charging and discharging to the same cell reading.
lessons.s: A pack has two temperature windows and they are not the same size, which is the single most common mistake in a homemade BMS. **Discharging** is allowed from about minus twenty to sixty degrees. Cold discharge is inefficient and sags badly, but it does not destroy anything.

lessons.g: Compute inrush current into bulk capacitance and size a precharge resistor and its delay.
lessons.s: Close a contactor between a pack and a robot full of bulk capacitors and, for an instant, the capacitors are a short circuit. The only thing limiting the current is the resistance of the path. An `11.1 V` pack through `20 mohm` of wiring and contacts delivers `555 A` into that capacitance.

lessons.g: Latch a protection fault and re-arm it only after a deliberate clear and enough clean samples.
lessons.s: A protection that clears itself the moment the condition goes away is not a protection, it is an oscillator. The overcurrent trips, the load disappears, the current falls, the protection re arms, the load comes back, and the pack is now being switched on and off several times a second. So faults **latch**.

lessons.g: Apply the Peukert relationship to find the usable capacity at a draw above the rated one.
lessons.s: A pack rated `100 Ah` is rated at a particular current, usually a very gentle one. Pull harder and you do not get 100 amp hours, you get fewer, and the effect has a name: **Peukert**. The rule of thumb is a power law with an exponent that depends on the chemistry.

lessons.g: Step a repeating mission profile until the usable energy is gone and count the missions completed.
lessons.s: Every runtime figure so far has been a division. That is fine for a robot with one steady load and useless for a robot with a **schedule**. The honest way is to step the profile. Spend the energy of each phase, add its hours, and stop when the usable energy is gone.

lessons.t: The Cold Keeps Some of It
lessons.g: Derate usable capacity by temperature and recompute the runtime at each one.
lessons.s: Cold does two separate things to a pack and this course has now met both. It raises the internal resistance, which is the sag, and it lowers the **usable capacity**, which is the runtime. The second effect is roughly this: about `85` percent of the nameplate at zero degrees, `75` at minus ten, `60` at minus twenty.

lessons.t: The Cost of a Deep Cycle
lessons.g: Compare cycle life at several depths of discharge and cost the energy the pack delivers over its life.
lessons.s: How long a pack lasts is decided less by how many cycles you run than by how **deep** they are. A lithium ion pack cycled to empty every day gives around `500` cycles. Cycled to eighty percent depth it gives about `900`, to sixty about `1500`, to forty about `3000`.

lessons.g: Add the electricity and the pack wear of one mission and see which of the two dominates.
lessons.s: A robot mission costs money in two ways and almost everybody counts only the first. The **electricity** is the energy taken from the wall, which is the mission energy inflated by the cell and charger losses. At a quarter of a unit per kilowatt hour, a `34.77 Wh` mission costs about one cent.

lessons.t: Buy the Pack for Its Last Day
lessons.g: Size a pack so the mission still fits when the cells have faded to their end of life capacity.
lessons.s: A pack that exactly meets the mission on the day it is unwrapped fails the mission a year later. Cells are normally considered worn out at **eighty percent** of nameplate, and that is a fully working pack, not a broken one. So the sizing has three divisions stacked on one multiplication.

lessons.t: The Pack You Have to Carry
lessons.g: Show that runtime grows more slowly than pack size because the extra mass costs power to move.
lessons.s: Doubling the pack does not double the runtime on anything that moves, because the robot now has to carry the pack it just bought. Model it simply.

lessons.g: Turn internal heating into a steady state pack temperature and judge it against the safe limit.
lessons.s: The internal heating from chapter three has to go somewhere, and where it goes is the temperature of the cells. In steady state the rise above ambient is the loss in watts multiplied by the **thermal resistance** of the pack to its surroundings.

lessons.t: The Numbers on the Shipping Form
lessons.g: Classify a pack against the transport thresholds using its energy in watt hours.
lessons.s: The last thing a pack design has to survive is a shipping desk, and the only number anybody there cares about is **watt hours**. Not cells, not amp hours, not chemistry beyond the word lithium. The thresholds worth knowing for passenger air travel are `100 Wh` and `160 Wh`.

lessons.g: Turn a delivery route specification into the pack energy the robot has to carry.
lessons.s: The machine for the rest of this chapter is a small indoor delivery robot. It runs a **route** of five deliveries, each one twenty eight minutes long, made of four phases: idle at the dock, drive out, wait at the door, drive back.

lessons.g: Build the phase power from the parts list and check each phase against the specification.
lessons.s: The customer gave you watts per phase. The robot has parts, and the parts do not know what a phase is. The bridge between the two is a table where every consumer carries a **duty per phase**, and it is the single most useful document in a power design. Read it as a grid.

lessons.g: Compute the pack current of the full rail tree including every converter quiescent draw.
lessons.s: The robot has three rails. The motors run from a `12 V` buck, the compute and the lidar from a `5 V` buck, and the analogue sensors from a `3.3 V` linear regulator that exists to keep switching noise out of them.

lessons.t: The Worst Instant of the Route
lessons.g: Sag the pack at peak current and check every rail input against its own minimum.
lessons.s: Now the parts of this course come together. The pack is `80 mohm` because 4S2P doubles and halves a `40 mohm` cell, the wiring and connectors add `17 mohm`, and at peak the tree pulls a little over four amps through all of it. Run it from the reserve floor, `14.0 V` open circuit, and the terminals sit near `13.6 V`.

lessons.g: Report charge, usable energy, deliveries left and the return decision from the cell voltages.
lessons.s: The gauge on this robot answers one question in four numbers, and it makes every one of them from the **lowest** cell rather than the pack. The charge comes from the open circuit curve. The usable energy is that charge with the reserve taken off, multiplied by the pack energy.

lessons.g: Combine the cell, temperature and current protections into one ordered verdict.
lessons.s: The protections have been written one at a time and now they have to answer as one voice, in a fixed order, with the most dangerous condition first. Cell voltage comes first, because a cell outside its window is being damaged right now.

lessons.g: Judge every number the design produced against its limit and print one verdict for the machine.
lessons.s: A power review ends with a sheet, and every line of it is a number this chapter produced next to the limit it had to respect. The route needs `96.25 Wh` and the pack holds `100.8`. At the reserve floor and full peak the terminals sit at `13.61 V` and the hungriest rail needs `12.5`.

lessons.g: Build the sample time grid from a sample rate and say how long a record lasts.
lessons.s: A signal in this room is two things that always travel together: an array of numbers and the rate at which they arrived. An ADXL345 accelerometer on the wrist of an arm, read over SPI at 400 samples per second, hands you the first half of that pair. The second half lives in your head until you write it down.

lessons.g: Split a reading into its constant level and its fluctuation, and show the fluctuation survives.
lessons.s: A load cell under a gripper reads 1.02 kg with the jaws empty. That 1.02 is not the measurement you care about, it is the tare, the weight of the jaws themselves. What you care about is the wiggle on top of it.

lessons.g: Compute the RMS of a fluctuation and relate it to the amplitude of a sine.
lessons.s: Peak to peak is a bad measure of how strong a fluctuation is, because one spike decides it. The **RMS**, root mean square, asks a better question: what constant magnitude would carry the same energy as this waveform. The recipe is in the name read backwards.

lessons.g: Express the signal to noise ratio of a channel in decibels from two RMS values.
lessons.s: How good is a measurement? Not by how big the signal is, and not by how small the noise is, but by the ratio between the two. That ratio is the **signal to noise ratio**, and because it spans several orders of magnitude on a real robot it is quoted in decibels.

lessons.g: Compute the voltage of one ADC code and show the quantisation error never exceeds half of it.
lessons.s: The converter inside an STM32F4 has 12 bits and a 3.3 V reference. It cannot return 1.7 V. It returns the nearest rung of a ladder with 4096 rungs, and every reading you will ever filter arrived already rounded onto that ladder.

lessons.g: Compute the Nyquist frequency of a sample rate and decide which tones a channel can carry.
lessons.s: A record sampled at `fs` hertz can only represent frequencies below `fs / 2.0`. That boundary is the **Nyquist frequency**, and it is not a rule of thumb, it is the hard edge of what the numbers are able to say. The intuition is short: you need at least two samples per cycle to know a wave went up and came back down.

lessons.g: Apply the folding formula to predict the apparent frequency of a tone above Nyquist.
lessons.s: A tone above Nyquist does not vanish. It **folds** back into the band and appears at a lower frequency, indistinguishable from a real one that was never there. Where it lands is arithmetic, not luck.

lessons.g: Show that a 27 Hz tone sampled at 40 Hz produces exactly the same numbers as a real 13 Hz tone.
lessons.s: The previous mission predicted the folding. This one proves it, and the proof has to be measured rather than asserted, because a badly chosen demonstration of aliasing shows you nothing but rounding dust. Sample a 27 Hz vibration at 40 samples per second. The folding formula says it should appear at 13 Hz.

lessons.g: Pick the lowest available sample rate that covers the highest frequency of interest with margin.
lessons.s: Nyquist gives you the floor, not the answer. Sampling a 120 Hz whine at 241 Hz is legal and useless: you get two samples per cycle, the amplitude you read depends on where they land, and any analog filter in front of the converter has almost no room to work in.

lessons.t: The Filter That Has To Be Analog
lessons.g: Compute the attenuation an RC anti aliasing filter gives at the folding frequency and judge whether one pole is enough.
lessons.s: Aliasing happens inside the converter. Once the sample is taken, the folded tone and a real one are the same number, so no filter written in Python can separate them. The only place to stop it is before the sample and hitting, which means resistors and capacitors.

lessons.g: Decimate a record with and without a pre filter and measure how much of the signal survives each way.
lessons.s: Keeping one sample in every four is called **decimation**, and it is what you do when a 200 Hz log is more data than the link can carry.

lessons.g: Predict the noise that sampling jitter adds to a tone and confirm the prediction by measurement.
lessons.s: Sampling assumes the samples arrive on a perfect grid. On a microcontroller with interrupts they do not: the conversion starts a few microseconds late whenever something else was busy. That wobble in the instant is called **jitter**, and it turns into amplitude noise. The mechanism is a first order Taylor step.

lessons.t: Samples That Arrive When They Feel Like It
lessons.g: Resample a record with wandering timestamps onto a uniform grid and compare the error against ignoring the timestamps.
lessons.s: A USB IMU logs a timestamp with every reading, and those timestamps are not on a grid. If you drop them and treat the array as uniform you have quietly told every tool in this course a lie, and the tools will believe you.

lessons.g: Detect missing samples from the timestamp gaps and report how many readings were lost.
lessons.s: Before any of this chapter applies, the record has to be complete. A dropped SPI transfer or a full buffer leaves a hole, and a hole in an array that you treat as uniform shifts everything after it in time without changing a single value. Gaps are found with `np.diff(stamps)`, which turns instants into intervals.

lessons.t: A Fixture You Can Trust Twice
lessons.g: Build a seeded noisy channel so the same code gives the same numbers on every run.
lessons.s: Every measurement in this room is going to be compared against another measurement. That only works if the data stops moving, and random noise moves by definition. The fix is a **seeded generator**.

lessons.g: Average blocks of independent samples and confirm the noise falls with the square root of the block size.
lessons.s: Averaging `n` independent samples divides the noise by the square root of `n`, not by `n`. That single fact decides most of the trade offs in this course. The reason is that variances add, not standard deviations.

lessons.t: The Noise That Averaging Cannot Touch
lessons.g: Show that averaging leaves a random walk untouched while it cuts white noise by root n.
lessons.s: The root n law of the previous mission has one condition printed in small letters: the samples must be **independent**. Real sensors produce noise that is not. A gyroscope bias wanders. A thermistor follows the temperature of the board.

lessons.g: Predict the RMS of quantisation noise from the code size and convert a bit count into a decibel ceiling.
lessons.s: Chapter zero showed that the quantisation error of a converter never exceeds half a code. That bound is useful but pessimistic, because the error spends most of its time nowhere near the bound.

lessons.g: Compare how many corrupted samples the mean and the median of a window can absorb before they lie.
lessons.s: The mean has no defence. One sample of a window is enough to move it anywhere you like, because every sample enters the answer with the same weight and nothing bounds the contribution of a large one.

lessons.t: The Detector That Does Not Believe Itself
lessons.g: Estimate the noise sigma from the median absolute deviation and flag outliers a three sigma rule misses entirely.
lessons.s: The usual outlier rule is to flag anything more than three standard deviations from the mean. It has a defect that hides in plain sight: the outliers themselves are inside the mean and inside the standard deviation, so a big enough group of them raises the bar until it is above their own heads.

lessons.t: The Hum You Did Not Ask For
lessons.g: Measure the amplitude of one known frequency by projecting the record onto a sine and a cosine.
lessons.s: Not all noise is random. A robot arm plugged into the mains picks up 50 Hz. A brushless driver injects its switching tone. These are **periodic interferences**, and to the standard deviation they look exactly like noise: one number, no explanation. A single frequency can be measured directly without any transform.

lessons.t: Noise Sold By the Root Hertz
lessons.g: Convert a datasheet noise density into an RMS figure for a given bandwidth and back again.
lessons.s: An accelerometer datasheet does not quote its noise as a number of milli g. It quotes a **density**, micro g per square root hertz, because how much noise you actually get depends on how much bandwidth you let through. The conversion is `density * np.sqrt(bandwidth)`.

lessons.g: Assemble one function that reports level, spread, robust spread, outlier count and hum amplitude for a channel.
lessons.s: A channel is never described by one number. The four missions before this one each produced a different question, and a report that answers only one of them will send you looking for the wrong fault. The RMS says how strong the fluctuation is.

lessons.t: Every Filter Is a Row of Weights
lessons.g: Express a moving average as a weight vector and apply it with a convolution.
lessons.s: A moving average is usually written as a loop over a circular buffer. That hides what it is. It is a **weight vector**, and applying it is a convolution: slide the weights along the record, multiply, add. Write the weights down and the filter stops being a special case.

lessons.t: Poke It and See What Falls Out
lessons.g: Recover the weights of a filter by feeding it a single impulse.
lessons.s: You can find out what a filter does without reading its code. Feed it a **unit impulse**, a record of zeros with a single one in it, and what comes out is the weight vector itself, in order. That output has a name, the **impulse response**, and it is the identity card of any linear filter.

lessons.t: The Step Tells You the Lag
lessons.g: Measure the delay a symmetric filter adds by finding where its step response crosses half.
lessons.s: The impulse response says what the filter is. The **step response** says what it costs you, because the quantity a control loop cares about is how late the answer arrives. Push a step through a moving average and the output ramps instead of jumping.

lessons.t: How Much of Each Tone Survives
lessons.g: Compare the measured gain of a moving average against its closed form and find the frequency it deletes completely.
lessons.s: A filter is best described by what it does to each frequency. For a moving average of `taps` samples that answer is known in closed form, and it is not the gentle slope most people picture. The magnitude is the absolute value of `np.sin(np.pi * f * taps / fs)` divided by `taps * np.sin(np.pi * f / fs)`.

lessons.t: Putting It Back Where It Belongs
lessons.g: Remove the group delay of a causal filter by shifting the output and measure the error before and after.
lessons.s: A filter running in real time on a microcontroller is **causal**: at sample `n` it has only seen samples up to `n`, so its output is late by the group delay you measured two missions ago. There is nothing to be done about that live. Offline is a different situation.

lessons.g: Cascade two moving averages by convolving their weights and measure what the second pass buys and costs.
lessons.s: Running a filter twice is the same as running one longer filter once, and you can build that longer filter without touching the data: `np.convolve(weights, weights)` gives the weights of the pair.

lessons.g: Show that convolution invents zeros at the edges and fix it by padding with the edge values.
lessons.s: Ask `np.convolve` for a result as long as the input and it has to make something up, because the first window hangs off the front of the record. What it makes up is zeros, and zeros are almost never what your signal was doing before the recording started.

lessons.g: Compare a moving average and a median filter on a step corrupted by spikes and measure what each one leaves behind.
lessons.s: Every filter so far has been a weighted sum, which makes it **linear**: scale the input and the output scales with it. A median filter is not, and that is exactly why it can do something no weighted sum can. Run both over a channel that steps from 0 to 1 while three samples are railed to 3 V by a loose connector.

lessons.g: Run the three time domain filters over one corrupted record and rank them by RMS error against the truth.
lessons.s: Three tools, three different faults, and no single winner. The only way to choose is to run all of them against a record whose truth you know, which is why every fixture in this course is built rather than loaded. The channel below carries a 2 Hz motion, gaussian noise at 0.25, and four railed samples.

lessons.g: Transform a record into its frequency bins and read the frequency axis that goes with them.
lessons.s: Chapter two measured one frequency at a time by projecting the record onto a sine and a cosine. Doing that for every frequency the record can represent, all at once and in a fraction of the time, is the **discrete Fourier transform**.

lessons.g: Scale the magnitudes of a transform so they read as the amplitudes of the tones that produced them.
lessons.s: The magnitudes that come out of `rfft` are not amplitudes. They grow with the length of the record, so the same tone measured for twice as long reports twice the number, which makes them useless for comparing anything. The scaling is `2.0 * mag / x.size`. Dividing by the count removes the length.

lessons.t: The Resolution You Bought With Time
lessons.g: Compute the bin spacing of a record and show that two close tones separate only when the record is long enough.
lessons.s: The spacing between bins is `fs / n`, and that number is the **frequency resolution** of the measurement. Because `n` divided by `fs` is the duration, the resolution is one over the length of the record in seconds. Nothing else enters.

lessons.t: Nothing Is Created and Nothing Is Lost
lessons.g: Verify Parseval by computing the energy of a record in the time domain and in the frequency domain.
lessons.s: The transform moves a record into another set of coordinates. It does not add or remove anything, and there is an equality that proves it: **Parseval**. The energy in time is `np.sum(x * x)`.

lessons.g: Convert an amplitude spectrum to decibels against a reference and put a floor under the logarithm.
lessons.s: A linear amplitude spectrum shows you the loud tone and hides everything else. A 0.001 component next to a 1.0 component is one pixel tall next to a thousand, so the interesting half of every real measurement is invisible. Decibels fix the scale: `20.0 * np.log10` of the amplitude divided by a reference.

lessons.t: The Trend That Is Not a Tone
lessons.g: Remove a linear drift before transforming and show it was polluting every low frequency bin.
lessons.s: A thermal drift is not periodic, so it has no business in a spectrum. The transform does not know that. It has to describe your ramp using only sines and cosines, and the only way to build a ramp out of sines is to pile up a large amount of everything at the low end.

lessons.g: Extract the frequency and amplitude of every peak in a spectrum, sorted by size, ignoring DC.
lessons.s: A spectrum is several hundred numbers and a diagnosis is three. The step between them is **peak picking**, and it is where most of the mistakes in vibration analysis live. A bin is a peak when it is larger than both of its neighbours and clears a floor you set.

lessons.g: Zero pad a record to refine where a peak sits and show that it does not separate two close tones.
lessons.s: Sticking zeros on the end of a record makes the transform longer, so the bins get closer together. It is tempting to call that better resolution. It is not, and the difference is worth being precise about. What zero padding does is **interpolate**.

lessons.t: The Spectrum of a Real Channel
lessons.g: Assemble detrend, transform, scaling and peak picking into one function that reports what a channel contains.
lessons.s: The five previous missions each produced one piece. Put them in the right order and you have the tool that the rest of the course uses: give it a record and a sample rate, get back a list of what is in it. The order is not negotiable. Detrend first, because a drift pollutes every bin and would win the peak ranking.

lessons.g: Measure how much of a tone escapes its own bin when its frequency does not land on the grid.
lessons.s: The transform assumes the record repeats forever. Cut one second out of a 20 Hz tone and the ends join perfectly, twenty whole cycles, and the spectrum is a single bin. Cut the same second out of a 20.5 Hz tone and the two ends do not meet: the loop has a step in it, and a step is broadband.

lessons.g: Build a Hann window and apply it to a record so the ends of the loop meet smoothly.
lessons.s: Leakage comes from the discontinuity where the end of the record meets its beginning. The cure is to fade both ends to zero before transforming, so there is nothing left to be discontinuous.

lessons.g: Correct the amplitude a window takes away using its coherent gain and see the scalloping that is left.
lessons.s: The Hann window sets half of your record to something close to zero, so the tone that comes out the other side is smaller. Measure a 20 Hz tone of amplitude one through it and the spectrum reports 0.4975. Nothing is broken, you multiplied the signal by a curve whose average is 0.4975.

lessons.t: Hamming Buys Near and Sells Far
lessons.g: Compare the near and far sidelobes of the rectangular, Hann and Hamming windows on the same tone.
lessons.s: There is no best window. There is a trade, and it runs between how much a window leaks close to the tone and how much it leaks far away from it.

lessons.g: Show that noise through a window scales with the root mean square of the weights, not with their mean.
lessons.s: A window takes a different bite out of noise than it does out of a tone, and using one correction for both is a mistake that quietly rescales every noise floor you report. A tone is coherent across the record, so every sample is scaled and the amplitudes add up in step: the right factor is the mean of the window.

lessons.t: The Weak Tone Beside the Strong One
lessons.g: Recover a tone sixty decibels below another one, which the rectangular window buries entirely.
lessons.s: This is what windows are for. Everything before it was preparation. The record holds a 20.5 Hz vibration of amplitude one and, fifteen bins away, a 35 Hz tone of amplitude 0.001, sixty decibels below it.

lessons.g: Estimate a frequency finer than the bin grid by fitting a parabola through the peak and its neighbours.
lessons.s: The grid says 20 Hz. The tone is at 20.3. The information needed to say so is already in the record, and it is sitting in the two bins next to the peak: the one on the side of the true frequency is taller. Fit a parabola through the three magnitudes and take its vertex.

lessons.g: Split a record into windowed frames and track a frequency that changes while the machine runs up.
lessons.s: One spectrum of a whole record assumes the machine did the same thing throughout. A run up does not: the shaft goes from 10 Hz to 80 Hz, and a single transform of the whole four seconds reports a wide smear that is true and useless.

lessons.g: Average the power of several frames and measure how much steadier the noise floor becomes.
lessons.s: The noise floor of a single spectrum is not a floor, it is noise. Each bin is a random number whose spread is as large as its own average, so the picture is a forest of spikes and any threshold you draw across it fires at random.

lessons.g: Build the impulse response of an ideal low pass by sampling a sinc around the middle tap.
lessons.s: Ask for the perfect low pass, one that passes everything below the cutoff untouched and deletes everything above it, and the mathematics answers with an impulse response that never ends. That response is a **sinc**, the function `np.sinc`, which numpy defines with the pi already inside it.

lessons.g: Evaluate the frequency response of a set of taps and measure the ripple that truncation leaves behind.
lessons.s: To judge a filter you need its response at any frequency, not only at the bins of some transform. That is one line: feed the taps a complex exponential and add up the result, `abs(np.sum(h * z))` where `z` is `np.exp(-2j * np.pi * f * k / fs)`. That expression is what a filter does to a tone, written down.

lessons.g: Multiply the truncated sinc by a Hann window and measure how much the stopband improves.
lessons.s: Truncating the sinc is the same as multiplying it by a rectangular window, and by now you know what a rectangular window does. The fix is the one from the last chapter, applied to the taps instead of to the data. Multiply the ideal response by a Hann window of the same length.

lessons.t: How Many Taps Do You Need
lessons.g: Choose the number of taps from a required transition width and verify the width you actually get.
lessons.s: Length is the currency of an FIR filter. It buys a sharper transition, and it costs delay and arithmetic, both of which are linear in the number of taps.

lessons.g: Scale a set of taps so the DC gain is exactly one and see what the unscaled filter did to a constant.
lessons.s: A filter that changes the level of a signal is a filter with a bug, and it is the easiest bug in this chapter to ship without noticing, because everything else about the response looks correct.

lessons.g: Turn a low pass into a high pass by subtracting it from an impulse and check both ends of the band.
lessons.s: You do not need a second design method for a high pass. Whatever a low pass keeps, the rest of the signal is what a high pass keeps, and subtraction says exactly that. Build an impulse the same length as the taps with the one at the centre, `delta[h.size // 2] = 1.0`, and return `delta - h`.

lessons.g: Build a band pass as the difference of two low passes and check the gain inside and outside the band.
lessons.s: A gear mesh tone lives at 140 Hz and everything else on the channel is in the way. What you want is a **band pass**: nothing below 80, nothing above 200, the band between them untouched. Subtraction again. Take a low pass at the upper edge, take a low pass at the lower edge, and subtract the second from the first.

lessons.t: Two Taps That Delete a Tone
lessons.g: Build a comb filter that puts an exact zero on the mains frequency and measure what it costs elsewhere.
lessons.s: The cheapest filter that removes a known tone has two taps. Average a sample with the one from half a period of that tone ago, and the two are always opposite, so they cancel: `comb[0] = 0.5` and `comb[delay] = 0.5` with `delay = int(fs / (2.0 * f_hum))`.

lessons.g: Design a low pass to a written specification, apply it to a noisy channel and report the improvement in decibels.
lessons.s: A filter specification is four numbers and nothing else: the sample rate, the cutoff, how wide the transition may be, and how quiet the stopband has to be. Everything in this chapter turns those four into taps.

lessons.t: A Filter That Remembers Its Own Output
lessons.g: Implement a one pole recursion and show its impulse response never reaches zero.
lessons.s: Every filter in the last chapter looked only at the input. A **recursive** filter looks at its own output as well, and that one change buys an enormous amount of shape for almost no arithmetic.

lessons.g: Decide the stability of a one pole filter from its coefficient and count how long it takes to settle.
lessons.s: The number `a` in the recursion is the **pole**, and everything about the filter follows from where it sits. Each pass through the loop multiplies the memory by it once more, so the impulse response is a geometric sequence. Below one in magnitude the sequence shrinks and the filter is **stable**: `abs(a) < 1.0`.

lessons.g: Choose the pole of a one pole filter from a wanted cutoff frequency and verify the gain at that frequency.
lessons.s: Picking `a` by feel is how most embedded code gets written and it is why nobody can say what the filter does. There is a formula, and it takes one line. A continuous first order low pass with cutoff `fc` decays with a time constant of one over two pi `fc`.

lessons.g: Implement the general difference equation with coefficient arrays and check it against the one pole case.
lessons.s: One pole gives you one shape. The general recursive filter takes two arrays, `b` for the input samples and `a` for the past outputs, and it can be any shape you can write down.

lessons.g: Evaluate the frequency response of a recursive filter from its coefficients without running any data through it.
lessons.s: Measuring a filter by pushing tones through it works and is slow. The response can be read straight off the coefficients, and for a recursive filter it is a ratio instead of a sum. The input side gives `np.sum(b * np.exp(-1j * w * np.arange(b.size)))`, exactly the FIR formula from chapter six.

lessons.g: Design a second order Butterworth low pass by hand and confirm its cutoff and its slope.
lessons.s: The analog world has a catalogue of filter shapes worked out over a century. The **bilinear transform** brings one of them into the digital world with pencil and paper, and the second order Butterworth is the one worth memorising. Start with the prewarped cutoff, `K = np.tan(np.pi * fc / fs)`.

lessons.t: The Notch That Keeps Its Neighbours
lessons.g: Place a pair of zeros on the mains frequency and a pair of poles just inside them to make the notch narrow.
lessons.s: The comb from chapter six deleted 50 Hz and took 41 percent of a 30 Hz signal with it. A recursive notch does the same job and leaves 30 Hz at 99 percent, because feedback can undo the damage that the zeros do away from the notch.

lessons.g: Measure the delay a recursive filter adds at two frequencies and compare it against a symmetric FIR.
lessons.s: A symmetric FIR delays every frequency by the same amount, half its length, which is why chapter three could undo the delay with a single shift. A recursive filter cannot do that, and the reason is structural: its impulse response is one sided, so its phase cannot be linear. Measure it.

lessons.g: Run a recursive filter forwards and then in reverse to get zero phase, and account for what that costs.
lessons.s: Offline you can have the shape of an FIR and the cheapness of an IIR at the same time. Filter the record forwards, reverse it, filter it again, reverse it back: `iir_filter(y[::-1], b, a)[::-1]`.

lessons.g: Find the period of a noisy repeating signal from the peak of its autocorrelation.
lessons.s: A wheel with a flat spot produces the same bump once per revolution. The spectrum can find that, but there is a more direct question: how far do you have to slide the record along itself before it lines up again. That is the **autocorrelation**.

lessons.g: Scale an autocorrelation by its own zero shift so the peak becomes a number you can threshold.
lessons.s: The raw correlation peak of 361 means nothing on its own. Record for twice as long, or turn the gain up, and it grows without the signal having changed. Divide the whole thing by its value at zero shift: `norm = r / r[0]`.

lessons.t: Where Did the Echo Come Back
lessons.g: Locate a known pulse inside a noisy record by correlating the record against the pulse.
lessons.s: An ultrasonic transducer sends a burst and waits. What comes back is the burst again, smaller, later, and sitting under the noise of the amplifier. Finding when is the whole measurement.

lessons.g: Measure the processing gain correlation buys and check it against the length of the pulse.
lessons.s: The previous mission found a burst that was invisible. That was not luck, and the amount of help it gives can be calculated in advance. Correlating against the transmitted pulse is the **matched filter**, and it is provably the best linear detector against white noise.

lessons.g: Refine a correlation peak to a fraction of a sample and turn it into a distance in millimetres.
lessons.s: The correlation grid is one sample wide, and at 100 kilosamples per second one sample of round trip is 1.7 millimetres of range. An echo that truly arrives at 37.4 samples gets reported at 37, and the measurement is 0.7 millimetres short before anybody has made a mistake.

lessons.g: Differentiate a noisy record with a plain difference and predict the noise the operation creates.
lessons.s: Speed from position, acceleration from speed, rate of change from anything: a robot asks for derivatives constantly, and taking one is where a clean signal goes to die. The plain difference is `np.diff(x) * fs`, the change between neighbours divided by the sample period.

lessons.t: Reach Across Instead of Next Door
lessons.g: Use the central difference to halve the derivative noise and measure what it costs at high frequency.
lessons.s: Comparing a sample with its neighbour uses the shortest possible baseline. Comparing the sample before with the sample after doubles the baseline for the same two measurements, and that is the whole idea of the **central difference**: `(x[2:] - x[:-2]) * (fs / 2.0)`. The noise halves, exactly.

lessons.t: Fit a Line and Take Its Slope
lessons.g: Estimate a derivative by least squares over a window and measure the noise it leaves.
lessons.s: Both differences so far use two samples and throw the rest away. Fit a straight line through seven of them instead and take its slope, and you get a derivative that uses every sample in the window. The least squares slope has a closed form when the samples are evenly spaced.

lessons.t: Order Matters Only When It Is Not Linear
lessons.g: Show that two convolutions commute exactly while a median and a difference do not.
lessons.s: Smooth then differentiate, or differentiate then smooth? For linear filters the question has no content: convolution commutes, and swapping the two stages gives the same array to the last bit.

lessons.g: Check a logged record for dropouts and put it back on a uniform grid before analysing it.
lessons.s: The project of this chapter is one channel: an ADXL355 on the wrist of a six axis arm, logged at 1000 samples per second while the arm holds a steady pose. Everything in the room gets used on it. Nothing else can start until the record is trustworthy.

lessons.g: Produce the peak list of the wrist channel with detrending, a window and correct amplitude scaling.
lessons.s: Now the record can be asked what it contains. The order is the one chapter four ended on, with the window from chapter five added: detrend, window, transform, scale, correct for the window, pick peaks. The window matters here because the tones are not on the bin grid and one of them is small.

lessons.t: Kill the Hum, Keep the Machine
lessons.g: Remove the mains tone with a zero phase notch and prove the gear mesh came through untouched.
lessons.s: The 50 Hz in this record is the building, not the arm. It has to go before anything is measured against a threshold, and it has to go without taking any of the machine with it.

lessons.t: Keep Only the Band That Matters
lessons.g: Isolate the gear mesh with an FIR band pass and confirm what the band kept and what it removed.
lessons.s: Trending one number over weeks is how a machine is actually watched, and the number has to mean one thing. The RMS of the whole channel does not: it moves when the mains gets noisier, when the room warms up, when anything at all changes. The RMS of a **band** does.

lessons.t: Track the Mesh While It Runs Up
lessons.g: Follow the gear mesh frequency across frames while the arm accelerates, ignoring the fixed mains tone.
lessons.s: The record so far was taken at a steady pose. A run up is the other useful test: the joint accelerates and every tone that comes from rotation moves with it, while everything from the building stays where it is. That is a diagnosis by itself.

lessons.g: Demodulate the ringing band into an envelope and read the repetition rate of the impacts from its spectrum.
lessons.s: The peak list found something around 317 and 324 Hz and could not say what it was. This mission answers it, and it is the one technique in the project that a spectrum alone cannot reach. A damaged bearing does not produce a tone.

lessons.g: Assemble the project into one function that turns a raw wrist log into a written diagnosis.
lessons.s: Everything is built. What is left is to put it in one place and let it write the paragraph that a maintenance engineer reads.

lessons.g: Build a feature matrix and a label vector from raw log rows and read their shapes.
lessons.s: Every machine learning method in this course eats the same two objects. `X` is a **feature matrix** with one row per example and one column per measured quantity, and `y` is a **label vector** with one entry per row of `X`. Nothing else.

lessons.g: Read a comma separated robot log into a float feature matrix and an integer label vector.
lessons.s: Robot logs arrive as text. A controller writes one line per window, the fields are comma separated, and the first line names the columns. Python reads that with `csv.reader` from the standard library, which handles quoting and line endings that a naive `split` gets wrong. The part that bites is types.

lessons.g: Label windows by comparing their start times against a logged fault interval.
lessons.s: Nobody hands you a labelled robot dataset. What you get is a stream of measurements and a maintenance note saying the joint was replaced on a certain date, or an operator log saying the arm was jammed between two timestamps.

lessons.g: Show that a lookup table scores perfectly on the rows it was built from and no better than a coin on new rows.
lessons.s: Here is the trap the whole field is built around avoiding. Build a dictionary from every training row to its label. Ask it about a training row and it answers correctly every single time. **Accuracy 1.0.** It has learned nothing: it memorized. The number that means something is accuracy on rows the model never saw.

lessons.t: The Number You Have to Beat
lessons.g: Compute the majority class baseline and compare a model against it instead of against zero.
lessons.s: An accuracy on its own is not a result. Accuracy of 0.95 sounds excellent until you learn that 95 percent of the windows in the log were healthy, in which case a constant predictor that always answers healthy scores the same 0.95 while being worth nothing. The **majority baseline** is that constant predictor.

lessons.g: Slice a continuous current log into fixed length windows and drop the incomplete tail.
lessons.s: A machine learning row has to be a fixed length vector, and a current log is a stream of unknown length. The bridge between them is **windowing**: chop the stream into blocks of a fixed number of samples and let each block become one example. The window length is a real engineering choice.

lessons.g: Compute per window mean and standard deviation and see which of the two responds to bearing wear.
lessons.s: The first two features anybody writes are the mean and the standard deviation of the window. With `axis=1` numpy computes them per row, giving one number per window instead of one number for the whole log. On a motor current signal they carry completely different information.

lessons.g: Compute the RMS of a window and the AC only RMS after removing each window's own mean.
lessons.s: RMS is the square root of the mean of the squares, and for a current signal it is the value that actually heats the motor windings. It is the feature a thermal model wants, so it belongs in any dataset about a joint that gets hot. There is a catch that ruins it as a health feature.

lessons.t: The Spike That Breaks Peak to Peak
lessons.g: Compare peak to peak against a percentile range on a window containing one contactor spike.
lessons.s: Peak to peak is the largest sample minus the smallest one. It is cheap, it needs no statistics, and it is the first thing a technician looks at on a scope. As a feature it has one fatal property: it depends on exactly two samples out of two hundred. A robot cell is full of single sample events.

lessons.g: Measure high frequency energy in a window as the mean absolute sample to sample difference.
lessons.s: A worn bearing does not change the average current, it adds **fast** content: small, rapid deviations riding on top of the smooth torque demand. Standard deviation counts all deviation regardless of speed, so a slow payload ramp inflates it just as much as real chatter does.

lessons.g: Compute the zero crossing rate of the AC part and separate two windows that have identical spread.
lessons.s: The **zero crossing rate** counts how often a signal changes sign, divided by the window length. It is a frequency estimate that needs no transform: a fast signal crosses zero often, a slow one rarely. It earns its place because it sees something spread cannot.

lessons.g: Build a ratio feature and measure that it no longer tracks the payload the way its parts do.
lessons.s: Chatter grows with wear, and it also grows with load, because a heavier payload drives more current through everything including the noise. A robot lifting a heavy part with a perfect bearing can produce more chatter than the same robot lifting nothing with a ruined one. The feature is **confounded**.

lessons.t: The Feature That Reads the Clock
lessons.g: Show that a window index feature scores perfectly on one session and lands below the baseline on the next.
lessons.s: Here is a feature that passes every test you can run inside one log and destroys the model in the field. In session A the bearing failed halfway through, so every window after number 40 is faulty. The window index therefore predicts the label perfectly.

lessons.g: Rank candidate features by the accuracy of the best single threshold measured on held out windows.
lessons.s: Before any classifier exists you can already ask how much each column is worth. Sweep a threshold across one feature, try both directions, keep the best accuracy. That number is what a one rule model would achieve using that column alone. Measure it on windows the sweep did not touch.

lessons.g: Show that an unscaled column with large units decides every nearest neighbour on its own.
lessons.s: Nearest neighbour, and every other method that measures distance, adds up the squared differences of all columns. That sum has no idea what the columns mean.

lessons.t: Statistics Belong to the Training Set
lessons.g: Standardize a dataset using the training mean and spread and apply the same numbers to the test rows.
lessons.s: Standardizing means subtracting a mean and dividing by a standard deviation so that a column comes out centred on zero with a spread of one. The question that decides whether you did it right is: **whose** mean and whose standard deviation. They have to be the training set's.

lessons.g: Compare min max scaling with and without a single outlier row and measure how far the normal rows get squashed.
lessons.s: Min max scaling maps a column into the range zero to one by subtracting the minimum and dividing by the range. It is popular because the output range is guaranteed, which matters when the next stage is a neural network or a fixed point implementation on a microcontroller.

lessons.t: The Leak in the Preparation Step
lessons.g: Select the best feature column using every row and see a pure noise dataset report accuracy far above chance.
lessons.s: This dataset has three thousand columns of pure noise and a label drawn by coin flip. There is nothing to learn. Any honest pipeline has to come back at the baseline, and if yours does not, the pipeline is broken rather than clever. The break happens in the **preparation** step.

lessons.t: The Seed Is Part of the Result
lessons.g: Reproduce a shuffled split from its seed and show that a different seed moves the reported accuracy.
lessons.s: A split has to be shuffled. Robot logs arrive in time order and often in class order too, so slicing the first seventy percent hands you a training set made entirely of healthy windows. Shuffling with a permutation fixes that. Shuffling has to be reproducible.

lessons.t: Keeping the Rare Class in Both Halves
lessons.g: Compare how many fault rows a plain shuffle leaves in the test set against a stratified split.
lessons.s: Faults are rare. A log with four percent faulty windows is a healthy dataset by industrial standards, and it is a trap for a plain shuffle. Shuffle three hundred rows with twelve faults, take sixty of them for testing, and the expected number of faults on the test side is under three. Some seeds give you one.

lessons.t: Windows That Overlap Are Not Independent
lessons.g: Compare a shuffled split against a split by time on overlapping windows cut from the same two recordings.
lessons.s: Overlapping windows are standard practice: a hop shorter than the window length gives you more rows out of the same recording. Two neighbouring windows then share most of their samples, so their feature vectors are nearly the same point. Shuffle those rows and you have put near duplicates on both sides of the split.

lessons.g: Compare a row level split against holding out whole robots when each unit has its own sensor offset.
lessons.s: Eight arms of the same model, four healthy and four with a worn joint. Each arm has its own current sensor with its own offset, a couple of decibels either way, fixed for that unit and completely unrelated to its health. Split the rows at random and every arm appears on both sides.

lessons.t: The Set You Choose On Is Not the Set You Report
lessons.g: Measure how much the winning validation score overstates the test score across twenty splits.
lessons.s: You have eight candidate values of k and one validation set. You score all eight, take the best, and report that number. It is too high, and it is too high for a reason that has nothing to do with leakage: the best of eight noisy measurements is biased upward, because whichever candidate got lucky on those particular ...

lessons.t: How Far Apart Are Two Windows
lessons.g: Compute the squared Euclidean distance from one query row to every training row without a loop.
lessons.s: Nearest neighbour needs one primitive: the distance from a query row to every row of the training set. In two dimensions that is the ordinary straight line distance, and in eight it is the same formula with more terms. Numpy does it by **broadcasting**.

lessons.g: Build a one nearest neighbour classifier and score it on held out rows.
lessons.s: One nearest neighbour is the smallest complete classifier there is. For a query row, find the training row closest to it and answer with that row's label. There is no training step: fitting means keeping the data. It is a serious method, not a toy.

lessons.t: A Perfect Score Means You Asked the Wrong Question
lessons.g: Score one nearest neighbour on its own training rows and on held out rows in the same run.
lessons.s: Ask one nearest neighbour about a row that is in its training set and the closest row is that row itself, at distance zero. It answers with that row's own label, every time. Training accuracy is exactly **1.000** and it is a property of the algorithm, not a measurement of anything.

lessons.g: Extend the classifier to take a majority vote among the k closest training rows.
lessons.s: One neighbour is one witness. If that witness happens to be a mislabelled window or a rare outlier, the answer is wrong and there is nothing to outvote it. Asking the **k** closest rows and taking the majority makes the classifier tolerate a bad neighbour or two. The implementation stays short.

lessons.g: Sweep k over a validation slice, pick the winner there, and report its score on the untouched test slice.
lessons.s: k is a **hyperparameter**: a number you choose rather than one the data fits for you. Choosing it is a fitting operation, so it needs its own slice of data, and reporting the score of the winner on that same slice gives you the optimistic number chapter 2 measured.

lessons.g: Replace the plain majority with a vote where each neighbour counts one over its distance.
lessons.s: A plain vote treats the closest neighbour and the fifteenth closest as equals. When a query lands in the middle of a dense cluster that is fine. When it lands out at the edge, where the fifteenth neighbour is four times further away than the first, it is not. Weighting by `1 / (distance + eps)` fixes it.

lessons.t: Delete the Feature and Look Again
lessons.g: Measure the classifier with both columns, with each column alone, and with one column shuffled.
lessons.s: The most useful test in this course takes three lines: **remove a piece and see whether the output changes**. If it does not, that piece was never doing anything, whatever the diagram says. Here the piece is a feature column.

lessons.g: Count the distance computations and stored numbers a neighbour model needs, and compare against a two prototype model.
lessons.s: Nearest neighbour has no training cost and an inference cost proportional to the size of the training set. Every query walks all 420 stored rows. On a robot controller that answers once per window at 5 Hz that is fine.

lessons.g: Reject a query whose nearest training row is further away than a radius taken from the training distances.
lessons.s: A classifier with two labels answers one of two labels, always, including when the window in front of it is a kind of failure nobody recorded. A cracked gearbox tooth produces a window that sits nowhere near either class, and the model reports worn with total confidence because worn is marginally closer.

lessons.g: Compare a trained detector against a constant predictor on a log where faults are four percent of the rows.
lessons.s: This log holds 1260 windows and 60 of them are faulty. That is four percent, which is a realistic and even generous fault rate for a machine that is still running. On a set shaped like this, accuracy stops being informative. A predictor that answers healthy to everything scores 0.952 on the test rows.

lessons.g: Build a two by two confusion matrix from predictions and true labels with boolean masks.
lessons.s: Every prediction on a two class problem falls into one of four boxes. **True negative**: healthy window called healthy. **False positive**: healthy window called faulty, an inspection nobody needed. **False negative**: faulty window called healthy, the one that costs a gearbox.

lessons.g: Compute precision and recall from the confusion boxes and say which question each one answers.
lessons.s: **Recall** is the share of real faults the model caught: true positives over all faulty rows. It is the number a maintenance engineer cares about, because a fault the model missed is a fault that keeps running until something breaks.

lessons.t: Why the Average of the Two Lies
lessons.g: Compare the arithmetic mean of precision and recall against their harmonic mean on a detector that fires once.
lessons.s: Take a detector so cautious it raises exactly one alarm in the whole test set, and that alarm is correct. Precision is 1.000, perfect. Recall is 0.067, because it found one fault out of fifteen. Average the two the ordinary way and you get 0.533, which sounds like a working detector and describes something useless.

lessons.t: The Two Mistakes Do Not Cost the Same
lessons.g: Choose between two thresholds by expected cost using a cost per false alarm and a cost per missed fault.
lessons.s: Put money on the two mistakes and the choice of threshold stops being a matter of taste. An unnecessary inspection on this cell costs about 120 units of technician time. A missed bearing failure costs about 9000 units in a seized joint, a stripped harmonic drive and half a shift of downtime.

lessons.g: Trace precision and recall across the whole range of thresholds and read the trade off from the table.
lessons.s: The model does not output a decision, it outputs a **score**. Here the score is the fraction of the fifteen nearest training windows that were faulty, so it lives on a grid between 0 and 1. The decision only appears when you compare that score against a threshold, and that comparison is yours to set.

lessons.g: Compute the recall of each class separately and average them into a balanced accuracy.
lessons.s: Plain accuracy weights each row equally, so on a set that is 95 percent healthy it is a report about healthy windows with a rounding error attached. **Balanced accuracy** weights each class equally instead: compute the recall of each class and average those. On the constant predictor the difference is total.

lessons.t: Three Faults and a Square Table
lessons.g: Build a three by three confusion matrix and find which pair of classes the model confuses.
lessons.s: The cell logs three states now: healthy, a worn bearing, and a loose belt. A loose belt raises the average current because the drive has to fight the slip, and it raises the high frequency content a little as well, so it shares part of its signature with a worn bearing.

lessons.t: The Report That Does Not Hide Anything
lessons.g: Print one block holding the baseline, the confusion boxes, precision, recall, balanced accuracy and the threshold.
lessons.s: Everything in this chapter goes into one block, printed by one function, so that no result of yours ever travels as a single number without its context. The minimum honest report has five parts. What the majority baseline was, so the reader knows the floor. The four confusion counts, so any metric can be recomputed.

lessons.t: When the Answer Is a Temperature
lessons.g: Set up a regression target and measure the error of the mean predictor in the units of the target.
lessons.s: Classification asks which of a few states a window belongs to. **Regression** asks for a number: how many degrees the winding of joint 3 will rise, how many millimetres of backlash the gearbox has, how many minutes of battery are left.

lessons.g: Build a design matrix with a leading column of ones so the fitted line can leave the origin.
lessons.s: A linear model computes `linear(X, w)`, a weighted sum of the columns. With two feature columns that expression can only produce planes that pass through the origin, which means a joint drawing zero current at zero duty must be predicted at exactly zero degrees of rise. Sometimes true, usually not.

lessons.g: Fit a linear model with least squares and predict the test targets with a matrix product.
lessons.s: Least squares picks the weight vector that minimises the sum of the squared residuals. There is a closed form, the normal equations, and numpy exposes a numerically better version of it as `np.linalg.lstsq`, which handles a rank deficient matrix instead of exploding on it.

lessons.g: Compute residuals on held out rows and find the structure a plain linear model leaves behind.
lessons.s: A **residual** is the truth minus the prediction, one number per row, in degrees. The set of residuals holds more information than the RMSE that summarises them, and looking at it is how you find out what the model is missing. The test is whether the residuals still depend on anything.

lessons.t: R Squared and Its Negative Half
lessons.g: Compute the coefficient of determination on training and held out rows and interpret a negative value.
lessons.s: R squared reports the share of the variance the model explains: one minus the sum of squared residuals over the sum of squared deviations from the mean. At 1.0 the model is exact, at 0.0 it is exactly as good as predicting the mean. Below zero it is **worse** than predicting the mean, and that is not a broken formula.

lessons.t: Putting the Physics in the Matrix
lessons.g: Add a squared and an interaction column to the design matrix and measure the drop in held out error.
lessons.s: Least squares fits a **linear combination of columns**, and nobody said the columns have to be the raw measurements. Copper losses go as current squared times the fraction of time the joint is energised, so a column holding `current ** 2 * duty` describes the heat directly and the fit stays linear in the weights.

lessons.t: The Degree That Went Too Far
lessons.g: Sweep polynomial degree on twelve training points and watch training error and held out error separate.
lessons.s: Give a model enough freedom and it will fit the noise. With twelve training points and a polynomial of degree nine the fit passes almost exactly through every one of them: training error falls towards zero and it means nothing at all. The held out error tells the other half of the story.

lessons.g: Add a ridge penalty to the normal equations and recover a usable degree nine fit.
lessons.s: The degree nine fit failed because its weights grew enormous, hundreds or thousands in size, with neighbouring terms cancelling each other to squeeze the curve through twelve points.

lessons.g: Read the fitted coefficients of the physical model against the constants that generated the data.
lessons.s: A weight in a linear model has units, and the units tell you what the number means. In this model the target is degrees and the physical column is amps squared times duty, so its weight is measured in degrees per amp squared per unit duty.

lessons.t: From a Score to a Probability
lessons.g: Turn a linear score into a probability with the logistic function and read what the shape does.
lessons.s: A linear model produces a score that runs from minus infinity to plus infinity. A probability has to live between 0 and 1. The **logistic function**, one over one plus the exponential of the negative score, is the map between them, and it is the only extra piece logistic regression adds to what you built in chapter 5.

lessons.t: The Cost of Being Confidently Wrong
lessons.g: Compute the log loss of a set of probabilities and compare a confident mistake against a hesitant one.
lessons.s: Accuracy cannot train a model, because moving a weight by a hair almost never flips a prediction, so the derivative of accuracy is zero nearly everywhere. **Log loss** replaces it: the negative average of the log of the probability the model gave to the correct answer. It punishes confidence.

lessons.g: Compute the gradient of the log loss and check it against a numerical derivative.
lessons.s: The gradient of the log loss with respect to the weights is the average over rows of each row's features scaled by that row's error `p - y`, where `p` is the vector of predicted probabilities.

lessons.g: Write the gradient descent loop and watch the loss fall while the held out accuracy rises.
lessons.s: The loop is three lines. Start the weights at zero, compute the gradient, step against it by a learning rate, repeat. There is no closed form for logistic regression the way there is for least squares, so this iteration is the fit. Starting at zero is a real choice and a safe one here.

lessons.t: The Step That Was Too Long
lessons.g: Run the same fit at four learning rates and identify the one that never converges.
lessons.s: The learning rate decides how far each step moves. Too small and the walk takes ten thousand iterations to cover ground a good rate covers in two hundred, which on a real dataset is the difference between a minute and an afternoon.

lessons.g: Read the sign and size of the fitted weights and check them against the physics of the feature bench.
lessons.s: The weights of a logistic model are readable in a way a neighbour model never is. On standardized columns each weight says how many units of score one standard deviation of that feature buys, so their sizes are comparable and their signs are statements about the machine.

lessons.g: Group the held out rows by predicted probability and compare each group's predicted rate against its true rate.
lessons.s: A logistic model outputs numbers between 0 and 1 and everybody calls them probabilities. Whether they deserve the name is a separate question with its own measurement, and the measurement is a **reliability table**. Sort the held out rows into bins by predicted probability.

lessons.g: Fit one logistic model per class against all the others and pick the class with the highest score.
lessons.s: Logistic regression answers one yes or no question. With three machine states you fit three of them: healthy against everything else, worn bearing against everything else, loose belt against everything else. That is **one versus rest**, and it is how most linear classifiers handle more than two classes.

lessons.t: The Fault a Straight Line Cannot See
lessons.g: Fit a linear model on a fault defined by disagreement between two sensors, then add the product column.
lessons.s: This joint is driven by two motors, each with its own current sensor, and the fault is a **cross coupled harness**. When the wiring is right both readings deviate together, because they share the payload.

lessons.g: Repeat the same fit over thirty random splits and measure how far the reported accuracy moves.
lessons.s: You have been reporting a single held out accuracy for six chapters. That number is a **measurement**, and like any measurement made on a finite sample it has a spread. Change the seed of the shuffle and nothing about the model or the data changes, yet the number moves.

lessons.g: Split the data into five folds, train on four and score on the fifth, and average the results.
lessons.s: A single split throws away most of your measurement. Seventy percent of the rows are never scored and thirty percent are never trained on. **k fold cross validation** fixes both: cut the shuffled rows into k blocks, and run k experiments where each block takes a turn as the held out set.

lessons.t: The Number and Its Error Bar
lessons.g: Report a cross validated accuracy with the spread across folds and compare two models with it.
lessons.s: The five fold scores are five measurements of the same quantity, so their standard deviation is an estimate of how uncertain the average is. Reporting the mean without it invites the reader to believe digits that are not there. Use it to decide whether a change is real.

lessons.t: Choosing the Penalty Inside the Training Set
lessons.g: Select the ridge penalty by cross validation on the training rows and report on a test set never touched.
lessons.s: Cross validation replaces the validation slice from chapter 2, and it comes with the same rule attached. The **test set is set aside first**, before any folds exist, and it is opened once at the end.

lessons.g: Plot accuracy against training set size as a table and read whether more data would still help.
lessons.s: A **learning curve** answers a question a single accuracy cannot: would collecting more windows help. Train on 20 rows, then 40, then 80, all the way up, scoring each model on the same held out set, and read the shape.

lessons.t: Two Curves and What Sits Between Them
