lessons.g: Draw the training and held out curves together and name the regime from the gap between them.
lessons.s: Add the training accuracy to the learning curve and the diagnosis becomes mechanical. Two curves, one gap, three regimes. Both curves low and touching: the model is too simple for the data, and no amount of extra rows will move it. A linear boundary on the crossed harness problem from chapter 6 sits here forever.

lessons.g: Build folds out of whole robots and compare the result against folds built out of rows.
lessons.s: Chapter 2 held out whole arms once. Cross validation has to do the same thing k times, and the version that ignores it is one of the most common broken pipelines in industrial machine learning. **Grouped k fold** assigns groups to folds instead of rows.

lessons.t: Ask the Data to Prove It Is Not Noise
lessons.g: Shuffle the labels many times, cross validate each shuffle, and place the real score against that distribution.
lessons.s: Here is the test that catches everything else in this chapter when you have missed it. **Break the link between the features and the labels** by shuffling the label vector, then run your entire pipeline on the broken data. Whatever it reports is what your pipeline produces from nothing.

lessons.t: The One Number You Are Allowed to Quote
lessons.g: Run the full protocol end to end and print the report that carries the result and everything needed to judge it.
lessons.s: Everything in this chapter assembles into one function and one printed block. Set the test rows aside. Cross validate the candidates on what is left. Refit with the winner. Open the test set once. Run the shuffled label control. Print all of it together. The report is not decoration.

lessons.g: Compute the Gini impurity of a set of labels and read what its extremes mean.
lessons.s: A tree splits the data into smaller and smaller groups, and it needs a number that says how mixed a group is so it can prefer splits that make groups purer. **Gini impurity** is that number: one minus the sum of the squared class shares. Read its two ends.

lessons.g: Find the column and threshold whose split lowers the weighted impurity the most.
lessons.s: A **decision stump** is a tree with one question in it. Search every column and every candidate threshold, split the rows in two, and score the split by the impurity of the two halves weighted by their sizes. Keep the best. Weighting by size is what stops the search from cheating.

lessons.g: Recurse the split into both halves and find the depth at which the extra questions start to pay.
lessons.s: A tree is the stump applied again to each side. Split the rows, then run the same search inside the left group and inside the right group, and stop when the depth runs out, the group is pure, or too few rows are left to say anything.

lessons.t: How Deep Before It Starts Lying
lessons.g: Sweep tree depth and read the training and held out curves against a linear model on the same rows.
lessons.s: Depth is to a tree what polynomial degree was to a regression. Each extra level doubles the number of leaves the tree can have, and past a point those leaves stop describing the machine and start describing individual windows. The curves separate exactly the way chapter 7 predicted.

lessons.g: Train many deep trees on bootstrap samples and take a majority vote across them.
lessons.s: A deep tree is **unstable**: change a handful of training rows and the split at the root can move, which rewrites the whole tree below it. That sounds like a fatal flaw and it is the property that makes the next trick work.

lessons.t: Which Column Is Carrying the Model
lessons.g: Measure feature importance by breaking one column at a time and watching the held out accuracy fall.
lessons.s: **Permutation importance** is the erasure test from chapter 3 turned into a routine. Take the fitted model, shuffle one column of the held out set so it keeps its distribution and loses its pairing with the rows, and measure how far the accuracy drops. Repeat for each column.

lessons.g: Fit a steering policy by least squares on a log of human demonstrations and measure its action error.
lessons.s: **Behaviour cloning** is supervised learning where the target is what a person did. An operator drives the corridor robot with a joystick, the controller logs the state and the commanded steering rate at 20 Hz, and you fit a model from state to command.

lessons.t: The States the Operator Never Visited
lessons.g: Evaluate the cloned policy far outside the demonstrated envelope and compare its commands against the actuator limit.
lessons.s: The held out demonstrations came from the same distribution as the training demonstrations, so the tiny error from the previous lesson only certifies the model inside the envelope the operator stayed in. That envelope is fifteen centimetres wide, because a competent operator does not let the robot wander.

lessons.g: Add recovery demonstrations from far off states, refit, and measure what the correction costs inside the envelope.
lessons.s: The fix for covariate shift is not a better fitting procedure, it is **data from the states the policy will actually meet**. Put the robot three metres off the centre line, hand the joystick back to the operator, log the recovery, and add those rows to the training set.

lessons.g: Cut the fleet logs into labelled windows and keep the unit each window came from.
lessons.s: The mission for this chapter: twelve arms of the same model have been logged for six seconds each at 1 kHz. Six run a bearing that a technician has confirmed as worn, six are known good. Build a detector that will be installed on an arm nobody has logged yet, and report a number that is worth acting on.

lessons.g: Reduce every window to three decibel features and check that each one responds to wear.
lessons.s: Three features, all in decibels, all from chapter 1. **Level** is the RMS of the raw window, which is dominated by the payload. **Chatter** is the mean absolute step between neighbouring samples, the high frequency proxy. **Wobble** is the RMS after removing the window's own mean, the AC amplitude.

lessons.g: Hold out four whole units, fit the scaler on the rest, and prove no unit appears on both sides.
lessons.s: The split happens now, before any model exists, and it holds out **whole units**. Arms 8, 9, 10 and 11 are the test fleet: two healthy and two worn, a hundred and twenty windows, and not one of their rows will be seen by anything until the last lesson of this chapter.

lessons.t: Choosing the Penalty on the Fleet
lessons.g: Cross validate the ridge penalty over folds made of whole training units and refit with the winner.
lessons.s: Four candidate penalties, four folds, and every fold is two whole units, one healthy and one worn. The pairing matters: units alternate healthy and worn, so taking them two at a time from an even number gives every fold the same class balance.

lessons.t: The Threshold Is an Engineering Decision
lessons.g: Collect out of fold probabilities on the training units and pick the alarm threshold that minimises expected cost.
lessons.s: The model gives a probability. Turning it into an alarm needs a threshold, and chapter 4 established where that number comes from: the cost of the two mistakes. On this cell an unnecessary inspection costs 120 units and a missed bearing failure costs 9000.

lessons.g: Write the deployment function that takes one raw window and returns healthy, worn or unknown.
lessons.s: Everything so far produced numbers. This produces the artefact: a function that takes one window of raw current, straight off the controller, and answers. It carries four frozen things and nothing else. The scaler's two vectors, the weight vector, and the threshold. It also carries a refusal.

lessons.g: Score the finished detector on the four held out arms once and print the report with its controls.
lessons.s: The test fleet opens now, for the first and only time. Everything that goes into the report has already been decided: the features, the split, the penalty, the threshold, the radius.

lessons.g: Write a reward function and add up what a walk through the arena pays.
lessons.s: A controller minimises an **error**. You hand it a setpoint, it measures, it subtracts, and the sign of the difference tells it which way to push. A reinforcement learner has no setpoint.

lessons.g: Run the agent and environment loop for a fixed policy and log every turn.
lessons.s: The loop has exactly four moving parts and never grows more. The agent reads a **state**, picks an **action**, the environment answers with a **reward** and the next state, and a flag says whether the episode is over. In code that is two lines, and they are the two lines the rest of the course keeps rewriting.

lessons.t: Two Ways a Run Can End
lessons.g: Separate a terminal state from a step budget that ran out.
lessons.s: An episode ends for one of two reasons and they are not the same reason. **Termination** is the environment saying there is nothing after this: the robot docked, or it went over the stair edge. **Truncation** is you saying you are out of patience: the step budget ran out while the world was still perfectly alive.

lessons.g: Score two policies by the return of an episode instead of by a single reward.
lessons.s: One reward tells you nothing. The dock pays 10 whether you reached it in eight steps or in eighty, and the step cost punishes you the same whether you were on your way somewhere or wandering. The quantity that ranks behaviour is the **return**: the sum of every reward collected in the episode. Write it `G`.

lessons.t: It Optimises What You Paid For
lessons.g: Measure a shaping bonus that pays a policy more for loitering than for docking.
lessons.s: The first thing engineers do when an agent will not learn is add a helpful bonus. The dock is far away and the reward is sparse, so they pay the robot a little for being **near** the dock, to point it in the right direction.

lessons.g: Turn a state and an action into the next cell of the arena grid.
lessons.s: The Reward Arena is a five by five patch of warehouse floor seen from the ceiling camera. A **state** is the cell the robot occupies, written as a `(row, column)` tuple with row 0 at the top. An **action** is one of four bearings, and `ACTIONS` holds their row and column offsets in the order north, east, south, west.

lessons.g: Refuse moves into shelving and count how many bearings each cell has left.
lessons.s: Four shelving units stand in the arena at the cells listed in `WALLS`. They are not states: the robot can never be inside one, and a bearing that points into one is refused exactly like a bearing that points off the floor. That detail matters more than it looks.

lessons.g: Write the environment step that returns the next state, the reward and the done flag.
lessons.s: The environment answers a state and an action with three things at once, and the whole course depends on those three arriving together: the **next state**, the **reward** for the transition, and whether the episode is **done**. Both terminals sit inside the arena.

lessons.g: Store a deterministic policy as one action per state and run an episode from it.
lessons.s: A **policy** is the answer to the only question the robot ever asks: I am here, what do I do. When the arena has 21 reachable cells, the honest form of that answer is a table with 21 entries. Writing it as a table instead of as a rule matters, because a table is what learning can change.

lessons.g: Seed a private random stream so an experiment repeats exactly.
lessons.s: Reinforcement learning is built on sampling, and a result you cannot reproduce is not a result. Two rules keep this course honest. First, **own your stream**. `random.Random(seed)` builds a generator that belongs to your function, and nothing else in the program can advance it.

lessons.g: Compute the size of a tabular policy and the number of policies it could be.
lessons.s: Before you learn anything, count what you are about to learn. A tabular method stores one number per state and action, so the table has `len(cells) * len(ACTIONS)` entries and there is no way around that product. The second number is the one that explains why search is not the answer.

lessons.g: Add a slip probability to the transition and measure how often the bearing survives.
lessons.s: A deterministic grid is a lie you tell yourself for one chapter. Real wheels slip on dust, on cable covers, on the shiny strip where the floor paint changed, and the bearing that leaves the planner is not always the bearing the base executes.

lessons.g: Wrap the arena in a reset and step object so later algorithms never touch its internals.
lessons.s: From here on the learning code should not know what an arena is. It resets, it steps, it reads three values back. That is the contract every simulator and every real robot driver in this field exposes, and keeping to it is what lets you swap a grid for a Gazebo model or for a real base without touching the learner.

lessons.g: Record complete transitions so later chapters can learn from stored experience.
lessons.s: Every algorithm after chapter 4 learns from the same five field record: the state, the action, the reward, the next state and the done flag. Store anything less and you will be re running episodes to recover it. The done flag is the field people drop, and dropping it is expensive.

lessons.g: Compute the discounted return of an episode for several discount factors.
lessons.s: The plain return adds every reward with equal weight, which says a charge in ten minutes is worth exactly as much as a charge now. No engineer believes that, and no battery does either. The **discount factor** `gamma` fixes it by multiplying the reward at step `t` by `gamma ** t`.

lessons.g: Accumulate the return in one reverse pass and count the multiplications you saved.
lessons.s: Raising gamma to a power on every step is the obvious way to discount and the wrong way to compute it. Walk the episode **backwards** instead and the recursion collapses to one multiply per reward, because the return from step `t` is the reward now plus gamma times the return from the next step.

lessons.g: Convert a discount factor into the number of steps the agent effectively sees.
lessons.s: Gamma is a number between 0 and 1 and it is useless as an intuition. Convert it into steps and it becomes a design parameter you can argue about. The standard conversion is the **effective horizon**, `1 / (1 - gamma)`.

lessons.g: Show that two discount factors pick different routes on the same arena.
lessons.s: There is a small auxiliary charger two cells from the start that pays 3, and the main dock eight cells away that pays 10. Which one is the right target is not a fact about the arena. It is a fact about gamma.

lessons.g: Show that an undiscounted continuing task has no finite return and a discounted one does.
lessons.s: Episodes end, so gamma 1.0 is legal there. A **continuing** task never ends: a patrol robot that circles a warehouse aisle forever, paying its step cost every turn. Add up that stream with gamma 1.0 and the answer is minus infinity, which ranks every possible policy equally badly.

lessons.g: Find the maximum distance a discount factor is willing to travel for a fixed payout.
lessons.s: Here is the version of gamma you can put in a design review. Given a payout at the end and a step cost along the way, there is a distance beyond which the discounted return of walking there goes negative, and past that distance the agent prefers to do nothing.

lessons.g: Compute the return remaining at every step of an episode and compare it to the reward there.
lessons.s: The reward at a step and the return from a step are different quantities and confusing them produces value tables that look plausible and are wrong. The reward is what that one transition paid. The **return from step t** is what the rest of the episode paid, discounted back to `t`.

lessons.g: Estimate an expected return by sampling and watch the estimate settle as episodes pile up.
lessons.s: On a slippery floor a single return is a coin flip, so the quantity that means anything is the **expected** return, the average over the distribution of episodes the policy produces.

lessons.g: Measure how much of a distant hazard penalty survives the discount.
lessons.s: The discount does not only fade rewards. It fades **penalties**, and that is the version nobody puts on the slide. A stair edge that costs -20 when you touch it costs `gamma ** distance` times -20 when it is that many cells away.

lessons.g: Estimate the value of a state under a policy by averaging sampled returns.
lessons.s: The **value** of a state under a policy is the expected return if you drop the robot there and let the policy run. Written `V(s)`, it is one number per cell and it is the object every method in this course is trying to get right.

lessons.g: Measure how badly a value table breaks the one step consistency condition.
lessons.s: Sampling is not the only way to know a value. A correct table obeys a local promise at every state: the value here equals the reward for the step the policy takes plus gamma times the value of where it lands.

lessons.g: Run one sweep of iterative policy evaluation and report the largest change.
lessons.s: Iterative policy evaluation fixes the residual the blunt way: visit every state, overwrite its value with the one step target, repeat. Each pass is a **sweep**, and the largest change in a sweep is the number that tells you whether another one is worth running.

lessons.g: Iterate policy evaluation to a threshold and report the sweeps it needed.
lessons.s: Sweeping once is not evaluation. Evaluation is sweeping until the table stops moving, and the stopping rule is a threshold on the largest change. The threshold is a real decision, not a formality.

lessons.g: Compare a sweep that reads its own updates against one that reads last sweep only.
lessons.s: There are two honest ways to run a sweep. **Jacobi** builds a fresh table from the old one, so every state in the pass sees the same snapshot. **Gauss-Seidel** writes into the table it is reading, so a state updated early in the pass helps the states updated after it.

lessons.t: The Value of a Bad Policy
lessons.g: Evaluate two policies on the same arena and read the gap at the start cell.
lessons.s: Evaluation does not judge. It answers what a policy is worth, and a policy that drives into the stair edge gets an honest number for doing so. The wall hugger goes east along the bottom and north up the last column, eight steps, no danger.

lessons.g: Print a value table as a grid and locate the worst cell on it.
lessons.s: A value table is 21 numbers, and 21 numbers in a column teach nothing. Printed on the floor plan they become a map, and the map is readable at a glance: values climb towards the dock and collapse around whatever the policy walks into.

lessons.g: Evaluate a policy under stochastic transitions by weighting every outcome.
lessons.s: When the floor slips, the one step target stops being a single number. The commanded bearing survives with probability `1 - slip` and each perpendicular bearing takes over with half the rest, so the value of a state is the **weighted average** over those three landings. Nothing else about evaluation changes.

lessons.t: The Residual Tells You When to Stop
lessons.g: Compare the theoretical error bound of a stopping rule against the error it actually left.
lessons.s: A threshold on the largest change is not an error. What you want to know is how far the table is from the truth, and there is a bound for it: if the last sweep moved nothing by more than `delta`, then no entry is further from the truth than `gamma * delta / (1 - gamma)`.

lessons.g: Build the action value of every bearing from a state value table.
lessons.s: A value table tells you what a cell is worth and says nothing about what to do there. To act you need one number per **state and action**, and that is the action value `Q(s, a)`: the worth of taking that bearing here and then following the policy afterwards. With a model you get it in one line of lookahead.

lessons.g: Extract a policy from action values with a tie break that never changes between runs.
lessons.s: Reading a policy out of action values is one `max` per state, and it is also the place where a reinforcement learning course most often stops being reproducible. At the start of training every bearing scores the same, so **every state is a tie**.

lessons.g: Show that acting greedily with respect to a policy value never makes any state worse.
lessons.s: The policy improvement theorem is the load bearing result of this chapter, and it is short. Take any policy, compute its values, then in every state act greedily with respect to those values. The new policy is at least as good **in every state**, and strictly better somewhere unless the old one was already optimal.

lessons.g: Alternate evaluation and improvement until the policy stops changing.
lessons.s: Policy iteration is the previous lesson in a loop. Evaluate, improve, repeat, and stop when improving changes nothing. It terminates and it terminates fast.

lessons.g: Solve the arena with value iteration and read the optimal policy off the result.
lessons.s: Policy iteration evaluates a policy to convergence and only then improves it, which is a lot of sweeps spent perfecting the value of a policy you are about to throw away. **Value iteration** cuts that short.

lessons.g: Check that policy iteration and value iteration agree, and compare what each cost.
lessons.s: Two algorithms that solve the same equation should produce the same policy, and if yours do not, one of them has a bug. Checking that is a five line experiment and it is worth doing every time you write a planner. Agreement on the **policy** is the right test, not agreement on the values.

lessons.g: Draw a policy on the floor plan and walk it to check where it ends.
lessons.s: A policy printed as 21 integers is unreadable. Printed as arrows on the floor plan it is inspectable in a second, and reviewing it that way catches the class of bug no metric catches: an optimal looking value table whose arrows point somewhere absurd in one corner. Draw it, then walk it.

lessons.t: The Model You Do Not Have
lessons.g: Count the environment queries a planner makes and price them as real robot moves.
lessons.s: Everything in this chapter called `step`. That call is the **model**: given a state and a bearing it returns the landing, the reward and the flag, instantly, for any cell, including cells the robot has never visited and cells beyond the stair edge. A real robot has no such function.

lessons.g: Confirm that the value at the start equals the discounted return the policy actually collects.
lessons.s: A value is a promise about a return. On a deterministic arena that promise is checkable to the last digit: run the policy from the start, discount every reward by how late it arrived, and the total must equal the table entry for the start cell.

lessons.g: Collect episodes without a model and measure how much of the arena they cover.
lessons.s: From here the model is gone. There is no `step` you may call on a hypothetical cell, only a robot that is somewhere, does something, and reports what happened. Everything the learner knows has to arrive through that stream. The first consequence is coverage.

lessons.g: Estimate state values by averaging the returns that followed each visit.
lessons.s: Monte Carlo prediction is the definition of value turned into code. The value of a state is the expected return from it, so wait until the episode is over, compute the return that actually followed each visit, and average. No model, no bootstrapping, no assumptions.

lessons.g: Compare first visit and every visit Monte Carlo on the same episodes.
lessons.s: An episode can pass through the same cell twice, which happens constantly on a slippery floor. That leaves a choice: average the return from **every** visit, or only from the **first** visit in each episode.

lessons.g: Replace stored sums with an incremental update and prove the two agree.
lessons.s: Keeping a total and a count per state works and it does not scale. Every learner from here on updates a single number in place, and the identity that lets you do it is the **incremental mean**. With `n` samples seen, the new average is the old average plus the new sample minus the old average, divided by `n`.

lessons.g: Track a value that moves, and show why a constant learning rate beats an exact average.
lessons.s: Dividing by the sample count is the right thing to do when the truth stands still. It weights the first episode as heavily as the ten thousandth, so after enough data the estimate stops responding to anything. Robots do not stand still.

lessons.g: Update a value from a single transition using the estimate of the next state.
lessons.s: Monte Carlo waits for the episode to finish. **Temporal difference** learning does not: it updates from one transition, using its own estimate of the next state in place of the return it has not seen yet.

lessons.g: Log the size of the TD error over training and show it shrinking.
lessons.s: The TD error is not only the thing that drives the update, it is the best progress signal a model free learner has. Big errors mean the table still disagrees with its own experience; small errors mean it has settled, right or wrong. Watch it rather than the values.

lessons.g: Compare Monte Carlo and TD on identical budgets and read where each one loses.
lessons.s: Monte Carlo is unbiased and noisy. Its target is a real return, so it is right on average from the first sample, and one unlucky slip near the stairs drags a whole episode of estimates with it. TD is biased and quiet.

lessons.g: Measure how long TD takes to recover from a badly initialised table.
lessons.s: TD builds its target out of the table it is writing, so whatever you put in that table at the start is an assertion the learner initially believes. Initialise every cell at 50 and the learner spends its first thousand episodes arguing itself out of a fantasy. It does recover.

lessons.g: Allocate an action value table and read a policy out of it.
lessons.s: Control needs one number per state **and bearing**, not one per state. That table is `Q`, it has `len(INNER) * len(ACTIONS)` entries, and unlike a value table it can be turned into behaviour without a model: look up the row, take the largest entry, drive. Store it as a dictionary from cell to a list of four floats.

lessons.t: The Rule That Learns Off Policy
lessons.g: Apply the Q-learning update to a stream of transitions and watch a policy appear.
lessons.s: Q-learning is the TD update with one substitution: the target uses the **best** bearing available in the next cell, not the one the robot is about to take. That single `max` is what makes it **off policy**.

lessons.g: Choose actions with an epsilon greedy rule and measure how often it explores.
lessons.s: A random behaviour learns everything slowly and a greedy behaviour learns nothing new. The standard compromise is **epsilon greedy**: with probability epsilon take a uniformly random bearing, otherwise take the current best. Epsilon is a budget for information, paid in steps.

lessons.g: Show a zero exploration learner failing to find the dock at all.
lessons.s: An agent that always takes its current best bearing is not being efficient, it is being circular. It believes what it has seen, it only sees what it does, and it only does what it believes. Start the table pessimistically, at a value below anything the arena can pay, and the loop closes hard.

lessons.g: Compare an optimistic and a pessimistic starting table by counting the pairs each one tried.
lessons.s: There is a way to explore without any randomness at all: start the table **above** what the arena can pay. Every bearing then looks better than it is, trying one drives its entry down towards the truth, and the untried bearings become the most attractive thing in the row.

lessons.g: Decay exploration over training and count the falls it saves.
lessons.s: A fixed exploration rate is a fixed tax. Early in training it is the only reason anything is discovered; late in training it is a robot that already knows the way and still drives off the stairs one time in ten. Decaying it fixes both ends.

lessons.t: The Learning Rate Is a Bet
lessons.g: Tune the learning rate on a slippery floor and find where a big step stops paying.
lessons.s: On a floor that never slips, a learning rate of 1.0 is correct. The target is exact, so overwriting the entry with it is not a gamble, it is an assignment. Add slip and the target becomes one sample of a distribution.

lessons.g: Track how many bearings of the learned policy match the planner over training.
lessons.s: Return curves are noisy and they hide where a policy is still wrong. When you have a planner, there is a much sharper measurement available: compare the learned bearings against the planned ones, cell by cell, and count the matches.

lessons.g: Plot a learning curve from training returns and separate it from the greedy score.
lessons.s: There are two curves and confusing them is the most common reporting error in this field. The **training return** is what the robot collected while exploring, so it carries the cost of every deliberate mistake and it can never reach the optimum while epsilon is above zero.

lessons.g: Implement SARSA and see it learn the value of the behaviour it is actually running.
lessons.s: Q-learning bootstraps on the best bearing available next. **SARSA** bootstraps on the bearing it is actually going to take, which it has to choose before it can update. That is the whole difference and it changes what the table means.

lessons.g: Train both learners on a cliff walk and read the two different routes they choose.
lessons.s: The arena moves to a service corridor: four rows by twelve columns, the robot starts at the bottom left, the charging point is at the bottom right, and the whole bottom row between them is an unguarded loading dock edge. Going over it costs 100 and puts the robot back at the start.

lessons.g: Count the cliff entries each learner pays for during training, not after it.
lessons.s: The previous lesson compared the two final routes and Q-learning won on paper: its route is two steps shorter. That comparison is the one every tutorial makes and it prices only the answer, never the search. So price the search.

lessons.g: Compare two policies that tie on a dry floor and separate as the floor gets slippier.
lessons.s: Two routes leave the start cell and reach the dock in eight steps. The planned one from chapter 4 climbs the left column and crosses the top row. The timid one runs along the bottom row and up the right column. On a floor that never slips they are worth exactly the same, 3.0, and no measurement can separate them.

lessons.g: Report a policy by its worst outcomes as well as its mean return.
lessons.s: Every method in this course optimises an **expectation**, and an expectation is a bad summary of a robot. A policy that docks nicely 95 times and falls down the stairs 5 times has a respectable mean and has destroyed five robots. So report the distribution, not the average.

lessons.g: Add a potential based bonus that speeds up learning and provably cannot change the optimum.
lessons.s: Sparse reward is the reason a learner wanders for a thousand episodes before anything happens. Extra reward for progress fixes that and usually breaks the task, as chapter 0 measured. There is one form that cannot break it.

lessons.g: Let a learner discover the loitering exploit that a hand written bonus creates.
lessons.s: Chapter 0 hand wrote a policy that farmed a proximity bonus and showed it scored better than docking. That was a demonstration you had to build. This one the agent finds on its own. Pay `NEAR_BONUS` for every step that ends next to the dock, with no matching subtraction, and let Q-learning optimise.

lessons.g: Separate training mode from deployment and count what leaving exploration on costs.
lessons.s: A trained agent has two switches that must both go off before it leaves the lab: the exploration rate and the learning rate. Leaving either on is a deployment that keeps experimenting on the customer. Exploration is the expensive one.

lessons.g: Find the cells where the learned policy is a tie break pretending to be a decision.
lessons.s: A table cannot say it does not know. Ask it for the bearing in a cell it has never visited and it answers, immediately, with whatever the tie break rule produces, and nothing in the interface distinguishes that answer from one backed by ten thousand visits. This is not a small corner of the arena early in training.

lessons.g: Instrument training to report the episodes, the steps and the falls a solution cost.
lessons.s: Every chapter so far reported what the agent learned. None of them reported what learning cost, and that omission is the reason people believe a robot can be trained by trial and error. So instrument it.

lessons.g: Convert a training budget into robot time using the speed of a real base.
lessons.s: A step is not a unit of anything until you attach a robot to it. A Kobuki class base crosses a 40 cm tile in about `SECONDS_PER_MOVE` seconds including the settle, and an episode reset means somebody carries the robot back to the start, which is `RESET_SECONDS` if the somebody is standing right there and much more if ...

lessons.g: Price the falls of a training run in parts and technician time.
lessons.s: A fall in the arena is a number on a screen. A fall on hardware is a robot that went over an unguarded edge, which in the fleet this course is written against means a cracked lidar mount, a bent bumper bracket, and a technician who stops what they were doing.

lessons.g: Grow the arena and measure how the training cost scales with the size of the table.
lessons.s: A tabular learner has to visit every state and bearing pair enough times to average out the noise. There is no sharing between cells: what it learns about one tile teaches it nothing about the tile next to it. So the cost grows with the table, and it grows faster than the table does.

lessons.t: The Arm That Cannot Be Tabled
lessons.g: Extrapolate the tabular budget to a jointed arm and read the answer in robot years.
lessons.s: The previous lesson measured how many steps a table entry costs. This one takes that number somewhere it does not want to go. Discretise a six joint arm at ten positions per joint and the state space is ten to the sixth. Give it two bearings per joint and the table has twelve million entries.

lessons.g: Filter unsafe bearings with a one step model and measure what the filter costs and saves.
lessons.s: The learner is allowed to be ignorant. It is not allowed to be ignorant about the stairs. A **shield** sits between the policy and the actuators and removes bearings that a one step model says can end badly.

lessons.g: Warm start a table from teleoperated demonstrations and measure the falls it saves.
lessons.s: Nobody sensible starts a robot from a table of zeros. Somebody drives it, badly and by hand, for twenty runs, and the learner updates on those transitions before it ever chooses a bearing of its own. The demonstrations do not have to be optimal and they do not have to be complete.

lessons.t: The Simulator Is Not the Floor
lessons.g: Train at one slip level, deploy at three, and measure both directions of the mismatch.
lessons.s: Training in simulation removes the falls, the resets and the years. It introduces one problem in their place: the simulator is wrong, and the policy is optimal for the simulator. The corridor from earlier in this chapter shows it in both directions, which is the part usually left out.

lessons.g: Put every measured cost into one comparison and let the arithmetic pick the plan.
lessons.s: The chapter has produced numbers instead of opinions, so the conclusion can be arithmetic instead of advice. On one side, training on hardware: the median steps and episodes from lesson one, priced at robot time and repairs.

lessons.g: Build the project arena and prove by search that the task is possible before training anything.
lessons.s: The project arena is a six by seven service bay. The robot starts in the bottom left corner, the charging dock is the top right cell, six shelving units block the middle, and there are **two** unguarded edges rather than one.

lessons.g: Solve the project arena with value iteration to produce the benchmark the learner will be graded against.
lessons.s: You have a model of this arena, so use it. Value iteration under the slip distribution produces the optimal value of every cell and the optimal bearing to take there, and those numbers become the yardstick for everything that follows. This is not what a robot would do.

lessons.g: Train a Q-learning agent with a decaying exploration rate and grade it against the planner.
lessons.s: Now the agent, with no model and no map. Q-learning, epsilon greedy starting at 0.5 and cooling towards a floor, and a stopping rule that asks the only question that matters: does the greedy policy drive the optimal eleven step route to the dock.

lessons.g: Add the safety filter to training and measure the falls it removes and the steps it adds.
lessons.s: The previous lesson produced a working policy and a body count. This one removes the body count. The shield is the same one as chapter 8, adapted to two hazards: a bearing is refused if the commanded landing **or either slip landing** is an edge.

lessons.g: Score four deployment configurations and find the one that is unsafe.
lessons.s: Two tables have been trained and each can be deployed with the shield on or off, which is four configurations, and they are not four flavours of the same thing. The bench runs 500 seeded episodes of each and reports the arrival rate, the fall rate, the mean return and the fifth percentile.

lessons.g: Price both training routes in robot hours, repairs and operator time.
lessons.s: Two ways to obtain the same table: run the learner on the real robot in the bay, or run it in a simulator and carry the numbers over. The bench in the previous lesson says both tables work. This lesson says what each one cost to obtain. Use the rates from chapter 8.

lessons.g: Freeze the policy and print an acceptance card that decides go or hold from the measurements.
lessons.s: The last artefact of the project is not the table. It is the card that says what the table is, what it was measured to do, and under what conditions it may be switched on.

lessons.t: The Weight You Have to Beat
lessons.g: Compute hover thrust per rotor and the thrust to weight ratio of the test frame.
lessons.s: A ground robot that loses power stops. An aerial robot that loses power falls. Nothing about a multirotor is stable by construction: the only thing holding 1.35 kg in the air is four propellers pushing down on the air hard enough to cancel gravity, and they have to keep doing it every millisecond of the flight.

lessons.g: Convert between rotor speed and thrust in both directions and show why the relation is not linear.
lessons.s: A propeller does not produce thrust in proportion to how fast it turns. It produces thrust in proportion to the **square** of how fast it turns. For a fixed pitch propeller in still air the useful model is `KF * omega * omega`, with omega in radians per second and `KF` a coefficient you measure on a thrust stand.

lessons.g: Lay out the X frame geometry and show that the reaction torques cancel only when all four rotors match.
lessons.s: The X layout puts the four rotors on the diagonals, so that a roll and a pitch each use all four motors instead of two. Rotor `i` sits at 45 plus 90 times `i` degrees around the body z axis, at a distance `ARM` from the centre, which on this frame is 0.17 m.

lessons.g: Compare the effective moment arm of yaw against roll and explain why yaw is given up first.
lessons.s: Roll and pitch are made by pushing harder on one side than the other. The lever is geometric: `ARM * math.cos(math.radians(45.0))`, which is 0.120 m on this frame. One newton of thrust difference buys 0.120 N m of roll torque. Yaw has no lever.

lessons.t: Six Places to Be, Four Ways to Push
lessons.g: Compute the tilt and the extra thrust a horizontal acceleration costs on an underactuated airframe.
lessons.s: A quadrotor has six degrees of freedom in the world and four independent inputs. It cannot move sideways without first pointing somewhere else, because all four propellers push along the same body axis. There is no rotor aimed left. So every horizontal move is a two step trade.

lessons.t: Four Numbers the Whole Aircraft Obeys
lessons.g: Turn four rotor thrusts into the collective thrust and the three body torques they produce.
lessons.s: Nothing above the mixer ever talks about motors. The whole flight stack commands four numbers: collective thrust along body z, and torque about x, y and z. Everything else is arithmetic on the frame geometry, and it belongs in one function that you can test on its own.

lessons.g: Build the inverse mixer that splits a commanded wrench into four rotor thrusts.
lessons.s: The controller produces a wrench and the motors need thrusts, so somebody has to invert dr1-1. On a symmetric X frame you do not need a matrix inverse, because the four sign patterns are orthogonal: each axis writes its own contribution and they never interfere.

lessons.g: Convert rotor thrust into a normalised motor command and measure what a linear throttle assumption costs.
lessons.s: The mixer speaks newtons. An ESC accepts a number between 0 and 1. Between them sits the square law of dr0-2, and skipping it is one of the most common reasons a machine that flies fine in a hover falls apart in a fast descent.

lessons.t: The Sign That Flies in Simulation
lessons.g: Show that one flipped column of the mixer leaves roll working and quietly destroys pitch.
lessons.s: A mixer sign error is the defect that does not announce itself. The machine still lifts off, still responds to the stick in roughly the right direction, and still holds a hover on the bench. It fails in the air, once, permanently. Here is why it hides.

lessons.t: The Ceiling Nobody Told the Controller
lessons.g: Clamp the rotor thrusts to the physical range and report what the clamp took away on every axis.
lessons.s: The mixer will happily ask rotor 2 for minus 1.9 N. The motor cannot pull. Every real mixer therefore ends in `min(MAX_THRUST, max(MIN_THRUST, f))`, with `MIN_THRUST` at 0.35 N because a stopped rotor takes a fifth of a second to come back and no controller can wait that long.

lessons.g: Move the collective so the attitude torque fits inside the motor range instead of clipping it.
lessons.s: The clamp of dr1-5 is the worst possible way to handle a wrench that does not fit, because it damages the axis that keeps the aircraft alive. Attitude is not negotiable. Height is. The fix is to notice that the collective is a free offset.

lessons.g: Scale the yaw demand down until roll and pitch fit, and report the scale factor instead of hiding it.
lessons.s: When the collective offset of dr1-6 is not enough, something has to be reduced. The order is not arbitrary. Losing roll or pitch means losing the aircraft in under a second. Losing heading means the machine points the wrong way while it stays perfectly in the air. Yaw goes first, always.

lessons.g: Compute the roll torque available as a function of collective and find the throttle where control is strongest.
lessons.s: Control authority is not a property of the airframe. It is a property of the airframe **at the current throttle**, and it goes to zero at both ends of the stick.

lessons.t: The Round Trip That Must Close
lessons.g: Push a commanded wrench through the mixer and back through the frame, and prove the loop closes only while nothing saturates.
lessons.s: Everything in this chapter is one claim: the mixer and the frame are inverses of each other. That claim is testable in four lines, and testing it is how you find a wrong sign, a wrong arm and a wrong yaw coefficient without leaving the desk.

lessons.t: The Gyro Is Not Telling You Angles
lessons.g: Convert body angular rates into Euler angle rates and find the attitude where the conversion blows up.
lessons.s: An MPU6000 gyro measures `p`, `q` and `r`, the rotation rates about the **body** axes, bolted to the frame and tilting with it. The attitude you want to hold is expressed in Euler angles relative to the world.

lessons.g: Build the quaternion attitude error and force it to take the shorter of the two possible rotations.
lessons.s: A quaternion has no singularity and no ordering convention to get wrong, which is why every flight controller written after about 2010 keeps attitude as `(w, x, y, z)`.

lessons.t: The Error the Controller Can Use
lessons.g: Turn an error quaternion into a rotation vector and show where the small angle shortcut stops working.
lessons.s: A rate controller needs a vector in radians, not a quaternion. The exact conversion is the axis angle form: the angle is `2.0 * math.atan2(norm, e[0])` with `norm` the length of the vector part, and the direction is that vector part normalised.

lessons.g: Close the body rate loop on the roll axis and measure the time constant it actually produces.
lessons.s: The rate loop is the fastest thing on the aircraft and the only loop that touches the mixer. It takes a body rate setpoint, subtracts the gyro, and produces a torque.

lessons.t: The Motor Is Not a Wire
lessons.g: Add the propeller spin up lag to the rate loop and measure the overshoot it introduces.
lessons.s: The loop of dr2-4 assumes the torque appears the instant you ask for it. It does not. An ESC changes the current quickly, but the propeller and rotor have inertia and take time to reach a new speed.

lessons.g: Sweep the rate gain against the motor lag and pick the highest one that still meets an overshoot budget.
lessons.s: Tuning is not taste once you have dr2-5. The propeller time constant sets a ceiling on the rate gain, the ceiling is computable, and the computation is a sweep. Fix the budget first. Ten percent overshoot on a rate step is a reasonable number for a camera platform: enough response to feel solid, not enough to bounce.

lessons.g: Split the attitude error into tilt and heading and weight the heading down so the aircraft never trades one for the other.
lessons.s: An attitude controller handed a large error will ask for torque on all three axes at once, and the mixer of dr1-7 will then quietly scale yaw down to fit. That works, but the decision was made in the wrong place: the mixer knows about motors, not about which axis keeps the aircraft alive. Do it properly one layer up.

lessons.t: Pointing Where You Want to Go
lessons.g: Turn a desired acceleration vector into the roll, pitch and collective thrust that produce it.
lessons.s: This is the hinge of the whole aircraft. Everything above it thinks in accelerations, everything below it thinks in attitude, and the conversion happens here in three lines. Take the acceleration you want, add gravity to it, and you have the direction the thrust vector must point.

lessons.g: Assemble the whole attitude layer: desired acceleration in, body rate setpoint out, with the tilt limit reported.
lessons.s: Time to make the chapter into one component with a clean interface. In go a desired acceleration, a desired heading and the current attitude. Out come three body rate setpoints and a flag saying whether the tilt the aircraft asked for was legal. The order matters.

lessons.g: Compute the loop rates of the cascade and how far the aircraft moves between two decisions of the outer loop.
lessons.s: A multirotor runs three loops at three speeds and they are not negotiable, because each one is fighting a different physical time constant. The rate loop runs at 1000 Hz because the airframe time constant is tens of milliseconds. The attitude loop runs at 250 Hz.

lessons.t: The Corner of the Angle Loop
lessons.g: Build the saturated angle loop and find the error above which it stops being proportional.
lessons.s: The angle loop is the simplest thing in the aircraft: an attitude error goes in, a body rate setpoint comes out, `min(MAX_RATE, max(-MAX_RATE, KP_ANGLE * error))`. There is no integrator and no derivative, because the loop below it already provides the damping and the aircraft has nothing pulling it off level.

lessons.t: A Tilt Limit Is a Braking Distance
lessons.g: Convert the tilt limit into a horizontal acceleration and into the distance the aircraft needs to stop.
lessons.s: Setting the maximum tilt to 35 degrees feels like a comfort setting. It is not. From dr0-5, the horizontal acceleration available is `G * math.tan(max_tilt)`, so 35 degrees is 6.87 m/s squared and that is the hardest the machine can push in any horizontal direction, forever, in both directions, including toward a ...

lessons.g: Build the outer chain and print the raw demand and the limited demand at every stage.
lessons.s: Above the attitude module of dr2-9 sit two more proportional stages. Position error becomes a velocity setpoint, `min(MAX_SPEED, max(-MAX_SPEED, KP_POS * error))`. Velocity error becomes an acceleration setpoint, `min(MAX_ACCEL, max(-MAX_ACCEL, KP_VEL * (v_sp - v)))`.

lessons.g: Fly a long dash and report how long each limiter was active and how much demand it removed.
lessons.s: This lesson exists because of a specific way of being wrong. A cascade prints its acceleration command during a hard manoeuvre and the number is 6.87. It prints the same number the next flight, and the next, in wind and in calm, at 40 m and at 4 m. The number is not measuring the aircraft.

lessons.t: The Height You Lose in a Bank
lessons.g: Compensate the collective for tilt and measure the altitude a bank costs when you do not.
lessons.s: When the aircraft leans, the thrust leans with it. The vertical component is what carries the weight, and it is the total times the cosine of the tilt, so a bank that is not paid for is a descent. The compensation is `MASS * (G + a_z) / math.cos(tilt)`, one cosine in a denominator.

lessons.t: The Setpoint That Is Already Old
lessons.g: Feed the rate loop from a slow attitude loop and measure the step it sees, with and without interpolation.
lessons.s: The attitude loop produces a new rate setpoint every 4 ms. The rate loop consumes one every 1 ms. Something has to happen on the three cycles in between, and the usual answer is nothing: the old value is held. That is a **zero order hold**, and it turns a smooth command into a staircase. The staircase is not free.

lessons.t: When the Loops Stop Being Separate
lessons.g: Run the position loop over a fast attitude loop and over a slow one, and measure the overshoot each produces.
lessons.s: The cascade works because the inner loop is finished before the outer loop looks again. Break that and the outer loop is no longer controlling a mass, it is controlling a mass behind a lag, and a proportional controller on a lagged plant rings.

lessons.g: Wire position, velocity, attitude, rate and mixer into one step function and fly it to a target.
lessons.s: Everything from dr0-1 to here is now one function. Position error goes in the top, four rotor thrusts come out the bottom, and each stage hands the next one a quantity the next one understands.

lessons.t: The Stick Is Not the Aircraft
lessons.g: Map a stick deflection to a body rate through an expo curve and measure the sensitivity it buys near centre.
lessons.s: In acro mode the stick commands a **rate**, not an attitude. Centre the stick and the aircraft holds whatever rate it has, which is zero, which is whatever attitude it happens to be in. Nothing levels it. That is the mode every racing pilot flies and the mode every autopilot uses underneath the others.

lessons.t: The Stick That Is Never Quite Centred
lessons.g: Add a rescaled deadband to the angle mode map and show what happens without the rescale.
lessons.s: Angle mode maps the stick to an attitude instead of a rate. Release the stick and the aircraft returns to level on its own, which is what makes it the mode a camera flies in and the mode a beginner survives. That creates a new problem.

lessons.t: The Throttle That Means Climb Rate
lessons.g: Turn the throttle stick into a climb rate command and measure what a mass error costs in each mode.
lessons.s: In manual throttle the stick is thrust. In altitude hold the stick is **climb rate**, `MAX_CLIMB * shape(stick)`, and centre means zero climb rather than a particular thrust.

lessons.g: Latch the position target when the stick returns to centre and show the flight the alternative produces.
lessons.s: Position hold maps the stick to a horizontal velocity, so a centred stick means stop and stay. The interesting question is where the target comes from, and it is the one that gets answered wrong. While the pilot is flying, `abs(stick) > STICK_EPS`, there is no target at all.

lessons.g: Seed a mode with the state the previous one was producing and measure the discontinuity you avoid.
lessons.s: Every mode switch is a handover, and the receiving controller starts from whatever its own state says. If that state is a fresh zero and the aircraft was in the middle of holding 16 N of thrust in a 25 degree bank, the first command out of the new mode is a step, and the aircraft moves before the loop catches up.

lessons.g: Write the arming gate as a named checklist and make it report which item refused.
lessons.s: Arming is the one moment where a robot is allowed to say no to its operator. Once the motors spin, a 9 inch carbon propeller at 5000 rpm is a hazard, and every check that is cheap to run before that moment is worth running.

lessons.g: Ramp the thrust into a takeoff, detect the liftoff from sustained vertical speed, and detect a takeoff that will not happen.
lessons.s: Takeoff is not a thrust setting, it is a search. The autopilot does not know the exact mass, the exact air density or how much the landing gear is stuck to wet grass, so it ramps the collective at a fixed rate and watches for the aircraft to answer. The answer is vertical speed.

lessons.t: Three Ways to Know You Have Landed
lessons.g: Build a landing detector on three simultaneous signals and show what each one alone gets wrong.
lessons.s: Landing detection decides when to cut the motors, and it is wrong in two directions. Declare a landing in the air and the aircraft falls. Fail to declare one on the ground and the machine sits there at hover thrust, tipping over on the first gust and cutting its propellers into the dirt. No single signal is enough.

lessons.g: Build the transition table with its per mode requirements and make every refusal come back with a reason.
lessons.s: The modes of this chapter are not a set, they are a graph. You cannot go from disarmed to position hold, you cannot go from land to takeoff, and you cannot enter return to home without a home point. Writing that as a table makes the aircraft's behaviour readable in one screen instead of scattered across nine handlers.

lessons.g: Learn the hover thrust in flight and remove the steady sink a mass error leaves behind.
lessons.s: The altitude loop of dr4-3 still sank 1.5 m under an unmodelled payload, because its feed forward was `MASS * G` and the mass in that expression came from a configuration file written before the flight.

lessons.g: Compute the vertical acceleration available in each direction and the descent rates the air will not allow.
lessons.s: A multirotor climbs and descends with entirely different physics, and treating the vertical axis as symmetric is how a machine ends up falling out of its own downwash. The first asymmetry is thrust.

lessons.g: Predict the steady position offset a proportional cascade leaves under a constant force, and confirm it in flight.
lessons.s: Put the aircraft of chapter 3 in a steady 3 N breeze and it will hold position badly, in a very specific and predictable way. It ends up sitting downwind of its target and staying there, perfectly stable, at a fixed distance. The distance follows from the loop having nothing but proportional terms.

lessons.g: Add the integral term, watch it converge on the disturbance, and read the wind out of it.
lessons.s: An integral term removes the offset of dr5-3, which is the usual reason to add one. On an aircraft it does something more useful: it **becomes a measurement**. Think about where it settles.

lessons.g: Model ground effect and show why an aircraft descending on a fixed thrust refuses to touch down.
lessons.s: Within about one rotor radius of the ground the downwash cannot get out of the way, and the rotor gets more thrust for the same power.

lessons.g: Measure hover quality as an RMS radius over a window and compare two gain settings against a spec.
lessons.s: Hover quality has to be a number or it is an opinion. The number is the root mean square radius over a window: `math.sqrt(sum(r * r for r in radii) / len(radii))`, taken over the last thirty seconds of a stationary hold.

lessons.g: Drop 300 g in mid flight and measure the height excursion and the time the learned hover thrust needs to recover.
lessons.s: A delivery drone releasing a package, a sprayer emptying a tank, a machine picking something up: the mass changes while the loop is closed, and the learned hover thrust of dr5-1 is suddenly wrong by exactly the weight that left. Release 300 g and the aircraft is instantly 2.94 N over thrusted.

lessons.g: Feed a noisy position estimate into two gains and measure the tilt activity each one produces.
lessons.s: Raising the position gain shrinks the wind offset of dr5-3 in exact proportion. It also multiplies whatever noise is on the position estimate by the same factor, and turns it into tilt commands, and tilt commands into motor current. The chain is short and mechanical.

lessons.g: Assemble learned hover thrust, the integral wind estimate and the quality metric into one holding controller.
lessons.s: The hover controller is now four pieces that have to run together: the learned hover thrust of dr5-1, the position latch of dr4-4, the integral term of dr5-4 with its freeze, and the quality metric of dr5-6 reporting on all of it. The order inside one cycle is fixed. Read the estimate.

lessons.g: Compute the drag force a steady wind applies and the lean the aircraft has to hold to stay put.
lessons.s: Wind does not push an aircraft sideways because it is windy. It pushes because the airframe is a bluff body moving through air at the wind speed, and the force is `DRAG_K * airspeed * airspeed`, with `DRAG_K` collecting half the air density, the drag coefficient and the frontal area.

lessons.g: Invert the tilt limit into a maximum holdable wind and set an operating margin under it.
lessons.s: There is a wind speed above which this aircraft cannot hold a position, and it is a property of the airframe, not of the tuning. At the tilt limit the horizontal force available is `MASS * G * math.tan(MAX_TILT)`, 9.27 N at 35 degrees.

lessons.t: Airspeed Is the Only Speed the Air Knows
lessons.g: Separate airspeed from ground speed and compute how fast the aircraft can still make progress upwind.
lessons.s: The autopilot works in ground coordinates. The air does not. Drag is produced by `airspeed = ground_speed + wind` when flying into the wind, and the two numbers are only equal on a still day, which is the day nobody has a problem. Hovering over a point in a 10 m/s wind, the ground speed is zero and the airspeed is 10.

lessons.t: The Gust That Arrives All At Once
lessons.g: Hit the position hold with a step change in wind and measure the excursion and the recovery.
lessons.s: A steady wind is a solved problem after dr5-4. A gust is a different question, because the integrator that solves the steady case is deliberately slow and a gust is not. Step the wind from nothing to 8 m/s in one sample and watch the sequence. The drag appears immediately, 3.9 N of it.

lessons.t: Reading the Wind Off the Controller
lessons.g: Turn the converged integral term into a wind speed and direction, and check it against the truth.
lessons.s: The aircraft has an anemometer and it did not cost anything. From dr5-4 the converged integrator holds the acceleration that cancels the disturbance, so `MASS * abs(integral)` is the force the air is applying, and dr6-1 inverts to a speed: `math.sqrt(force / DRAG_K)`. Three things make this estimate honest.

lessons.t: Out and Back Is Not Twice One Way
lessons.g: Compute the round trip time in wind and find the wind at which the outbound leg never finishes.
lessons.s: Intuition says a headwind out and a tailwind back cancel out. They do not, and the reason is that you spend a long time in the slow half and very little in the fast half. Fly 200 m out and back at an 8 m/s airspeed. In still air the trip takes `distance / ground` twice over, 50 s.

lessons.g: Drive the hold with correlated turbulence and compare it against a steady wind of the same average.
lessons.s: Real wind is a mean with a rough surface on it, and the roughness has memory: a gust lasts a second or two rather than one control cycle. White noise is the wrong model, because a controller filters it out for free and the simulation flatters itself.

lessons.g: Model the wind gradient with height and decide what a climb costs before a long leg.
lessons.s: The wind at 100 m is not the wind at the launch site, and the difference is large enough to change a decision. Friction with the ground slows the lowest layer of the atmosphere, and the standard engineering model is a power law: `reference * (height / REFERENCE_HEIGHT) ** alpha`, with an exponent near 0.14 over open ...

lessons.g: Turn the wind estimate into a latched advisory level that escalates and never quietly relaxes.
lessons.s: The estimate of dr6-5 is only worth having if something acts on it. That something is a monitor with four levels, `ORDER` from `ok` through `caution` and `return` to `land`, and two rules about how it moves between them. The first rule is escalation only: `ORDER.index(level) > ORDER.index(current)`.

lessons.g: Compute the induced velocity and the electrical power a hover consumes on this airframe.
lessons.s: A ground robot at rest costs nothing. An aerial one at rest costs everything it has, and the bill comes from momentum theory: to hold itself up the rotor has to throw air downward, and the power is the thrust times the speed it throws it at.

lessons.g: Convert the pack capacity into flight minutes and justify the fraction of it you are allowed to use.
lessons.s: The pack on this frame is a 4S 5.2 Ah lithium polymer, which at a 14.8 V nominal is 77 Wh of stored energy. At the 146 W of dr7-1 that would be 31 minutes of hovering, and anyone who plans a 31 minute flight will land by parachute. Two thirds of the missing time is chemistry.

lessons.t: The Voltage That Runs Away From You
lessons.g: Solve the loaded pack voltage against its own internal resistance and read the thrust it can still produce.
lessons.s: A battery quoted at 16.0 V is 16.0 V with nothing attached. Pull current through it and the internal resistance takes its cut, and the aircraft never sees the number on the label. The awkward part is that the sag depends on the current and the current depends on the voltage, so there is no closed form to copy.

lessons.g: Price a payload in power and in flight minutes, and show the exponent that makes it worse than linear.
lessons.s: Ask what a 300 g camera costs on a 1.35 kg aircraft and the intuitive answer is 22 percent, because that is how much heavier it is. The real answer is 35 percent of the power and a quarter of the flight time, and the gap between those numbers is the whole reason aerial engineering is conservative about mass.

lessons.g: Sweep the pack mass against endurance and find the point where more battery stops helping.
lessons.s: More battery is more energy and also more weight, and weight costs power at the 1.5 exponent of dr7-4. Somewhere those two curves cross, and past that point every extra cell you bolt on makes the aircraft fly for less time than it did before. Write it out.

lessons.g: Integrate the power actually drawn and compare the energy a flight cost against the energy it was planned to cost.
lessons.s: A percentage gauge derived from voltage is a guess, because voltage under load depends on current, temperature and how old the pack is. Integrating the power is not a guess. Every cycle, `used_wh += power * DT / 3600.0`, and what is left is `usable - used_wh`.

lessons.g: Price the return leg in watt hours against the wind and decide when the aircraft must turn around.
lessons.s: The decision to come back is not about how much battery is left. It is about how much is left compared to what the trip home costs from **here**, in **this** wind, and that second number moves during the flight. Build it from parts you already have.

lessons.t: The Margin That Drains With the Pack
lessons.g: Track the thrust to weight ratio down the discharge curve and find the voltage where a laden aircraft loses its authority.
lessons.s: Everything chapter 1 computed about mixer authority assumed a fixed maximum thrust. From dr7-3 that maximum falls with the pack, so the aircraft ends its flight with much less margin than it began with, and the machine that was easy to fly at takeoff is not the machine that is landing.

lessons.g: Combine the remaining energy, the return cost and the thrust margin into one latched advisory that can refuse to stay out.
lessons.s: Three separate measurements, one decision. The integrated energy of dr7-6 says what is left. The return cost of dr7-7 says what going home is worth right now. The margin of dr7-8 says whether the aircraft still has the authority to fly at all. The supervisor turns them into a level and the level never goes backwards.

lessons.t: The Point You Are Allowed to Call Home
lessons.g: Set the home point under explicit conditions and refuse every request that does not meet them.
lessons.s: Return to home is only as good as the home. Every serious incident report that begins with an aircraft flying confidently into a hedge ends with a home point that was recorded before the position estimate had settled. So home is not recorded when the operator presses a button.

lessons.g: Choose a return altitude from the obstacles below and check the wind that lives up there.
lessons.s: The default answer is to climb before returning, and it is right for the reason everyone gives: the aircraft does not know what is between it and home, so it goes over. The altitude is `max(obstacles) + CLEARANCE`, the tallest thing on the route plus a margin, 15 m here. It is not right for the reason nobody mentions.

lessons.t: The Distance You Cannot Come Back From
lessons.g: Compute the furthest the aircraft may be from home given what is left in the pack and the wind against it.
lessons.s: Range is usually quoted as how far a machine can fly. The number that matters is half that, and it moves with the weather: how far it can be and still get back. Build it from dr7-7.

lessons.g: Debounce the radio link so a dropped frame is not a failsafe and a real loss still is.
lessons.s: A 2.4 GHz radio link drops frames. It drops them when the aircraft turns and puts its own battery between the antennas, when a car goes past, and when the transmitter is held at the wrong angle.

lessons.g: Grow the position uncertainty after a navigation loss and decide how long the aircraft may keep going.
lessons.s: When the position estimate dies, the aircraft does not stop knowing where it is. It starts knowing worse, at a predictable rate, and the useful question is how many seconds of that it can afford before the answer is not worth flying on. Model it as a straight line: `accuracy0 + DRIFT_RATE * t`.

lessons.g: Work out what a quadrotor can still do with one motor dead and when that is not enough.
lessons.s: A quadrotor with a dead rotor cannot balance its torques with the remaining three. The standard survivable answer is to shut down the **opposite** rotor as well and fly on one diagonal: two rotors, both spinning the same way, so the aircraft yaws continuously and nobody can stop it.

lessons.t: The Fence That Has to Brake in Time
lessons.g: Limit the speed by the distance left to the fence and show what a tailwind does to the margin.
lessons.s: A geofence written as a test on position is a fence the aircraft crosses. By the time the position is outside, the machine is still doing 8 m/s and needs the 7.3 m of dr3-3 to stop, so the breach happens whatever the code does next. A fence that works limits the speed on the way in.

lessons.g: Build the staged descent profile, keep every stage out of the vortex ring band and time the whole descent.
lessons.s: Descending at one rate from cruise altitude to the ground is wrong at both ends. Fast is right at 50 m, where there is time to recover from anything, and completely wrong at 2 m, where the aircraft has to arrive gently and the ground effect of dr5-5 is already lifting it.

lessons.g: Map every failure to an action, take the worst of the ones that are active, and never allow the result to relax.
lessons.s: Failures arrive together. A pack that has been pushed hard is a pack that sags, and a sagging pack browns out a receiver, so low battery and link loss show up in the same second and both want to be handled. The arbiter is the thing that decides what actually happens. Two pieces.

lessons.g: Write the plant: rotor thrusts and attitude in, new position, velocity and attitude out, with the wind.
lessons.s: The final chapter builds one aircraft out of the nine before it, and the first piece is the part that does not obey anybody: the airframe. Everything else in this chapter is a controller, and a controller is only as honest as the plant it is graded against. Four lines of physics.

lessons.g: Assemble position, velocity, attitude, rate and mixer into one controller call that returns rotor thrusts and a saturation flag.
lessons.s: The controller of this chapter is chapters 3, 5 and 1 stacked in a single function, and its interface is the thing to get right: state in, four rotor thrusts out, plus every flag the layers above will need. The order is the one dr3-9 established. Position error to a velocity setpoint.

lessons.g: Build the wind field: a mean that grows with height and a seeded gust process on top of it.
lessons.s: The aircraft is finished and the room it flies in is not. A mission run against a constant wind proves very little, because the two things that actually decide the flight are the gradient with altitude from dr6-8 and the roughness from dr6-7. Two lines, both already written earlier in the course.

lessons.g: Charge the battery for the thrust the aircraft actually delivered and price the trip home from wherever it is.
lessons.s: The energy module has one input and it is the delivered thrust of dr9-2, not the commanded one. Every cycle, `used_wh + hover_power(total) * DT / 3600.0`, using the momentum theory power of dr7-1 on whatever the rotors really produced.

lessons.t: The Supervisor That Knows It Is Losing
lessons.g: Combine the gated wind estimate, the losing ground detector and the energy reserve into one latched level.
lessons.s: This is the piece the whole course has been building toward, and the reason it is not simply a threshold on wind speed is worth spelling out. The wind estimate of dr6-5 is only valid when the loop has converged, so it is gated: read it only when `abs(v) < 0.5 and abs(error) < 2.0`.

lessons.g: Drive the phases from takeoff to landing and let the supervisor preempt any of them.
lessons.s: The last module is the smallest and it is the one that decides what the aircraft is trying to do. Four phases: `outbound` to the waypoint, `hold` there for a while, `return` to the home point, and `landed`.

lessons.g: Fly the whole mission at four wind speeds and one overload, and print the four acceptance checks of the flight.
lessons.s: Final mission. Wire the plant of dr9-1, the controller of dr9-2, the energy meter of dr9-4, the supervisor of dr9-5 and the sequencer of dr9-6 into one loop and fly it: out 250 m downwind, hold 40 s, return upwind, land at home. What you check at the end is not that it ran.

lessons.g: Write a step function that takes a state and a timestep and returns the next state.
lessons.s: A simulator is two things and nothing else: a **state** and a **step** function. The state is every number you need to continue from here. The step function takes that state, takes a timestep `dt`, and returns the state one `dt` later.

lessons.g: Turn a duration and a timestep into a step count and drive the state that many times.
lessons.s: A step function alone does not simulate anything. Something has to call it, and that something owns time. The rule is `steps = duration / dt`, rounded to an integer because you cannot take two thirds of a step.

lessons.g: Compare the simulated height against the closed form solution and print the error.
lessons.s: Free fall has an exact answer written down two centuries before anyone had a computer. The height after `t` seconds is the initial height plus the initial velocity times `t` plus half of gravity times `t` squared. That exact answer is worth more to you than any plot.

lessons.g: Store several bodies in a list and advance all of them inside one step of the world.
lessons.s: Two loose variables were fine for one body. For three they are a mess, and for three hundred they are impossible. The state of a world is a **list of bodies**, and each body is a small mutable record. Here each body is a list of two numbers, `[height, velocity]`.

lessons.t: The Same Second, Three Step Sizes
lessons.g: Measure how the simulated result changes when only the timestep changes.
lessons.s: Here is the fact that makes a simulator different from a calculation: **the answer depends on the timestep**. The same physics, the same half second, the same starting state, and three different numbers come out.

lessons.g: Implement explicit Euler on a mass spring and measure the energy it invents.
lessons.s: Free fall was forgiving because the acceleration never changed. A spring is not: the force depends on where the mass is, so the acceleration changes inside every step, and the integrator has to guess. **Explicit Euler**, also called forward Euler, guesses with the values from the **start** of the step.

lessons.g: Implement semi implicit Euler and show its energy stays bounded where explicit Euler grows.
lessons.s: One line moved and the problem disappears. **Semi implicit Euler**, also called symplectic Euler, updates the velocity first and then moves the position with the velocity it just computed. That is the entire change.

lessons.t: Halving the Step Halves the Error
lessons.g: Measure the order of accuracy of explicit Euler by comparing errors at three step sizes.
lessons.s: An integrator has an **order**. It is the exponent in the relation between the timestep and the error left after a fixed amount of simulated time: halve `dt` on a first order method and the error halves, on a second order method it drops by four, on a fourth order method by sixteen.

lessons.g: Implement the midpoint method and measure that its error falls by four when the step halves.
lessons.s: Explicit Euler uses the slope at the start of the step for the whole step. That is why it is only first order: it is a straight line approximating a curve, anchored at the wrong end. The **midpoint method**, the classic second order Runge-Kutta, buys a big improvement with one extra evaluation.

lessons.t: Four Slopes and a Weighted Average
lessons.g: Implement classical fourth order Runge-Kutta and measure the sixteenfold error drop.
lessons.s: Classical **RK4** samples the derivative four times per step: once at the start, twice at the midpoint using each previous sample as the trial, and once at the end using the third sample.

lessons.g: Compare integrators at equal derivative evaluation cost instead of equal timestep.
lessons.s: Comparing methods at the same `dt` is comparing a bicycle to a lorry by the size of the wheels. RK4 at `dt` of 0.02 is not four times better than Euler at `dt` of 0.02, it is four times more **expensive**, because every step costs four calls to `deriv`. In a real simulator `deriv` is the expensive part.

lessons.g: Reproduce the instability of explicit Euler on a stiff decay and find where it starts.
lessons.s: Accuracy is one failure mode. **Instability** is the other, and it is louder: instead of a slightly wrong answer you get a number that doubles every step until it becomes infinity. A **stiff** system is one with a rate much faster than the interval you care about.

lessons.g: Find the stability limit of explicit Euler by scanning and check it against 2 over lambda.
lessons.s: The boundary you just crossed has a formula. Explicit Euler on `dx/dt = -LAMBDA * x` is stable when the magnitude of `1 - LAMBDA * dt` is at most one, which happens exactly when `dt` is at most `2 / LAMBDA`. That is the number every stiff simulator lives under.

lessons.g: Implement implicit Euler for the stiff decay and show it stays bounded at any timestep.
lessons.s: **Implicit Euler**, or backward Euler, evaluates the derivative at the **end** of the step instead of the start. That gives `x_next = x - LAMBDA * x_next * dt`, an equation with the unknown on both sides. For this decay you can solve it by hand: `x_next = x / (1 + LAMBDA * dt)`.

lessons.g: Show that feeding the simulator the real frame time makes the same run give a different answer.
lessons.s: The obvious way to drive a simulator from a program is to measure how long the last frame took and pass that as `dt`. Every tutorial does it. It is wrong, and this lesson measures how wrong. Chapter one established that the answer depends on `dt`.

lessons.g: Decouple the physics timestep from the frame time with a leftover time accumulator.
lessons.s: The fix is to stop letting the frame decide the timestep. The physics runs at a **fixed** `FIXED_DT` forever. The frame only delivers a quantity of time into an `accumulator`, and the loop spends that time in whole fixed steps, keeping the remainder for the next frame.

lessons.g: Interpolate between the last two physics states and measure the frame to frame jitter it removes.
lessons.s: The accumulator leaves the display in an awkward place. When a frame ends there is leftover time that has not been simulated, and how much leftover there is changes every frame. Draw the newest state as it stands and the amount of staleness jumps around, which on screen is judder even at a perfectly steady frame rate.

lessons.g: Reproduce the runaway accumulator and stop it with a maximum frame clamp.
lessons.s: The accumulator has a failure mode that only appears when the machine is too slow. If one physics step costs more real time than it simulates, then every frame hands the loop more work than the work it just finished, the accumulator grows, the next frame is longer, and the loop never catches up.

lessons.g: Split one frame into substeps and show it stabilises a contact stiff enough to blow up.
lessons.s: Sometimes the physics needs a smaller step than the frame rate can afford to call.
