lessons.s: An **IMU** (inertial measurement unit) is a small chip that senses how the robot moves. It usually holds two sensors and sends their readings as digital messages: - An **accelerometer** measures acceleration along three directions.

lessons.g: Pick a DC motor, a servo or a stepper motor for a job.
lessons.s: Three kinds of motor do most of the work in small robots. A **DC motor** spins quickly and keeps spinning as long as it has power. Swap its two wires and it spins the other way, and PWM changes its speed. It has no idea where it is pointing, so add an encoder if you need to know.

lessons.g: Work out a motor's stall current and see why a motor cannot run from a microcontroller pin.
lessons.s: Never connect a DC motor straight to a microcontroller pin. A pin can give about **20 mA** safely, and a motor needs far more. A motor is a coil of wire with some resistance, called the **winding resistance**. When the motor stands still, only that resistance limits the current.

lessons.g: Choose the right sensor for a robot task by asking what it must detect, and where.
lessons.s: Picking a sensor is easier if you ask four questions. - **What must the robot know?** A distance, a brightness, a tilt, how far the wheels turned, or whether it touched something? - **Where is the thing you want to detect?** A sensor only notices what it is pointed at.

lessons.g: Know which holes on a breadboard are connected, and avoid the classic mistakes.
lessons.s: A **breadboard** lets you build circuits without soldering. Under the holes, metal spring clips grip the legs of your parts and connect them. The holes are connected in groups: - In the middle, each **row** of 5 holes is one connected strip.

lessons.g: Measure voltage, current and resistance with a multimeter the right way.
lessons.s: A **multimeter** measures voltage, current and resistance. It has a dial, two probes (black and red) and a few sockets. - **Black probe:** always in the socket marked **COM**.

lessons.g: Recognise the basic schematic symbols, and read which way an LED points.
lessons.s: A **schematic** is a map of a circuit. It shows what is connected to what, not where the parts sit on the board. Lines are wires. The symbols you will meet most: - **Battery:** a long line and a short line side by side. The long line is **+**, the short line is **−**. Several pairs mean several cells.

lessons.g: See why a short circuit is dangerous, and handle batteries safely.
lessons.s: Batteries store a lot of energy and can release it fast. Common types: - **Alkaline** cells, such as the AA (1.5 V) and the 9 V block. - **Lithium** cells, lithium-ion and LiPo: about **3.7 V** each, and 4.2 V when full. They store a lot of energy for their weight.

lessons.g: Learn the safety rules for soldering and for working at the bench.
lessons.s: **Soldering** joins parts for good with melted metal called solder. The tip of a soldering iron runs at about **350 °C**, hot enough to burn skin instantly and to melt plastic. The iron: - Always put it back in its **stand**, even for a few seconds. Never lay it on the bench. - Hold it by the grip, like a pen.

lessons.t: Challenge: The LED That Won't Light
lessons.g: Use your multimeter and a clear method to find out why an LED circuit does not work.
lessons.s: When a circuit does not work, do not pull it apart. Measure it. A useful fact: in a series loop, **if no current flows, a resistor has 0 V across it**, because V = I × R and I is 0. The whole supply voltage then appears across the **gap**: the one place that blocks the current.

lessons.g: Name the three jobs every robot does, over and over.
lessons.s: A robot is a machine that does three jobs, again and again, many times every second. - **Sense**: it measures the world with sensors. A camera sees, a bumper feels a wall, a counter on each wheel measures how far it turned. - **Think**: a small computer reads those measurements and decides what to do next.

lessons.g: Use the sense, think, act test to tell a robot from a machine that only moves.
lessons.s: Lots of machines move, but not every machine is a robot. Engineers argue about the exact line, so in this course we use a simple test built on the loop from the last mission: a robot **senses** its surroundings, **decides** something by itself, and **acts** on the physical world. Try the test on a few machines.

lessons.g: Recognise the main families of robots and match one to a job.
lessons.s: Robots come in many shapes, and the shape follows the job. Here are the main families you will meet. - **Robot arms** (also called manipulators) are bolted to one spot and move a tool through space. Factories use them to weld car bodies, paint and pack boxes.

lessons.t: From Remote Control to Fully Autonomous
lessons.g: Place a robot on the scale of autonomy, from remote control to full autonomy.
lessons.s: **Autonomy** means how much a robot decides by itself. It is not a yes or no question. It is a scale, and most real robots sit somewhere in the middle. - **Remote control** (also called teleoperation): a person makes every decision through a controller or a screen.

lessons.g: Recognise the jobs robots do well today, and the ones they still find hard.
lessons.s: Robots do best at jobs people describe with three words: **dull, dirty and dangerous**. - **Dull**: the same motion thousands of times a day, such as welding car bodies or packing boxes. A robot does not get bored or tired, and it repeats a motion very precisely.

lessons.g: Learn the safety rules around robots and work out how far a robot moves before it can react.
lessons.s: Robots are strong and fast, and they do not know you are there unless a sensor tells them. So safety comes first, every time. Rules people follow around robots: - Big **factory arms** work inside fences or behind light curtains, beams of light that stop the robot if someone walks through.

lessons.g: Know what a chassis does and how to keep a robot from tipping over.
lessons.s: The **chassis** is the robot's skeleton: the frame that everything else attaches to. Motors, wheels, battery, sensors and the computer all bolt onto it. A good chassis does three jobs. - It is **stiff**. If the frame bends, the wheels point in slightly different directions, sensors shift and measurements go wrong.

lessons.g: Choose between wheels, tracks and legs for the ground a robot must cross.
lessons.s: How a robot moves across the ground is called **locomotion**. There are three main choices, and each fits different ground. - **Wheels** are simple, cheap and efficient. On smooth floors and roads they use the least energy and are easy to control. They struggle with steps, deep mud, sand and big rocks.

lessons.g: See how a two-wheeled robot steers, and work out how far its wheels roll when it spins in place.
lessons.s: The most common way to build a small wheeled robot is **differential drive**. It has two driven wheels, one on each side, each with its own motor. A free-rolling **caster** wheel or ball at the front or back stops it from tipping. There is no steering wheel. The robot steers by giving its two wheels different speeds.

lessons.g: Tell a revolute joint from a prismatic joint.
lessons.s: A robot arm is a chain of stiff pieces called **links**, connected by **joints**. Each joint lets two links move against each other in one way. Two joint types cover almost every robot you will meet. - A **revolute joint** rotates, like a hinge or your elbow. Its position is an angle, in degrees.

lessons.g: Count the degrees of freedom of a robot arm.
lessons.s: **Degrees of freedom** (DOF) count the independent ways something can move. Each one is a number you would need to say exactly where it is. A box lying on a flat floor has **3 DOF**: it can slide forward and back, slide left and right, and turn to face a new direction.

lessons.g: Pick the right gripper or tool for an object and a job.
lessons.s: The part at the end of a robot arm that touches the world is the **end effector**. The arm brings it to the right place; the end effector does the actual job. Choosing it well matters as much as choosing the arm. - **Two-finger grippers** close on an object from both sides, like a pair of pliers.

lessons.g: Know why robots need sensors, and tell internal sensors from external ones.
lessons.s: Without sensors a robot is blind. It can only follow a fixed plan, like the toaster in chapter 0, and it has no idea whether the plan is working. Sensors give the think step something to work with. Robot sensors fall into two groups.

lessons.g: Compare ultrasonic, infrared and lidar sensors, and turn an echo time into a distance.
lessons.s: Knowing how far away things are is one of the first things a robot needs. Three sensors do this job, and each has trade-offs. - **Ultrasonic** sensors send a short click of sound, too high for you to hear, and time how long the echo takes to come back. They are cheap and do not care about light or colour.

lessons.g: Know what a camera tells a robot, and what it cannot tell on its own.
lessons.s: A **camera** gives a robot more information than any other sensor. One picture shows colours, shapes, text, faces, lines on the floor and signs on the wall.

lessons.g: Know what an accelerometer and a gyroscope measure, and turn a gyro reading into an angle.
lessons.s: An **IMU** (inertial measurement unit) is a small chip that feels how the robot moves, without looking at anything outside. Phones, drones, game controllers and balancing robots all have one. It combines two sensors. - An **accelerometer** measures acceleration: speeding up, slowing down and the pull of gravity.

lessons.g: Turn encoder ticks into wheel turns, and wheel turns into distance.
lessons.s: A **wheel encoder** is a sensor on a wheel or motor shaft that counts how far it turns. Inside, a disc with slots or magnets passes a detector, and every slot or magnet gives a small pulse called a **tick**. The encoder has a fixed number of ticks per turn, for example 500.

lessons.g: Tell a touch switch from a force sensor, and know when a robot needs each.
lessons.s: Sometimes the simplest way to know you have hit something is to feel it. Robots use two kinds of touch sensing. - A **bumper switch** or **limit switch** is either on or off. When something presses it, a contact closes and the computer sees a click. Robot vacuums have a bumper all around the front.

lessons.t: GPS and Choosing the Right Sensor
lessons.g: Know where GPS works and where it fails, and choose a set of sensors for a real job.
lessons.s: **GPS** works by receiving radio signals from satellites high above Earth. From the timing of several signals, a receiver works out where it is. Outdoors under open sky, an ordinary receiver like the one in a phone is usually accurate to a few metres.

lessons.g: Know what an actuator is and the main kinds robots use.
lessons.s: If sensors are a robot's senses, **actuators** are its muscles. An actuator turns energy into motion. It is the part of the robot that does the **act** step of the loop. - **Electric motors** turn electrical energy from a battery into rotation.

lessons.g: Know what DC motors, servos and stepper motors are each best at.
lessons.s: Three kinds of electric motor do most of the work in small robots. - A **DC motor** spins continuously when you connect it to power. More voltage gives more speed, and swapping the two wires makes it spin the other way.

lessons.g: Use a gear ratio to work out the speed and torque at the output of a gear pair.
lessons.s: A small DC motor spins fast but weakly. A robot wheel or arm joint usually needs the opposite: slow and strong. **Gears** make that trade. The strength of a turning motion is called **torque**, a turning force. It is measured in **newton-metres** (N·m). Opening a tight jar lid takes torque.

lessons.t: From Motor RPM to Robot Speed
lessons.g: Turn a motor speed in RPM into a driving speed in metres per second.
lessons.s: Motors are rated in **RPM**, revolutions per minute. Your robot's speed is in metres per second. Here is how to get from one to the other. Every time a wheel turns once, the robot rolls forward by one circumference, π × diameter, just as in odometry in chapter 2.

lessons.g: Know why a motor needs a motor driver between it and the microcontroller.
lessons.s: A robot's brain is often a **microcontroller**, a tiny computer on a single chip, like the one on an Arduino board. It controls things through its **pins**, which it can switch on and off. So why not wire a motor straight to a pin? Because the pin is far too weak.

lessons.t: Air and Oil: Pneumatics and Hydraulics
lessons.g: Know when a robot uses compressed air or oil instead of an electric motor.
lessons.s: Electric motors are not the only muscles. Two others push with fluids. **Pneumatics** use compressed air. A compressor squeezes air into a tank, and valves let it into a **cylinder**, where it pushes a piston out fast.

lessons.g: Tell a microcontroller from a single-board computer and pick the right one for a job.
lessons.s: Every robot needs a brain: a small computer that reads the sensors and tells the motors what to do. Hobby robots use two kinds. A **microcontroller** is a whole tiny computer on one chip. The Arduino Uno is the classic example.

lessons.g: Describe the sense, think, act cycle and spot what breaks it.
lessons.s: Every robot brain, big or small, runs the same cycle again and again, as long as the robot is switched on: - **Sense:** read the sensors. - **Think:** decide what to do with those readings. - **Act:** send commands to the motors. - **Repeat:** go back to the start. This cycle is called the **control loop**.

lessons.g: Calculate a loop rate in hertz from the time one pass takes.
lessons.s: How often your control loop runs is called its **loop rate**. It is measured in **hertz (Hz)**, which means "times per second". A loop rate of 50 Hz means the robot senses, thinks and acts 50 times every second. The time one pass takes is called the **period**.

lessons.g: Explain why feedback matters, and measure what happens without it.
lessons.s: There are two ways to give a robot a job. **Open loop** means the robot follows a command without checking the result. "Run both motors at 50% power for 4 seconds" is open loop. A toaster is open loop too: it heats for a set time, whether the bread is pale or burnt.

lessons.g: Say what each of the three parts of PID reacts to, and which one fixes an error that will not go away.
lessons.s: A closed loop needs a rule that says how hard to correct. The most popular rule in robotics is called **PID**. It has three parts, and each one looks at the error in a different way: - **P, proportional:** reacts to the error **now**. A big error gives a big push; a small error gives a small push.

lessons.g: Follow a state machine through a series of events.
lessons.s: A robot does different things at different times: waiting, searching, working, stopping. A **state machine** is a tidy way to organise that. - The robot is always in exactly one **state**, and each state has its own simple behaviour. - **Events** are things the robot notices, like a button press or a sensor reading.

lessons.g: Explain what a good emergency stop does and why it must not depend on the program.
lessons.s: Robots are strong, fast and sometimes wrong. A bug, a frozen program, a loose wire or a sensor fooled by sunlight can all send a robot where it should not go. That is why real robots have an **emergency stop**, or **e-stop**: a big red button that anyone nearby can hit to stop the robot at once.

lessons.g: Read a battery's voltage and capacity, and work out the voltage of cells in series.
lessons.s: Every battery label has two important numbers. **Voltage**, in volts (V), is how hard the battery pushes current through a circuit. Motors and electronics are designed for a certain voltage, so it must match. **Capacity**, in milliamp-hours (mAh), is how much charge the battery stores.

lessons.g: Estimate a robot's runtime from battery capacity and current draw, with a safety margin.
lessons.s: Once you know the capacity of the battery and how much current the robot draws, you can estimate how long it will run: - runtime in hours = capacity in mAh ÷ current draw in mA Example: a 2000 mAh battery powering a robot that draws 500 mA lasts 2000 ÷ 500 = 4 hours. Watch the units. Both numbers must be in milliamps.

lessons.g: Explain why a robot needs voltage regulators and how much heat a linear regulator wastes.
lessons.s: The parts of a robot rarely want the same voltage. Small DC gear motors often run on 6 to 12 V, because more voltage gives them more speed. A microcontroller or sensor wants a steady 5 V or 3.3 V, and a Raspberry Pi needs 5 V. Feed 7.4 V straight into a 5 V pin and you can destroy the board.

lessons.g: Wire a robot neatly and choose and place a fuse correctly.
lessons.s: Most robot faults are wiring faults: a wire pulled loose by a wheel, or a **short circuit**, where bare metal on the positive side touches the negative side. A short on a lithium battery can push tens of amps or more through a wire, make it glow hot, and start a fire.

lessons.g: Explain why parts that share signals must share a ground.
lessons.s: Voltage is always measured **between two points**, a bit like height is measured from the floor. In a circuit, that floor is called **ground**: GND on the pin labels, 0 V, the negative side of the battery.

lessons.g: Charge, store and handle lithium batteries safely.
lessons.s: Lithium batteries (LiPo and Li-ion) pack a lot of energy into very little weight. That is why robots and drones use them, and it is also why they must be treated with respect. A damaged or misused lithium battery can swell, get very hot and catch fire.

lessons.g: Compare the two classic first robots and match each to its sensors.
lessons.s: Two projects are the classic first robots, and both are great. A **line follower** drives along a dark line on a light floor. Two or more **IR reflectance sensors** sit under the front, pointing down.

lessons.g: Check a parts list against the job, part by part.
lessons.s: A parts list is where many first robots go wrong, before a single wire is connected. Go through it part by part and ask two questions: what does this part do, and do its numbers match the rest of the robot?

lessons.g: Put the steps of a robot build in an order where each step can be checked before the next.
lessons.s: Build your robot in an order where every step can be checked before the next one hides it. Then, when something fails, only the newest step can be to blame. A good order: - **Plan:** sketch the robot, draw a wiring diagram and write the parts list. - **Chassis:** mount the motors, wheels and caster.

lessons.t: Test One Part at a Time
lessons.g: Test parts separately and use your measurements to predict runtime.
lessons.s: Before you run the whole robot, give every part its own small test. - **Motors:** does each wheel turn the right way, at slow and fast speeds? - **Sensors:** show the readings while you move your hand or the line under the sensor.

lessons.g: Find the most likely cause of a robot fault from what you observe.
lessons.s: Every builder's first robot misbehaves. Debugging is detective work: - Describe exactly what you see, not what you think is wrong. - List the likely causes, and check the easiest and most likely one first. - Change **one** thing at a time, then test again.

lessons.g: Combine ideas from the whole course to judge a complete robot design, and see where to go next.
lessons.s: You now know what a robot is made of: body, senses, muscles, brain, power and wiring. Here is where the academy's Python courses take each idea further: - **Python for Robotics:** write real control loops, read sensors and build a robot simulator. - **Control Theory and PID:** build and tune your own PID controller.
